19742-the-heather-moon:
The Heather Moon, dated 1912, is a novel of Scotland in the C. N. and A. M. Williamson manner. Its early mystery is a garret that only Mrs. Muir ever enters. She locks the stairway door behind herself every time. She performs the same ceremony on letting herself out. To young Barrie, watching, this seems thrillingly strange. A locked garret in a novel always hides something.

Scottish settings gave romance writers mist, heather, and old houses. Secrets kept upstairs drive such plots toward discovery. The child's-eye view sharpens the puzzle here. Barrie notices what adults pretend is normal. That gap between seeing and knowing pulls readers on. The novel is period romance built on a household secret.
19922-the-scientific-evidences-of-organi:
George J. Romanes wrote The Scientific Evidences of Organic Evolution as a popular defense of Darwin. He marvels at the ignorance of Darwin's work among educated people. The Origin of Species had an effect without parallel, he says. That effect touched both science and philosophy of the age. Yet many who could not be called uncultured misstate it daily. Romanes, Darwin's younger friend, sets out the evidence plainly.

Romanes was a working biologist, not only a popularizer. His lectures compress anatomy, fossils, and breeding into one case. The book belongs to evolution's first great wave of advocacy. It shows how Darwin's circle argued in public. Clear and combative, it still reads well. Science historians use it to trace Darwinism's spread.
19935-critical-miscellanies-vol-1-essay-:
John Morley's Critical Miscellanies gather his essays on great writers. Volume one's fifth essay treats Ralph Waldo Emerson. Morley opens with a puzzle about interpreters of life. A great interpreter ought not himself to need interpretation, he says. Contemporaries, least of all, should need him explained. Yet Emerson plainly did need explaining to England. Morley's essay supplies that explanation with care.

Morley was Victorian England's leading man of letters and editor. His Emerson essay introduced American transcendentalism to British readers. He weighs Emerson's style, optimism, and spiritual radicalism evenly. The Miscellanies set the tone of serious literary journalism. This essay remains a landmark in Emerson's English reception. It shows two cultures translating each other.
19964-regeneration:
Charles Dye wrote Regeneration, a science fiction tale of a far-future tribe. Morge, an old man of the tribe, fears the death-things around him. His ancestors left those things lying about before they vanished. Builder, wisest of the tribe, teaches what the ancestors were. The tribe both hates and fears that inheritance. Dye sets civilization's ruins under primitive eyes. The death-things are old machines and weapons, plainly.

Post-collapse stories ask what knowledge survives its makers. Dye's tribesmen read our world as magic and menace. The title promises some form of rebirth for humankind. Pulp magazines loved the ancient-astronaut angle in reverse. This tale shows the theme in early, earnest form. It is a fable about technology outliving understanding.
20016-home-rule-second-edition:
Home Rule, in its second edition, argues Ireland's case for its own parliament. Nearly a generation had passed since Gladstone's first Home Rule bill. He expounded it in the House of Commons in 1886. Nearly twenty years had passed when this edition appeared. The preface measures that long defeat and persistence. Irish self-government remained the era's unresolved question. The book collects the argument in one place.

Home Rule dominated British politics from 1886 to 1914. Gladstone's two failed bills split his party permanently. Advocates restated the case for each new Parliament. This second edition updates the brief for another round. It preserves the movement's official reasoning and tone. Readers meet the question that would end in 1921's settlement.
20063-theodoric-the-goth-barbarian-champ:
Theodoric the Goth ruled Italy after Rome's western empire fell, and his life fills this biography. The subtitle calls him a barbarian champion of civilisation. He was born as that empire staggered toward ruin in the West. Barbarian attacks over two generations had worn it down, the book says.

For six centuries Rome had been the strongest power in Europe. Theodoric tried to keep its laws, cities, and learning alive under Gothic rule. That clash of old Rome and new kings drives the story. Readers get a clear case of how one ruler can both end and save an age.
20202-walnut-growing-in-oregon:
Walnut Growing in Oregon is a farm guide on a growing American nut trade. Imports of English walnuts rose fast in the early 1900s, it reports. In 1906, imports reached near twenty-five million pounds of walnuts. By 1907, the United States grew twelve million pounds of its own.

Oregon alone ate some four hundred thousand dollars' worth each year. That demand made local orchards a clear chance for Oregon farmers. The guide covers soils, planting, care, and the profits in view. Readers get a crisp record of how the Pacific walnut trade began.
20220-the-mind-and-its-education:
George Herbert Betts published The Mind and Its Education in 1906, a study of how minds learn. Betts asks how we can study a thing we cannot touch. The material world can be seen, weighed, and measured with ease. The mind, by contrast, is intangible to every sense we have.

Yet teachers must know how consciousness works to teach it well. Betts turns psychology into plain guidance for schools and homes. His book links brain, habit, interest, and will to daily lessons. Readers get an early, clear text of educational psychology for teachers.
20230-jane-journeys-on:
Jane Journeys On, from 1918, follows a young woman's path through work and love. One young man in her world is marked for swift promotion. He will be assistant cashier at the first chance, all agree. His habits are exemplary, and he dresses with the greatest care.

His mother boasts at the Ladies' Aid and the Tuesday Club freely. He is as perfect a son as any woman ever had, she says. He will make some girl a perfect husband one day, she adds. Readers get a period tale where pride and praise may hide flaws.
20236-fair-to-look-upon:
Mary Belle Freeley wrote Fair to Look Upon, a novel of society and desire. A woman sits on a luxurious divan with a man beside her. He holds her milk-white hand in his as they talk. She states that fact plainly, as no startling news at all.

That calm opening hints at a world of practiced charm and flirtation. Fair looks open doors, yet they can mask sharp aims beneath. Novels of this kind probe beauty, money, and the marriage market. Readers get a period romance told in a smooth, knowing voice.
20332-tabitha-s-vacation:
Ruth Alberta Brown wrote Tabitha's Vacation, volume three in the Ivy Hall Series. Tabitha Catt stands on the doorstep of her little desert home. She shakes a dingy dusting cloth and sniffs the sweet morning air. Silver Bow nestles in a cup-like hollow among Nevada mountains.

The first week of June has gone, yet summer heat has not yet fallen. A vacation for a desert schoolgirl promises travel, friends, and change. Brown's series follows Tabitha through school terms and holidays alike. Readers get a bright western girls' tale with a lively, singing heroine.
20343-the-spinners-book-of-fiction:
The Spinners' Book of Fiction gathers tales from a famed San Francisco literary circle. Verse in the book sings of halls girdled round by summer gardens. A nightingale's song rings beyond the eastern walls at dusk. Sweeter than love's first hearing, that song draws replies from hidden dells.

Faint faery bells seem to wake in answer across the garden. The Spinners were writers who met to share and judge new work. Their book collects fiction and verse from that bright company. Readers get West Coast letters at a lively, hopeful moment in its growth.
20402-beside-the-still-waters-a-sermon:
Preached on Sunday, February 19, 1871, Beside the Still Waters takes its title from the twenty-third Psalm. The preacher turns the psalm's quiet water into a long look at how streams work through the world. It is a single sermon, printed for readers to study at home.

The sermon follows every running stream, from the tiniest mountain rill to the muddy Po and the Nile that feeds Egypt's fields. Water, it argues, works without pause, while men miss how much of what they love is being carried away. The piece blends natural observation with a call to notice God's steady hand.
20429-the-seventh-noon: The Seventh Noon is a novel that opens in a laboratory. A young man sprawls on a lean sofa in one corner, his long legs stretched over its end. He holds a test tube up to the light, studying it idly while work waits around him. From that room the story sets its scheme in motion.
20478-strong-souls-a-sermon:
Strong Souls is a sermon preached on Sunday, October 29, 1882. The preacher asks what makes one life stronger than another. His measure is not wealth or fame but reach: how widely a soul touches the lives around it.

A strong soul, he says, is known by the width of its sympathies and the largeness of its hopes. There is also a quality of intensity in which lives differ. Some people live more in a week than others live in a year. The sermon urges hearers to widen their sympathies and deepen their days, rather than merely lengthen them.
20506-the-laws-of-euchre-as-adopted-by-t:
The Laws of Euchre, adopted by the Somerset Club of Boston in 1888, sets down the official rules of the card game. H. C. Leeds and James Dwight prepared the code. Club rules mattered because euchre was then America's favorite card game, and disputes needed settling.

The rubber, the book states, is the best of three games. If the first two games go to the same players, the third is still played. Should the score of the third game lap, a fourth game follows. Around such points the little book builds a full code for dealing, trump, and scoring.
20638-from-plotzk-to-boston:
Mary Antin's From Plotzk to Boston tells how a Jewish family left the Russian town of Plotzk for America. Antin wrote it as a young immigrant, in letters full of wonder. She later expanded the story into her famous book The Promised Land.

In Plotzk, the elders shake their sage heads over the evening fire. They prophesy no good for those who brave the terrors of the sea and the foreign goal beyond it. All talked of America, but scarcely anybody knew one true fact about this magic land. Antin's crossing turns rumor into experience, storm by storm.
20653-checking-the-waste-a-study-in-cons:
Checking the Waste: A Study in Conservation surveys America's squandered natural wealth and how to stop the loss. Forests, soils, waters, and minerals all come under its eye. The book belongs to the conservation movement that rose under Theodore Roosevelt.

Our inventions and discoveries, it grants, have developed a great nation at home. They have done much to better the condition of the world. But the very size of our natural wealth has made us careless of it. The study counts the waste resource by resource, and argues that thrift with nature is a public duty.
20666-the-debs-decision:
The Debs Decision examines the Supreme Court case that sent labor leader Eugene V. Debs to prison. Debs had been convicted under the Espionage Act for a speech against the draft. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes read the Court's decision upholding the verdict.

The book introduces Holmes with care. He has been a member of the Supreme Court for twenty-two years, it notes, and was born in Boston in 1841. He is seventy-seven years old, was admitted to the bar in 1866, and served in the Civil War. The study then weighs the famous ruling and its danger to free speech.
20738-diccionario-ingles-espan-ol-tagalo:
Words in three tongues fill this dictionary, which gives English terms with Spanish and Tagalog matches. Entries mark parts of speech and give short, plain glosses. A word like abate is shown as a cut or lessening, then matched in both tongues.

Such a book served schools, clerks, and traders in the Philippines under American rule. It shows how English was taught through Spanish into local speech. Word lists like this one froze a moment when three languages met each day. Language students and historians can mine it for old spellings, lost senses, and the feel of that mixed world.
20772-agriculture-for-beginners-revised-:
Teachers need not fear a simple farm textbook, argues Agriculture for Beginners. A teacher need not know calculus to teach sums, the preface notes. Nor must one master all history to teach a first United States book.

Soil, crops, stock, and tools fill lessons made for school use. The book brought farm science into rural classrooms in plain terms. Its authors served North Carolina schools, where most pupils lived close to the land. Readers today can see an early push to make schooling match the daily work of farm children, lesson by plain lesson.
20781-heidi-gift-edition:
Johanna Spyri's Heidi appears here in a gift edition of 1919, turned into English by Elisabeth P. Stork. Fourteen plates in colour by Maria L. Kirk grace the book. An intro by Charles Wharton Stork sets the tale for new readers.

Heidi, a Swiss orphan girl, brings warmth to her gruff grandfather in the Alps. Fresh air, goats, and mountain life heal more than one sad heart. The tale has charmed children in many tongues for well over a century. This fine edition shows how dear the book had grown by the time of the First World War.
20815-a-soldier-of-the-legion:
Eight dances pass at a grand ball, yet the great event of the night still waits. A Soldier of the Legion, from 1914, by C. N. and A. M. Williamson, sets that tense calm first. All prior fun, the tale says, is a mere curtain-raiser.

The Williamsons wrote tales of travel, motors, and daring deeds for wide audiences. France's Foreign Legion gives this one its harsh, romantic stage. Honour, disguise, and desert perils drive the plot at speed. Readers who like swift, glossy adventure in exotic dress will find the pair's smooth craft on full show here.
20879-critical-miscellanies-vol-1-essay-:
No land hates fresh ideas like England, writes Morley in his essay on Byron. No class there clings to old ways like the peerage (aristocracy). Yet Byron, a lord, broke every rule of that world in life and verse.

Morley traces how Byron's pride, pain, and genius made him Europe's voice of revolt. Childe Harold, Manfred, and Don Juan mark the climb of his fame. The essay weighs the man apart from the myth with care. Readers get a crisp Victorian verdict on a poet whose fire still warms and scorches readers now.
20919-the-status-civilization:
A man wakes by climbing through all time, from primal ooze to ape to self, in The Status Civilization. Robert Sheckley's hero rises layer by layer through sleep's deep strata. Each form, down to the amoeba, holds his own strange essence intact.

Sheckley strands a man with no memory on Omega, a prison world of rigid ranks. Crime is law there, and status is won by dark deeds. The satire bites at caste, fame, and rule-bound worlds with glee. This 1960 tale shows Sheckley's wit at its sharpest, a funhouse mirror held to human pride and place.
20991-follow-my-leader-the-boys-of-templ:
Ulsters, gloves, and top hats mark boys bound on a grave trip in Follow My Leader. No trunks crowd the lobby, and no homeward joy lights their glum faces. Talbot Baines Reed sets his Templeton boys on a path far from Mountjoy ease.

Reed, a master of the school tale, follows his boys into city life and work. Templeton's lads face tests no classroom set them, with grit as their guide. His tales prize honour, pluck, and fair play above mere marks. This one shows Reed widening his range, from school walls to the stern school of the world beyond.
21054-people-s-handy-atlas-of-the-world-:
Published in Chicago in 1911 by the Geographical Publishing Company, the People's Handy Atlas of the World calls itself the 1910 Census Edition. It packs more than one hundred specially engraved maps into a compact reference book. Thousands of indexed entries list towns and countries around the globe.

Populations come from the 1910 United States federal census for American places and from the latest sources then available abroad. A table of maps runs from Abyssinia and Africa to the individual states, and essays cover topics like the Panama Canal locks. For a modern reader it freezes world geography as Americans saw it just before the First World War.
21060-the-congo-rovers-a-story-of-the-sl:
A letter from Captain Vernon changes young Dick's life at the breakfast table in Harry Collingwood's novel of the slave squadron. Dick is offered a midshipman's place aboard the sloop Daphne. She is commissioned for service on the west coast of Africa and sails within days.

Dick must get his outfit fast and join a navy force sent to stop the slave trade. Collingwood tells the tale in the manner of W. H. G. Kingston, the boys' sea writer he often followed. Sea duty, slavers, and the Congo coast give the young midshipman a hard first education in command.
21064-a-middy-in-command-a-tale-of-the-s:
A young midshipman serves with the Royal Navy's anti-slavery squadron in Harry Collingwood's tale. It opens aboard the gun-brig Shark near the mouth of the Congo. First Lieutenant Seaton scans the sky at dawn and orders the light sails set again. The squadron's work is to catch slave ships off West Africa.

Accidents, swims, and chases fill the young officer's service. He wins promotion through his strong part in capturing a slaver. Collingwood, a naval architect by trade, handles sails, hulls, and shipboard routine with care. Readers who like exact sea detail get plenty of it here.
21075-the-cruise-of-the-thetis-a-tale-of:
Two old school friends meet in Piccadilly in July 1894 at the start of Harry Collingwood's Cuban tale. Singleton, a broad young English athlete, runs into Carlos, a slim friend of foreign birth with perfect English. Their meeting leads aboard the Thetis, a fast motor cruiser bound for Cuba.

Cuba is in the grip of an insurrection, and the young men are drawn into it. The cruise visits places around the island, including Guantanamo. Collingwood mixes a modern motor vessel with revolution, smuggling-era adventure, and youthful loyalty. Old school ties from their Alleynian days bind the heroes as danger grows.
21131-amos-huntingdon:
The Reverend T. P. Wilson's novel follows a well-off Derbyshire family and the two sons of old Mr Huntingdon. Each brother receives an allowance from their father. Amos manages his money well; his brother does not. Their maiden aunt Kate, the old man's sister, steadies the household.

Their sister Julia married a good-for-nothing and was shown the door by her father, leaving her children in real want. Amos spends his whole allowance quietly supporting Julia's family, which is why he cannot lend to his brother. Wilson keeps the cast small and draws each character closely, so readers follow the family's moral choices with real interest.
21135-nearly-lost-but-dearly-won:
The Reverend T. P. Wilson wrote this temperance tale in the late 1880s. It opens with Mr Tankardew, an educated gentleman whose house and person are anything but clean. Only his towels, people joke, are clean in the whole house. He lives on the edge of the small town of Hopeworth.

Wilson had won a prize from the Band of Hope for an earlier book. That society urged the young never to take up drinking. Nearly Lost but Dearly Won carries the same cause in story form. Ten lively line drawings by an artist signing MDH illustrate children, horses, and the turns of the plot.
21342-the-principles-of-english-versific:
Paull Franklin Baum, a Harvard scholar, published The Principles of English Versification with Harvard University Press in 1922. He begins with rhythm itself, arguing the word has grown from its strict senses into a name for any regular variation. Chapters then separate the rhythm of prose from the rhythm of verse.

Metre comes next, then metrical forms: the line, the stanza, and larger structures. Baum uses special marks for stressed and unstressed syllables, rests, and accents, explained in a transcriber's note for this edition. The book remains a careful, technical guide to how English verse keeps time, aimed at students who want rules grounded in the ear.
21379-marcus-the-young-centurion:
Marcus, eighteen, farms quietly in southern Italy with his father Cracis, once a great Roman general now fallen from favour. Old soldier Serge also lives there, raising the boy on war stories. His father forbids talk of soldiering. Then a stranger comes to the door: Caius Julius, later Caesar, begging Cracis to join his war against the Gauls.

Cracis goes, making Marcus and Serge promise not to follow. Both break the promise separately and meet by chance when Marcus rescues Serge from bandits. They reach Rome with their dog Lupe in time to join the last unit marching for Gaul. In battle the pair rescue generals and win notice, launching Marcus's career in George Manville Fenn's Roman tale.
21385-on-the-banks-of-the-amazon:
A long voyage down a great river drives W. H. G. Kingston's On the Banks of the Amazon. The tale opens with boyhood scenes under high peaks, where one peak pours out flame and smoke. From there the party moves into the vast lands drained by the Amazon.

Kingston fills the trip with natural history, told in clear and lively terms. Readers meet the plants, beasts, and birds of the river banks as the boats push on. Strange meetings and close calls keep the pace up between the science. The book recalls older tales of South America, yet it holds its own as a full, rich travel adventure.
21388-exiled-for-the-faith-a-tale-of-the:
France in the days of Huguenot suffering forms the scene of W. H. G. Kingston's Exiled for the Faith. Two cousins talk in the gardens of the Louvre, by the clear Seine, as danger grows around French Protestants. One guest arrives travel-stained, with a Scottish accent and plain dress.

The tale follows folk forced to flee home for their faith. Kingston writes as a firm Protestant, and he speaks hard words against the Catholic powers of that age. Modern readers may find those parts sharp, yet the story is clear and fast. It gives a vivid sense of what exile cost such families.
21395-the-last-look-a-tale-of-the-spanis:
Seville, some three hundred years back, glows at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's The Last Look. An archbishop calls on the widow of a great noble, a woman who once refused him in love. Her young daughter chats with him, free and unaware of risk.

Without meaning harm, the girl lets slip that her family now holds Protestant beliefs. Her father had met Luther on trips to Germany, and the faith took root at home. Years pass, the girl grows up, and two suitors seek her hand. Secret meetings of Protestants draw the eye of the Inquisition, and peril closes in fast.
21491-the-trapper-s-son:
An old trapper and his son prepare for winter in W. H. G. Kingston's short tale The Trapper's Son. Their camp sits in a valley under snow-touched heights in North America. Cree, Dakota, and Peigan peoples still hunt over that land.

Wolves or raiders kill their horses, so the pair cache most of their skins. They must walk to a nearby fort with what they can carry. The boy, Laurence, was raised by his Indigenous mother, apart from his father Michael. At the fort, both father and son hear the Christian faith for the first time, and the tale turns on their change.
21529-the-chauffeur-and-the-chaperon:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson send their travellers through Dutch waterways in The Chauffeur and the Chaperon, copyrighted in 1907. The tale is told from three points of view, starting with Nell van Buren's. Karl Anderson draws the pictures for the tour.

Nell and her stepsister Phyllis lodge cheap at Clapham, with a makeshift bath in the box room. From such plain starts the pair launch into boating, roads, and romance. The book is dedicated to a Rotterdam sailing club chief who helped the authors' own voyage. Light talk, fine scenes, and a chaperon problem carry this Edwardian holiday tale.
21533-reincarnation-a-study-in-human-evo:
Dr Th. Pascal sets out the theosophical case in Reincarnation, a study in human evolution, issued in London in 1910. Fred Rothwell translated the book from the French. Pascal had been a French naval doctor before turning to homeopathy and theosophy in a great seaport.

A Schopenhauer line opens the work: Europe is haunted by the belief that each birth is a first entrance into life. Chapters treat the soul and its bodies, rebirth and the moral law, and rebirth and science. Pascal then claims the backing of ages of faith and thought. The book is a clear period statement of theosophy.
21610-the-secret-of-the-creation:
Dr Howard D. Pollyen claims a mighty secret in The Secret of the Creation, sold for twenty-five cents. The book calls itself the great wonder of the literary age. It holds the first and second chapters of his full secret, with songs and poems added.

Pollyen styles himself the world's greatest author, with the deepest and most puzzling songs ever made. His first chapter treats the creation of the heavens, where Jehovah divides the waters. Minerals and kingdoms form at the creator's hands in his telling. The pamphlet is a curio of grand claims and home-made theology, offered as a touch of heaven's torchlight.
21611-the-runaway-or-the-adventures-of-r:
Two lads walk by Buttermilk Creek near Albany on a May morning in 1828 in The Runaway. The elder is sixteen, the younger fourteen, and the day is a lovely Sabbath. Their walk opens the adventures of Rodney Roverton, issued in Boston in 1852.

The New England Sabbath School Union approved the book for young readers. A line from Crabbe fronts it, of a vagrant who stole away to rove. The preface calls the tale a truthful narrative, not a fiction. Rodney's flight from home, and the cheats and prowlers of the road, teach their lesson in the Sunday-school manner.
21668-the-complex-vision:
John Cowper Powys sets out his philosophy in The Complex Vision, published at New York in 1920. Powys calls his method an instrument of research, free of technical terms where he can. Only our rare, finest moments of insight, he argues, show reality truly.

Average moments mislead, so we must recall the exceptional ones and build on them. Within the body, he holds, lives a real soul where mind and matter fuse. Powys names the gathered result the eternal vision, or complex vision of man. The book is a dense, personal metaphysic from a novelist of vast and strange gifts.
21677-milton:
Sir Walter Raleigh, the critic and man of letters, studies Milton in a short life first issued in his English Men of Letters manner. The copy given here is a tenth impression, printed in 1915. Raleigh dedicates it to his lost friend R. A. M. Stevenson.

Contents promise Milton's birth, schooling, early poems, and the intrusion of politics. Raleigh quotes Milton on the reader who brings a judgment equal to the book. Intensity, simplicity, and egotism mark his sense of Milton's temper. The farewell to mirth and the coming of the Restoration close the tale of England's blind epic poet.
21762-on-the-firing-line-in-education:
War gives A. J. Ladd his title and his question in this 1919 book: had the schools been disgraced by what the war revealed? Ladd, a professor of education at the State University of North Dakota, argues that social betterment must drive the schools. His chapters roam widely, from child study and physical training to surveys and vocational guidance.

Other chapters take up the state university and the high schools, the training of teachers, and eye problems among schoolchildren. He writes on the home, the church, and the school as partners in raising children. The book is a reformer's tour of American education just after the First World War, practical in aim and earnest in tone.
21783-a-manual-of-pronunciation:
Words most often mispronounced in English fill this 1904 manual by Otis Ashmore, superintendent of schools in Savannah, Georgia. Ashmore gathers each word's sound as given by the best authorities in England and America. He weighs Webster's, Worcester's, the Standard, the Century, and Murray's great dictionary, then still in preparation, against each other.

A key at the front explains his marks for long and short vowels and other sounds. The book was made for practical use in schools and families. It belongs to a time when careful speech marked a person's schooling, and a wrong vowel could betray it. As a snapshot of American speech standards in 1904, it remains a handy and curious reference.
21791-the-aeroplane-speaks-fifth-edition:
Flying in the Great War is explained by a pilot for plain readers in The Aeroplane Speaks, by H. Barber, a captain in the Royal Flying Corps. Barber gives two reasons for writing: to help the ordinary man grasp the aeroplane, and to share the joys and troubles of its pilot. The book sold fast: five editions ran from December 1916 to December 1917.

Thirty-six full pages of aircraft types and eighty-seven sketches and diagrams fill out the text. Reviewers praised its gift for making hard principles easy to swallow. Barber writes with the ease of a man teaching friends, not lecturing pupils. It remains a vivid primer from the years when flight itself was new and war made it urgent.
21879-the-sins-of-se-verac-bablon:
A mysterious millionaire's sins drive this thriller by Sax Rohmer, The Sins of Séverac Bablon, first published in January 1914. Julius Rohscheimer, the great financier, boasts that he could sell up half a score of ancestral halls tomorrow. His secretary Adeler shows no feeling; Sir Richard Haredale veils his scorn in tobacco smoke. Around them gathers the shadow of Bablon himself.

Chapters promise thirty men who were all alike, a mystic hand, a Damascus curtain, and a corner in millionaires. Rohmer, soon to be famous for Fu Manchu, builds the tale from dressing rooms, hotels, and midnight calls. It is early Rohmer: society London on the surface, and beneath it a masked power moving money and men like pieces.
21972-george-washington:
Washington's whole career is told for young readers in Calista McCabe Courtenay's George Washington, a 1917 volume in the Makers of American History series. February twenty-second is a national holiday, the book begins, because it is Washington's birthday. Chapters follow the surveyor's first trip into the wilderness and his errand to the French. Braddock's staff, the French and Indian War, and command of Virginia's forces come next.

The Revolution fills the heart of the book: Boston relieved, the Delaware crossed, Valley Forge, Arnold's treason, and Yorktown beyond. A. M. Turner and Harriet Kaucher drew the pictures. Courtenay writes plain, patriotic history pitched at school readers. The life ends, as it should, with the farmer-president honored by all loyal Americans.
21986-the-dash-for-khartoum-a-tale-of-th:
The Nile expedition to relieve Gordon drives G. A. Henty's The Dash for Khartoum, one of his long shelf of historical tales. Joseph Nash and John Schönberg drew its ten page illustrations for Blackie of London. Henty's young heroes race up the Nile with the relief force, through desert, cataracts, and Mahdist resistance. The dash of the title was real: Britain's soldiers rowed and fought hundreds of miles against the river's clock.

The publisher's list at the front shows the company the tale keeps: Cat of Bubastes, Young Carthaginian, Beric the Briton, Lion of St. Mark. Henty wrote history as a boy's adventure with the dates left in. Khartoum's fall hangs over every chapter, giving this one a somber race-against-time power.
22038-the-evolution-of-the-dragon:
Grafton Elliot Smith, an anatomist who had studied Egyptian mummies, argued that the dragon was born in Egypt. His book The Evolution of the Dragon grew from a lecture on incense and libations. Smith held that early Egyptian beliefs about gods, shells, and precious stones travelled the world by trade. As the ideas spread, they changed, and the dragon changed with them.

Smith follows dragon lore through Babylon, India, China, and the Americas. He treats myths as evidence that can be tracked like goods on a trade route. Fellow scholars fought his sweeping claims hard. The book still marks a bold, early attempt to explain why far-apart peoples tell such similar tales.
22055-dame-duck-s-first-lecture-on-educa: Dame Duck's First Lecture on Education belongs to Uncle Toby's Series of cheap colour picture books for small children. Old Mother Duck has hatched a brood of ducklings, small and callow. Their wings are short and their lessons are just beginning. In verse, the dame warns, scolds, and instructs her young ones by the pond.
22125-the-venetian-painters-of-the-renai:
Bernhard Berenson was twenty-nine when he published The Venetian Painters of the Renaissance in 1894. The book is a bold handbook, not a narrative history. Berenson lists the works of each Venetian master and says where those works could be seen. This third edition adds painters like Andrea Schiavone and Girolamo da Treviso to the lists.

An index to the paintings lets collectors and students check attributions fast. Berenson's sharp eye for who painted what made him the great connoisseur of his age. Dealers and museums hung on the judgments first tried out here. The little volume still marks the start of modern art attribution as a profession.
22154-creatures-of-vibration:
Harl Vincent wrote Creatures of Vibration as a sequel to his story Vagabonds of Space. Vincent was an engineer who helped shape early magazine science fiction. His space vagabonds fall into the hands of the natives of Titan, Saturn's great moon. The blurb calls those natives vibration-maddened, and the heroes' plight drives the tale.

Romance crosses the stars here: a hero measures a girl from Paladar against every woman he knew on Earth. On Europa he had neither wealth nor influence, only his wits. Vincent mixes love, exile, and strange science in the pulp manner. The story shows Astounding-era science fiction in its brisk, inventive youth.
22177-morality-as-a-religion:
W. R. Washington Sullivan published Morality as a Religion in 1898, expounding first principles of the ethical movement. His title page carries Kant's saying that religion is morality recognised as a divine command. Emerson's words stand beside it: the age has fallen away from theology to morals, and Sullivan calls the change an advance.

Sullivan argues that right living can bind people together as creeds once did. He leans on the French thinker Guyau and on the Ethical societies then spreading. Duty, sympathy, and service form his creed. The book documents a real Victorian experiment: building churches of conduct for people who had lost faith in doctrine.
22203-my-contemporaries-in-fiction:
David Christie Murray turned critic in My Contemporaries in Fiction. The novelist here judges the novelists he worked beside. He insists the book is not meant to instruct the instructed. It makes no pretence to be infallible, only to help the average reader form just opinions on contemporary art.

Murray also hopes to check interested or over-enthusiastic puffers of bad work. Chapters weigh the reputations of living writers one by one. Praise and blame come from a man who earned his bread by the same trade. The book is a period document of literary London: who was up, who was down, and what a working novelist thought of both.
22216-project-mastodon:
Clifford D. Simak first published Project Mastodon in Galaxy magazine in March 1955. Simak, a Minnesota newspaperman, became one of science fiction's most humane voices. His story opens in the State Department with a protocol problem. The chief announces "Mr. Hudson of — ah — Mastodonia," and the Secretary of State must greet a country that does not exist.

Hudson's party has used a time machine to found a tiny republic in the age of the mastodons. They want diplomatic relations, trade agreements, and foreign aid, all quite politely. Simak plays the absurdity deadpan. The tale is a gentle satire of diplomacy wrapped in a time-travel joke.
22251-the-teacher-or-moral-influences-em:
Jacob Abbott, the famous writer of the Rollo books, published The Teacher in 1833. Its subject is the moral influence a teacher holds over a school. Abbott promises a system for organising and managing a school in a clear, practical manner. The system rests, so far as possible, on moral influences rather than force or fear.

Abbott describes classrooms he ran, with their rules, signals, and quiet appeals to conscience. He treats pupils as reasonable beings who respond to trust. The book shaped American teaching for decades and trained a generation of schoolmasters. It still reads as a humane classic of education, written before corporal punishment went out of fashion.
22269-the-autobiography-of-madame-guyon:
Jeanne-Marie Guyon, the French mystic, wrote her autobiography at the command of her spiritual director. She says she complies willingly, though the labour is painful. Her earnest wish is to paint in true colours God's goodness to her and the depth of her own ingratitude. Numberless small circumstances, she admits, have escaped her memory.

Madame Guyon taught a prayer of pure, passive love that the Church condemned as Quietism. She was imprisoned in the Bastille for her doctrine. Her life tells of convents, bishops, persecution, and an inner stillness she never surrendered. The Moody Press edition carried her story to evangelical readers, who prized her devotion while doubting her errors.
22286-milton:
John Bailey, a critic of French poetry and Dr. Johnson's circle, wrote this short life of Milton for a series of brief biographies. Bailey sets Milton's verse ringing from the start, quoting the armouries and bowery loneliness of his early poems. Brooks of Eden, cedar arches, and crimson palm-woods show the young poet's gorgeous ear before the epic singer emerged.

The life follows Milton through Cambridge, Italy, prose warfare for Parliament, blindness, and Paradise Lost. Bailey writes appreciation rather than archive work; his Milton is a poet first. Such pocket lives introduced the great dead to busy readers. Bailey's is a warm, literate example, strong on the poetry and brisk on the politics.
22294-robert-louis-stevenson:
Robert Louis Stevenson had been dead only a few years when this life of him appeared. The writer thanks the helpers who supplied facts and kindness during the work. For dates and particulars he leans on Sidney Colvin's article in the Dictionary of National Biography. Colvin was Stevenson's friend and editor, and every early biographer stood on his ground.

The life follows Stevenson from Edinburgh childhood through engineering, law, and Bohemian London to Samoa. Treasure Island, Kidnapped, and Dr. Jekyll made him famous; illness made him an exile. Early lives like this one fixed the beloved "RLS" of legend: brave, gay, and doomed. It remains a document of the cult that followed him.
22353-early-theories-of-translation:
Early Theories of Translation, published in 1920, studies how past writers rendered foreign works. It begins with Anglo-Saxon writers and the medieval period. Their comments reveal the attitude then common toward borrowed material.

Prefaces to works linked with King Alfred give suggestive evidence. One method appears in the English version of Pope Gregory's Pastoral Care. Alfred's circle thought hard about turning Latin into English. Their choices shaped English prose at its start. The study follows such thinking across early centuries. Scholars of language get a compact history of translation before it had settled rules or a settled name.
22359-an-essay-on-professional-ethics-se:
George Sharswood wrote An Essay on Professional Ethics for the legal profession. It began as lectures on the aims and duties of law. Part was read at the University of Pennsylvania on October 2, 1854.

That lecture opened the fifth session of the university's Law Department. The second edition carries the fuller title plainly. Sharswood treated lawyering as a calling with moral duties. His compend of lectures set standards for students entering practice. American legal ethics grew partly from teaching like his. Readers get a founding voice on what lawyers owe clients, courts, and the public beyond mere skill.
22431-dave-darrin-on-mediterranean-servi:
Dave Darrin on Mediterranean Service sends a young naval officer to European duty. Dan Dalzell, his friend, shares the service named in the subtitle. Trouble in a Spanish cafe opens the story's action.

One speaker predicts a lively time within four minutes. A fellow under an Alpine hat, he says, equals four spindling Spanish waiters. That judgment sets up a brawl the heroes must handle. Dave Darrin books followed cadets into the real navy fleet. Readers got sea service, foreign ports, and quick fists. This volume trades American waters for the Mediterranean. It delivers period naval adventure written for boys who dreamed of the fleet.
22455-adam-johnstone-s-son:
F. Marion Crawford wrote Adam Johnstone's Son, a novel published in 1895. Crawford was a popular novelist of Italy and international society. The preserved passage watches a woman read time in her own face.

Lines on a face are years, the passage reflects. Streaks are months, weeks, or sometimes only hours of storm. Tear-storms have bleached the brown, black, or gold of hair. One little wrinkle, she says, was so very little then. It came when she doubted for a single day. Such tender attention to aging opens the novel's emotional world. Readers get Crawford's polished, feeling prose on love and loss.
22549-space-prison:
Space Prison is a science fiction novel of a ship fleeing in terror. Her communicators are silenced as she runs like a hunted thing. Her drives moan and thunder under the strain of escape.

Up in the control room, Irene has been told the news. Needles of the dials dance against red danger lines constantly. Day and night they hold at those lines without relief. Such pressure sets up life aboard a prison ship in space. Tom Godwin wrote the novel, also known as The Survivors. Castaways and captors share its harsh survival stakes in deep space. Readers get a grim, driving tale of endurance among the stars.
22577-practical-grammar-and-composition:
Practical Grammar and Composition is a school textbook on English grammar, published through Project Gutenberg as a public-domain work. Its author is not named in the catalog record. The book teaches the parts of speech and sentence building step by step, in the formal style of older American classrooms.

The contents run from basic grammar into connectives, covering relative pronouns, conjunctions, and prepositions. Later sections treat independent and dependent clauses, plus the case and number of pronouns. Review questions close the main sections, followed by a general exercise on grammar. Students of older teaching methods, and anyone curious about how grammar was once taught, will find a complete period course here.
22636-a-middle-high-german-primer-third-:
A Middle High German Primer, here in its third edition, is a textbook for the German language of the medieval centuries. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Students of old literature need this stepping stone to read the epics and lyrics written between the Old High German and modern periods.

The author states the aim plainly: an elementary introduction that prepares readers for the larger German works on the subject. Its grammar leans, with thanks, on Paul's and Weinhold's standard Middle High German grammars of the 1880s. Sounds, forms, and sample texts build in order. The primer still serves its purpose for beginners, and it shows how German universities of its day trained philologists.
22821-the-blot-on-the-kaiser-s-scutcheon:
Newell Dwight Hillis aimed The Blot on the Kaiser's 'Scutcheon squarely at wartime readers in 1918. His contents page reads like an indictment. Chapters cover the Kaiser's hatred of the United States, his friendship with the Sultan, and General Pershing's charges against Germany. One chapter asks where Wilhelm learned to treat a signed treaty as worthless paper.

Hillis, a well-known Brooklyn preacher, writes as a prosecutor rather than a historian. He marshals speeches, reports, and atrocity stories to blacken Wilhelm II and rally American opinion. The book has little balance, and that is the point. Today it serves as a clear sample of home-front persuasion during the First World War, worth reading as such.
22847-official-views-of-the-world-s-colu:
Chicago's great fair gets an official record in Official Views of the World's Columbian Exposition. The idea of marking the third centennial of Columbus's voyage with a world's fair, the text notes, arose years before the anniversary itself. Congress organized the show as early as 1890 and fixed Chicago as its seat.

Commissions, boards, and committees fill the opening pages, including a National Commission and a Board of Lady Managers. The views that follow present the White City as its organizers wished it seen, hall by hall and lagoon by lagoon. As a souvenir and a document, the volume preserves the fair's official face. Historians still mine such records for how America presented itself in 1893.
22900-erasmus-and-the-age-of-reformation:
Johan Huizinga wrote Erasmus and the Age of Reformation, and its foreword recalls a spring morning in Oxford. Rather more than twenty years earlier, the foreword's writer had acted as guide to Huizinga on a visit there. It was not his first stay, and he knew the principal buildings already, so they sought out lesser-known corners.

Huizinga's subject is the Dutch humanist who stood between medieval faith and the Reformation storm. Erasmus prized learning, moderation, and peace in an age that rewarded none of them. The Dutch historian tells that story with rare grace and sympathy. His book remains a standard portrait, as much literature as history, and a fine door into Renaissance thought for new readers.
23038-quiet-talks-on-the-crowned-christ-:
S. D. Gordon opens Quiet Talks on the Crowned Christ of Revelation with a hymn. The opening hymn recalls how Christ pictured his love. He chose the figure of a shepherd laying down his life for the flock, before the crowd bore him to the cross. Gordon's talks keep that devotional key throughout.

The Quiet Talks series made Gordon one of the most read devotional writers of his generation. This volume walks through the Book of Revelation as a portrait of Christ crowned, rather than as a puzzle of dates. His manner is intimate, as if speaking to one listener in a quiet room. Readers seeking the period's warm, personal evangelicalism will find it here in its most practiced form, gentle and certain.
23073-villegagnon-a-tale-of-the-huguenot:
Ships fight off Brazil in Villegagnon, a tale of the Huguenot persecution. Ships return to France for more Protestant emigrants, braving a hostile Catholic crowd stirred up by a scheming monk. At sea, five Portuguese vessels attack the French squadron and are beaten off, losing one ship taken.

Villegagnon, the French commander who founded a colony in Rio's bay in 1555, stands at the story's center. Protestants and Catholics carried Europe's wars across the Atlantic, and this tale follows them there. Historical fiction of this kind taught young readers their confessional past as adventure. The sea fights are brisk, the theology earnest, and the colony's strange fate hangs over both.
23099-the-fourth-invasion:
Alien ships leave evidence in The Fourth Invasion. Clayton rustles a pile of newspapers. The reports in here vary, he says. The reports, Clayton says, missed the jets of flame from the alien ships, flame blamed for a house fire. Nobody recorded the great black wings the invaders glided down on, either.

Four invasions mean a pattern, and patterns mean the witnesses can finally compare notes. The story builds its case like a hearing, testimony against testimony, until the official version cracks. That method gives the fantasy a reporter's spine. Readers who enjoy invasion tales argued from evidence, rather than announced by narrators, will appreciate the discipline here, and the slow chill as the reports begin to agree.
23208-how-janice-day-won:
Helen Beecher Long published How Janice Day Won in 1917, a novel for young readers about a girl named Janice Day. Janice attends the Middletown Seminary. On a holiday from that school, she is back among the boys of her home town at an hour when they should be under a watchful eye.

Their principal, Mr. Nelson Haley of the Polktown school, is meant to keep order, yet the voices Janice hears are all boys' voices. Long sets school routine against small-town freedom. Readers get a story of a capable girl, her school friends, and the scrapes and contests of town life.
23209-the-life-of-friedrich-schiller-com: The Life of Friedrich Schiller sets out to give both a biography of the German writer and an examination of his works. Its early pages worry over the fate of books themselves. A poor book, the writer says, must walk this world in clean linen, so to speak, carrying no blotches but its own. Care over print and reputation frames the life that follows.
a-blot-in-the-scutcheon:
Robert Browning's verse tragedy turns on the honor of the house of Tresham. The introductory note sets Browning apart from aristocratic poets: a bank clerk's son, a dissenter, educated by tutors and his widely read father. His play puts that outsider's intensity into an old family's pride. The scenes move between a lodge in Lord Tresham's park, the mansion's saloon, and his sister Mildred's chamber.

Lord Tresham discovers that a lover visits Mildred by night and reads disgrace into the visits. Truth comes too late to stop the sword. Browning builds the tragedy on silence: three people who love each other refuse the one plain talk that would save them. The verse is swift and stage-worthy, rare in his work.
a-complete-account-of-the-settlement-at-:
Watkin Tench resumes his subject, as his preface says, having already published a narrative of the colony brought up to July 1788 that passed through three editions. He resided at Port Jackson nearly four years, from January 20, 1788, to December 18, 1791, and this fuller account covers the whole term. Gratitude, he writes, must be shown by fresh information, not by claims on indulgence.

Nineteen chapters follow the settlement's hunger, discipline, building, and exploring, and its dealings with the Aboriginal people of the harbor. Tench writes of friends and enemies among them by name. His two books together form the classic first history of Sydney, valued for fairness rare in first accounts of colonization.
a-dream-of-john-ball-and-a-king-s-lesson:
William Morris wrote these two short prose works of revolt and counsel in a medieval dress. The contents list twelve chapters for A Dream of John Ball. Its narrator dreams himself into Kent at the time of the rising of 1381. He hears John Ball preach. Ball is the hedge priest of the revolt. His theme is that fellowship is heaven, and the lack of it hell. The chapters move from a meeting at the cross to a township battle. They end with talk of the days to come.

A King's Lesson, printed after the dream tale, is a brief fable. In it a king learns what his rule rests on. Morris was a socialist as well as a poet and craftsman. He used the fourteenth century to argue with his own age. The dreamer keeps asking whether the old fight for fairness was lost. The book refuses a simple answer.
a-march-on-london-being-a-story-of-wat-t:
G. A. Henty opens his preface with the chroniclers Froissart, Monstrelet, and Holinshed. They make the fourteenth century unusually well known. He grants at once that the uprising of the Commons was in itself justifiable. Serfs owed their lords labor and labored under grievous disabilities. His hero is young Edgar, drawn into the march on London in 1381.

Nineteen chapters follow Wat Tyler, the rescue of prisoners, death to the Flemings, a combat in the Tower, and Tyler's death before the boy-king Richard. The tale then carries Edgar to the wars in Flanders, a starving town, and civil war. Henty teaches solid medieval history inside a fast boys' adventure, as was his signature method.
a-narrative-of-the-life-of-mrs-mary-jemi:
James E. Seaver took this narrative carefully from Mary Jemison's own words on November 29, 1823, as the title page states. She was taken by the Indians in 1755, when only about twelve years of age, and remained among them for life. The title page also promises what the book holds: the murder of her father and family, her sufferings, and her marriages to two Indians.

Her account covers the French and Revolutionary wars on the frontier, the customs of the Seneca among whom she lived, and the loss of her sons. An appendix adds the tragedy at the Devil's Hole and Sullivan's expedition. Jemison's story, told in old age, is one of the most remarkable captivity narratives in American letters.
a-psychological-counter-current-in-recen:
William Dean Howells wrote this essay on a turn he saw coming in the fiction of his day. Fiction, he argues, moves in tides. Realism had swept romance aside. Then romance flooded back. The flood sank the novel's good name once more. Yet Howells spots a drift against the tide. He names it psychologism. It means close care for motive and inner life. He finds it at work in the newest books.

He tests the idea on recent novels. The first case is Gilbert Parker, a popular writer of romance. Parker's latest book, Howells says, is saved by its inner study of character. The essay is criticism with a program. Howells was the dean of American letters. He argues that the novel's future lies past the fight of romance and realism. It lies in the study of character from inside.
a-question:
A Question, by Georg Ebers and translated from the German by Mary J Safford, begins as a poem before it becomes a tale. Ebers tells how a picture in an art palace on the river Isar held him spellbound in his seat. A year later, wintering with his family on a palm shaded shore in the south, the image kept returning to his mind unbidden.

The prelude explains that the words for the story arrived one bright day without searching, as if the painting itself supplied them. Alma Tadema, the painter of classical scenes, is the friend whose picture Ebers credits. What follows the verses is a prose idyl, a short tale in an ancient setting, built scene by scene from that canvas. Readers meet the artwork first as the author did: as a question that would not let go.
a-simpleton:
Charles Reade defends his method in a fighting preface before his novel begins. He borrows facts from every source, he says. But a man who takes only facts, not treatment, is no plagiarist. All fiction worth a button, he argues, is founded on facts. The novel then tests that method on a hero of unusual simplicity.

His simpleton is a good-hearted, trusting young man set among sharper people who live by their wits. Reade follows him through love, business, and betrayal, using documented fact to fill in the worlds he crosses. The book runs long, in nineteen chapters, with Reade's usual energy, research, and moral heat on every page.
a-spirit-in-prison:
A Spirit in Prison is a 1908 novel by Robert Hichens, an English writer whose career produced more than forty novels. Hichens, full name Robert Smythe Hichens, also worked as a journalist, dramatist, and music critic. He gained notoriety with The Green Carnation and his widest popularity with The Garden of Allah, and A Spirit in Prison was among the books that won him critical praise.

Written at the height of that reputation, the novel belongs to Hichens's serious fiction rather than his satires. Its title suggests a self trapped by circumstance, a theme his psychological novels pursued in polished, atmospheric prose. The book stands as a sample of the literary craftsmanship that set Hichens apart from ordinary popular novelists of his time.
acts-peter-twelve-mattison:
Peter and the twelve sail, preach, and face marvels in a tale from the Nag Hammadi codices. The Acts of Peter and the Twelve Apostles, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives that story in English. It is a work of adventure first and doctrine second.

A pearl merchant named Lithargoel draws the apostles to a strange city and a hard lesson. The tale praises care for the poor and turns the hunt for a pearl into a sign of the soul's quest. Its mix of travel yarn and teaching is rare among the codices. Mattison's version keeps the tale brisk and plain.
alfred-tennyson:
Andrew Lang writes a brief life of Alfred Tennyson from the 1901 Blackwood edition. He rests, as he says in his introduction, on two sources. The first is the official biography by the poet's son. The second is the text of the poems. He refuses the anecdotes and local researches Tennyson disliked. The contents run from boyhood and Cambridge through the poems of 1831 to 1833 and the long silence after.

Chapters treat The Princess, In Memoriam, the Idylls of the King, Enoch Arden, the dramas, and the last years. Lang, himself a poet, gives his own impressions of the poems rather than the commentators'. The book is a compact, admiring portrait of the laureate by a fellow craftsman.
alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland-html-ed:
Lewis Carroll sends young Alice down a rabbit hole after a White Rabbit with a watch, in this Millennium Fulcrum edition of his famous story. Alice had been sitting bored beside her sister, whose book had no pictures or talk in it. Underground, size, sense, and manners all stop behaving.

Twelve chapters bring the pool of tears, the caucus race, the Caterpillar, the Cheshire Cat, the Mad Tea-Party, and the Queen's croquet ground, where flamingos serve as mallets. Alice ends in a courtroom where the Knave stands trial for stolen tarts. The mix of logic games, songs, and nonsense has kept the story loved by children and adults alike.
amphitryon:
Molière's comedy was first played in Paris at the Palais-Royal on January 13, 1668, as A. R. Waller's translation notes, and it held the stage for months. The cast list gives the trick plainly: Jupiter, under the form of Amphitryon, visits Alcmène while her husband the general is at war. Mercury likewise doubles the valet Sosie.

The doubled masters and servants collide in scenes of perfect confusion, with Sosie beaten by himself and Amphitryon shut out of his own house. Beneath the farce sits an uneasy point about power: gods may do what would hang a mortal. Molière based his play on Plautus and sharpened it with courtly verse and nerve.
an-essay-on-the-principle-of-population:
Thomas Robert Malthus's Essay on the Principle of Population, in its first form of 1798, grew out of a conversation about Godwin's speculations on society's future. The title page promises remarks on Godwin, Condorcet, and other writers who dreamed of human perfectibility. Malthus's preface says he sat down only to state his thoughts to a friend more clearly. The thought was his principle: population, unchecked, grows geometrically, doubling by generations, while food grows only arithmetically.

From that disproportion the essay derives its machinery: misery and vice, the checks balancing mouths and meals. Perfect societies, Malthus argues, founders on arithmetic before they reach philosophy. Readers get the founding text of the dismal science here in its sharp, short first edition, before the data and the softened doctrine of later versions. Few pamphlets have argued with the future so successfully.
androcles-and-the-lion:
George Bernard Shaw's fable play Androcles and the Lion, written in 1912, retells the old story of the slave who pulled a thorn from a lion's paw. Shaw's prologue shows the lion limping and roaring in the Libyan forest while Androcles, a Greek tailor, hides with his shrewish wife Megaera. Kindness to the beast, done in terror, becomes the debt the arena will collect. Shaw frames the tale as a parable about religion.

Inside the play, Roman soldiers round up Christians for the Colosseum, and Androcles joins converts like the gentle Lavinia and the giant Ferrovius. Shaw gives each prisoner a different faith to argue: some love doctrine, some love courage, some simply love life. The Emperor demands sacrifice to his own godhead as the price of pardon. Readers get Shaw's wit turned on martyrdom itself, ending with the lion remembering its friend in the arena, and a tailor dancing free.
annette-the-metis-spy-a-heroine-of-the-n:
Edmund Collins sets his tale on the prairie at sunset, where two riders hurry their ponies along a blind trail toward purple hills along the Red River. His contents announce the shape at once: Le Chef falls in love with the half-breed maiden, Annette forms a heroic resolve, and her lover falls into danger. The setting is the North-West Rebellion in Canada.

Nine chapters give Annette escapes, a fight, a capture, and a guardian swan, as she carries word between camps at the risk of her life. Collins adds notes and a further tale, Nancy the Light-Keeper's Daughter. The novel is popular adventure fiction of its moment, written while the rebellion of the Métis under Riel was still fresh news.
apocalypse-adam-mattison:
Adam speaks to his son Seth at the end of his life in a revelation found at Nag Hammadi. The Apocalypse of Adam, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives that Sethian text whole. The codex that holds it was buried in Egypt and found again in 1945.

Adam tells Seth of the flood to come, of fire and quake after it, and of a savior to rise at the end. He warns that the world's rulers will fight the truth in each age. The tale is dark, vast, and told in the voice of the first man. Mattison's version lets readers meet this rare apocalypse in full.
apollonius-argonautica-seaton:
Apollonius of Rhodes composed the Argonautica in the third century BCE. R. C. Seaton translated the Greek epic into English prose. Jason leads the Argonauts aboard the Argo toward distant Colchis.

Their goal is the Golden Fleece, guarded by King Aeetes. The sorceress Medea falls in love with Jason and makes success possible. Apollonius writes a polished, learned epic quite unlike Homer's rougher power. Scholars value his psychology, especially Medea's divided heart. Seaton's clear prose lets modern readers follow the voyage, the monsters, and the uneasy triumph at its end.
apuleius-golden-ass-adlington:
Apuleius, a Roman writer of the second century, composed the novel called Metamorphoses, or The Golden Ass. William Adlington Englished it in 1566, in lively Tudor prose. It is the only Latin novel to survive complete.

Young Lucius, dabbling in magic, turns himself into a donkey by mistake. As a beast he witnesses theft, cruelty, comedy, and human folly everywhere. The tale of Cupid and Psyche sits at the book's heart. After long suffering, the goddess Isis restores his human shape. Bawdy and strange, the novel still feels fresh. Adlington dedicated his translation to the Earl of Devonshire in print.
archibald-malmaison:
Julian Hawthorne called Archibald Malmaison a true story, and his long introductory essay argues with himself about whether truth or invention makes better fiction. The tale concerns Archibald, second son of Sir Clarence Butt Malmaison of Malmaison in Sussex, a family of Huguenot descent, and the strange mental affection that sets him apart from other men.

The narrative rests on the professional notebooks of Dr. Forbes Rollinson, the family physician, whose own father held the same trust before him. Family history, childhood signs, and later episodes are arranged as evidence in a case the reader must judge. Hawthorne leaves the doctor's material explanation and his own doubts standing side by side, which gives the novel its uneasy, casebook air.
around-the-world-in-eighty-days-junior-d:
Jules Verne's race around the world appears here in a Junior Deluxe Edition made for young readers. The contents open with Phileas Fogg hiring Passepartout, then the club conversation that leads to Fogg's famous wager: around the world in eighty days. A detective named Fix soon betrays a very natural impatience.

Chapter by chapter the pair cross the Red Sea and Indian Ocean, India, China, Japan, and America, by train, ship, elephant, and sled. Passepartout talks too much, loses his shoes, and saves the journey more than once, while Fix follows, sure Fogg robbed a bank. The final twist turns on a day gained by traveling east. This edition keeps the full, swift plot.
b09-melanchthon-augsburg-confession:
Philipp Melanchthon, Luther's close ally, wrote the Augsburg Confession and saw it presented to Emperor Charles V in 1530. Lutheran princes and cities had been called to state their faith before the empire. Melanchthon, a scholar of calm temper, drafted a text meant to show unity with the old church where unity held.

The confession sets out teaching on God, sin, faith, the church, and the sacraments in orderly articles. Its tone seeks peace, yet it concedes nothing on the core of the gospel. The text became the chief doctrinal standard of Lutheranism worldwide. The rendering here is by F Bente and W H T Dau.
beric-the-briton: Beric the Briton, G. A. Henty's Roman Britain tale. The British chief. This book preserves that historical novel. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
beric-the-briton-a-story-of-the-roman-in:
G. A. Henty's Beric the Briton tells the Roman invasion of Britain for boys. Henty argues that his series on England's wars would be incomplete without the period when Romans mastered the country, and he praises the valour with which the natives defended themselves.

Only Roman discipline, Henty says, finally triumphed over British bravery and superior physical strength. The conquest brought Roman civilisation and ended perpetual tribal wars, yet it proved disastrous in the end, since Britons defended by Roman soldiers could not resist the Saxons when the legions left. Young readers will find Beric a vigorous introduction to Roman Britain.
captain-brassbound-s-conversion:
George Bernard Shaw set his play Captain Brassbound's Conversion in Morocco, opening in a missionary's garden above the harbor of Mogador. Missionary Rankin receives a Cockney visitor, Drinkwater, with news of travelers. Sir Howard Hallam, a hanging judge, and his sister-in-law Lady Cicely Waynflete are coming to tour the country. Their guide is the outlaw Captain Brassbound.

Brassbound nurses a revenge plot against Hallam, who he believes ruined his mother. Lady Cicely, calm and charming, manages men the way others manage weather. She talks her way through an ambush, a tribal court, and the captain's grievance. Shaw turns melodrama into comedy about justice, revenge, and feminine diplomacy. Readers watch a would-be avenger converted not by force but by a woman who refuses to take his tragedy seriously.
cashel-byron-s-profession:
Cashel Byron's Profession, by George Bernard Shaw, begins in a schoolroom world far from the prize ring. Shaw's prologue sets Moncrief House on Panley Common, a scholastic establishment for the sons of gentlemen. Fifty boys in tailless jackets fill a bare back yard. It holds a pump, a worn ball alley, and a door carved thick with initials. Strollers on the common climb the wall to watch.

From that yard comes Cashel Byron, who runs from respectability into professional boxing, the profession of the title. Shaw makes his hero a pugilist with a gentleman's manners and a theorist's mind, then sets him among patrons, trainers, and a heroine who studies him as a social problem. The novel argues that prize fighting is skilled labor judged by snobs. In Shaw's earliest fiction manner, a boxer may be the most honest professional in a room full of amateurs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aaron:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Aaron treats Moses' brother, the high priest of the Old Law. The entry first weighs two views of the Pentateuch as a source. One is the traditional Catholic view of a single work under Moses' supervision. The other is the critical view of a late compilation from several documents.

On the traditional reading, Aaron was the great-grandson of Levi, second child of Amram and Jochabed, with Miriam eldest and Moses youngest. Exodus gives Aaron's age as eighty-three at the Exodus, against Moses' eighty. The entry follows Aaron's life under both aspects, dwelling longer on the traditional account, and treats his priesthood, his part in the Exodus, and his death as the sources present them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abaddon: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Abaddon explains a Hebrew word meaning ruin or destruction, and by extension the place of destruction, the abyss or realm of the dead. In the Apocalypse the word appears personified as Abaddon, rendered in Greek by Apollyon, the hellish prince who deals death and wreaks ruin on earth. The Latin Vulgate renders Apollyon as Exterminans, meaning Destroyer. An asserted identity with Asmodeus, demon of impurity, is noted but not proved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-corn:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Cornillon describes a Norbertine abbey founded in 1124 by Albero of Liège, three years after St. Norbert formed the Premonstratensian Order. Canons from Floreffe near Namur staffed the house, which stood on Mont Cornillon above the Meuse, overlooking Liège.

Early Norbertine abbeys were double houses, with canons on one side of the church and nuns, who ran a women's hospital, on the other. At Cornillon the nunnery and hospital stood at the hill's foot. St. Juliana of Cornillon, nun of this convent and patron of the Corpus Christi feast, and Blessed Lucas, its first abbot, give the entry its human centre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abdias-of-bab: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Abdias of Babylon describes a writer of doubtful credit, counted among the seventy-two disciples and Babylon's first bishop, ordained by Simon and Jude. Very little is known of him. He matters chiefly for the ten-book Historia Certaminis Apostolici imputed to him, telling the apostles' labours and deaths. The work claims translation from Hebrew to Greek by Eutropius, then to Latin by Julius Africanus. It is really a Latin work citing Jerome's Vulgate and Rufinus' history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abdication:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on abdication, in church law, means the giving up of a benefice or clerical rank. Every such honour, from the papacy down to the lowliest chantry, may be given up by its holder.

Church law requires the benefice to be given up into the proper superior's hands, for a just cause, freely and with no paid bargain. Giving up may carry terms, such as bestowing the benefice on a named person or giving the holder another office. A holder in sacred orders must also hold other sure means of support matching his rank. Giving up may also be tacit, presumed when a cleric takes an office or does an act that clashes with holding a church rank.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abduction:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on abduction treats it both as a public crime and as a matrimonial diriment impediment. As a crime it is the forcible carrying off, physically or morally, of a virtuous woman, or even a man. The victim is taken from a free and safe place to a place morally different and unsafe under the captor's power, intending marriage or lust.

As an impediment it is the violent taking of any woman, chaste or unchaste, from a free and safe place. The abductor detains her under his power until coerced into consenting to marry him. The crime is wider in covering men and lustful intent, while the impediment is wider in covering all women. The state suppresses the crime as a public menace, while the church guards marriage consent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abjuration:
Abjuration means denial, disavowal, or renunciation under oath. In church language it covers only a penitent heretic's renunciation of heresy on reconciliation to the Church. Such a renunciation has always been demanded by the Church, joined to fitting penance. Sometimes abjuration alone sufficed, while in other cases it was followed by the laying on of hands, by anointing, or by both.

St. Gregory the Great set out the ancient practice in a letter to Quiricus and the bishops of Iberia on reconciling Nestorians. Where heretical baptism counted as invalid, as with Paulinists, Montanists, and Eunomians, the penitent was baptized, while converts with valid baptism returned by chrism, hands, or profession of faith. Later decrees refined these forms, and the entry gathers its sources from canonists and liturgists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abortion:
Abortion is defined here, from the Latin for perishing, as the loss of fetal life. It covers a fetus dying within the mother or ejected before it can live on its own. The entry uses the word widely, for any time from conception to safe delivery. It sets the term beside miscarriage and premature birth, which medical writers use more narrowly. Viability may exist in the seventh month but cannot safely be presumed before the eighth.

Much of the piece turns on the long debate over when the embryo gains a rational soul. It weighs civil and canon law, with their technicalities, and the decisions of Roman tribunals. Those decisions claim Catholic respect, the entry notes, though they are not irreformable or definitive judgments, and strong reasons could one day prompt reconsideration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-absolution:
Absolution means the Church's remission of sin, or of sin's due punishment. Absolution proper is the act of the priest in the Sacrament of Penance by which he frees a person from sin. It presupposes contrition, confession, and at least a promise of satisfaction on the penitent's part. On the minister's part it requires valid priestly ordination and jurisdiction over the person receiving the sacrament.

The Council of Trent declares that Christ instituted Penance when, risen from the dead, he breathed on his disciples and gave them power to forgive and retain sins. The classical texts are Matthew 16:19 and 18:18 and John 20:21-23. A later part of the long entry turns to Anglican and Ritualist views, including the discussion of 1898 in which Dr. Temple wrote a pastoral on confession.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abstraction:
Abstraction names the mind's way of picking one attribute of a thing for consideration and setting the rest aside. With some writers, including the Scholastics, the selected attributes are said to be abstracted. With others, like Kant and Hamilton, the term marks the exclusion of the attributes ignored, though both work the same way. Even the simplest-seeming things are complex, and abstraction begins with sensation, as sight takes in certain qualities and taste takes in others.

All generalizations depend on abstracting a shared phase from different objects. A further step comes when the mind handles abstractions like extension, motion, species, being, and cause, which ground science and philosophy. There they are worked almost like symbols in algebra, without direct reference to the concrete. The process risks fallacy, but knowledge would not progress far without it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-accaron:
Accaron, or Ekron, was the northernmost of the five principal Philistine cities. Whether it was founded by Philistines or Hevites is not known. Juda's tribe received it first, then Dan. Juda conquered it for a time, but it fell again to the Philistines, who brought the captive ark here via Azotus and Geth.

Israel nearly reconquered it after Goliath's defeat. The city held a famous sanctuary of Beelzebub and was often denounced by the prophets, in Jeremiah, Amos, Zephaniah, and Zechariah. King Alexander Bales later gave the city to Jonathan Machabeus, and Robinson identified it with Akir village, a railway station between Jaffa and Jerusalem.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-accession:
Accession means acquiring ownership of a thing because it is joined to, or grows from, something already one's own. It happens in three ways: naturally, artificially, and from nature and industry combined. Natural accession covers animals' increase, fields' yield, and a house's rent, each belonging to its owner. The offspring of a female animal belongs to her owner, even if sired by another's male, under the rule partus sequitur ventrem.

Artificial accession covers specification, where labour on another's materials makes a new thing, adjunction, where labour and material join another's property inseparably, and blending, where equal materials of different owners are mixed. The mixed kind covers building a house on another's ground or planting in another's field. The house or trees pass to the master of the soil, with compensation to the builder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acclamation:
Acclamation, from Latin words for crying out, was the general term in Republican Rome for any shout expressing popular feeling. At weddings, funerals, and triumphs the cries took set forms, like Io Hymen at a bride's procession or Io Triumphe at a triumph. An applauded orator heard cries like bene et praeclare, where a modern crowd would say hear, hear. Under the Empire the practice grew, above all in circus and theatre.

At the emperor's entrance the audience rose, greeting him with shouts, reduced under Nero to prescribed rhythmic forms, repeated a set number of times. The senate saw the same custom invade it, where addresses of congratulation or censure took the form of carefully drafted shouts in chorus. The long entry follows acclamation into church use, coronations imperial and papal, and the laudes of the liturgy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-accusations-o:
This entry attacks a common misrepresentation of the persecution of English and Irish Catholics under Elizabeth from 1570 onward: that its victims suffered for treason, not religion. The view was officially promulgated by William Cecil, Lord Burghley, in 1583, repeated by judges and Protestant controversialists, and passed into popular histories. It still reappears among Anglican controversialists today.

The simple fact that many condemned for treason were offered life and liberty for attending Anglican worship, showing they died for religion. Yet religion and politics were so tangled that individual cases do not settle the general charge, as the Anglican historian Pollard notes. Everything centres on St. Pius V's 1570 excommunication of Elizabeth. The entry closes by insisting the treason charge against the martyrs is false and unfounded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-easton:
Adam Easton was a cardinal born at Easton in Norfolk who died at Rome on 15 September, or by other accounts 20 October, 1397. He entered the Benedictines at Norwich, probably accompanied Archbishop Langham to Rome, and, as a man of learning and ability, won a post in the Curia. Urban VI made him cardinal-priest of St. Cecilia, probably in December 1381, and in 1381 or 1382 he gained York's deanery.

In 1385 Urban imprisoned him for allegedly conspiring against the pope with five other cardinals, and stripped him of cardinalate and deanery. Boniface IX restored his cardinalate on 18 December 1389. For a time Easton returned to England, holding a Salisbury prebend later swapped for Heygham's living in Norwich.
