He wrote many works, none extant, and is credited with composing the Visitation of Our Lady's Office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adjuration:
Adjuration, from Latin adjurare, to swear by oath, is an urgent demand on another to act or desist. Coupling it with God's name or some sacred person or thing makes it more solemn and irresistible. Theologically, however, adjuration never implies an oath. It is more an earnest appeal, or a stringent command, demanding action or inaction under pain of divine visitation.

Thus when Christ stayed silent before Caiphas, the High Priest said: I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us if thou be the Christ, the Son of God. Adjuration may be deprecatory, implying deference and prayer, or imprecatory, implying authority and menace. The first may address any rational creature except the demon, while the second addresses only inferiors and the demon. A long adjuration ceremony in the Roman Ritual, rarely used without the bishop's leave, closes the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adolphe-napol:
Adolphe-Napoleon Didron, also called Didron aine, was an archaeologist and, with Viollet-le-Duc and Caumont, a principal reviver of Christian art in France. Born on 13 March 1806 at Hautvillers near Reims, his father a tax collector there, he died at Paris on 13 November 1867. After seminaries at Meaux and Reims, Paris took him in 1826, where he became a professor of history, and spent leisure hours on law, medicine, and other courses.

Reading Victor Hugo's Notre Dame de Paris sparked his taste for medieval antiquities, and in Hugo's circle in 1829 he planned a tour of Normandy, famed for historic buildings. His knowledge of saints' legends, scripture, and theology led him to iconography. Guizot named him secretary in 1835 to the committee publishing unedited documents on French history. His greatest work is the Annales archeologiques, and he also founded an archaeological library and built a glass manufactory in 1849.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adoption:
Adoption in canon law's sense is foreign to the Old Testament, this entry argues. Exodus 2:10's and Esther 2:7-15's incidents cannot count as counterexamples. The original text holds only a vague expression instead of adopted, implying merely that Moses and Esther were their benefactors' proteges. Israel's people enjoyed a similar privilege from God. The facts in Genesis 48:5, however, closely resemble adoption in its strict sense.

St. Paul introduces adoption in the New Testament, houiothesia, at Romans 8:15 and 23, Galatians 4:5, and Ephesians 1:5, applying it to sonship toward God through the indwelling Spirit of God. That Spirit gives a new, supernatural life, the life of grace. It brings the consciousness that this life comes from God, making us his children, privileged to call him Abba, Father, and to be his heirs. This adoption is consummated when bodily redemption joins the Spirit's first fruits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adoration:
Adoration, strictly, is a religious act offered to God acknowledging his supreme perfection and dominion, and the creature's dependence on him. More loosely it means reverence for anything sacred or morally excellent. The rational creature, seeing God as infinitely perfect, cannot in justice stay indifferent to that perfection. It is the source and fulfilment of all good we possess or shall possess.

This worship, given exclusively to God as God, is called by the Greek name latreia, latinized latria, best translated as adoration. Adoration differs from supplication, confession of sin, and other worship acts, since it formally means self-abasement before the Infinite and devout recognition of his transcendent excellence. The Apocalypse 7:11-12 gives an admirable example, with angels falling before the throne and adoring God. The entry also repudiates worship by mystic numbers or magical phrases as cabbala or pagan myth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adrien-greslo:
Adrien Greslon was a French missionary born at Perigueux in 1618, who died in 1697. He entered the Society of Jesus at Bordeaux on 5 November 1635. Literature and theology filled his teaching in his order's houses until 1655, when China called him as a missionary. He arrived there in 1657.

After mastering Chinese and Manchu, he went to Kiang-si province, which he calls a veritable Garden of Eden. There he remained in missionary labour until 1670, returning to France. Greslon wrote two books. One is Lives of the saintly patriarchs of the Old Testament, with reflections in Chinese. The other is a History of China under Tartar domination from 1651 to 1669, published at Paris in 1671. The entry cites Moreri's historical dictionary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-advowson:
Advowson, from Latin advocatio and Old French avoenson, is, in English law, a church or benefice's right of patronage. It is exercised by nominating a clergyman to that church or benefice. English law recognizes two kinds, presentative and collative. Until 1898 there was also a third, donative. In the early Saxon period, English parishes and dioceses were coterminous, with bishops residing alongside their clergy at their cathedral churches.

Clergy went forth to distant parts of the diocese, preaching and administering sacraments. Tithes and oblations went into a common fund for bishop and clergy, church repair, and works of piety. In time parochial churches arose, some through inhabitants' liberality, some through bishops' action. By the eighth century great lords began building and endowing churches for families, tenants, or friends. Bishops let a church's founder nominate its resident priest. Its income could also be restricted to that church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aeneas-mcdonn:
Aeneas McDonnell Dawson was an author born in Scotland on 30 July 1810. He died at Ottawa, Canada, on 29 December 1894. He studied at the Paris seminary and was ordained priest in 1835, labouring until 1840 on the Dumfries mission in Scotland, then in Edinburgh. Before Canada called him in 1855, he held charge of Fife, Kinross, and Clackmannan.

On arrival in Canada he took Ottawa's St. Andrew's parish, later becoming the cathedral's preacher. A lecturer of repute and frequent press contributor, he wrote The Temporal Sovereignty of the Pope in 1860, Ottawa's first printed and published book. He also wrote a life of St. Vincent de Paul in 1865 and Pius IX and His Time in 1880, and translated French works including de Maistre on the pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aenon:
Aenon, Greek Ainon and Vulgate Aennon, is named in John 3:23 as the place where Christ's forerunner baptized. It is described as near Salim, with much water. Where it stood is disputed, and this entry weighs the rival identifications. Barclay's hypothesis, identifying Salim with Jerusalem and choosing Wady Fara, is judged improbable.

Nor should Aenon be sought in Palestine's southern extremity, where much water would be sought in vain. Conder and others favour Ainun, northeast of ancient Salim, but that site lies as near Nabulus as Salim, and deep in Samaritan territory Jews avoided, ill-suited to the Baptist's mission. The most probable opinion places Aenon in the Jordan valley, two miles west of the stream and seven miles south of Beisan, where Van de Velde found a Salim and seven wells.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-affirmation:
Affirmation is a solemn declaration taken in legal procedure instead of the requisite oath, universal in England, Canada, and the United States. In England and Canada, statutes provide that false statements under affirmation constitute perjury just as false statements under oath do. The same provision, direct or implied, appears in the legislation of the various American states.

This right to affirm instead of swearing is generally granted out of respect for scruples, conscientious or religious, against swearing, such as Quakers, Moravians, Dunkers, and Mennonites entertain. In the court of conscience, however, an affirmation lacks an oath's standing, for the obvious reason that the intention to swear, to call God as witness, is formally excluded. The short entry thus separates legal equivalence from moral and theological standing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-age-of-reason:
Age of reason is the name for the period when persons begin to be morally responsible. As a rule this happens at about seven, though moral discernment may come earlier or much later. At this age Christians come under church laws such as Sunday Mass, abstinence on certain days, and annual confession after mortal sin.

Easter Communion literally applies to all who reach the years of discretion. In practice the church does not bind children just turned seven. At the age of reason a person may witness a marriage, sponsor at baptism or confirmation, and contract betrothal. One may receive extreme unction, take first tonsure and minor orders, and hold a simple benefice if its founder so provided. Church censures apply, though penalties generally wait until puberty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexandre-eti:
Alexandre-Étienne Choron was a French musician and teacher of music, born at Caen in October 1772 and dead in June 1834. Denied by his father the chance to study music, he mastered the theories of Rameau and his school on his own, then studied harmony with Abbé Roze and Bonesi. Through Bonesi he learned Nicolò Sala's treatise on fugue and counterpoint and Italian musical art in general.

In 1811 the government charged Choron with reorganizing the church choirs of Paris and other cities and directing music for solemn public and religious occasions. He directed the Grand Opera in 1816 for only a year. He then reopened the Conservatoire as the Royal School of Song and Declamation and founded the Royal Institution of Classical and Religious Music in 1817. The institution spread the choral works of Palestrina, Bach, and Handel. The loss of its subsidy after Charles X crippled the school and hastened Choron's death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alimentation:
Alimentation means support or maintenance: whatever sustains human life: more than food and drink — lodging, clothing, sickness care, burial. A parent must supply it to a child, legitimate or illegitimate, as a natural-law duty binding the father and claiming his estate. Husbands owe it to wives, children to parents and needy relatives, with civilized countries' common law fixing these duties.

A professed religious, incorporated into his order as a monastery son, holds aliment rights even in penance elsewhere, on trial, or after unjust expulsion. Once his vows are pronounced and accepted, his monastery owes him nothing. Clerics need a title guaranteeing honourable subsistence before major orders, by benefice, patrimony, or stable income. Mission-title priests burden dioceses, with bishops encouraging clerical funds for pecuniary help. A parish pension after infirmity resignation requires ten years' service, capped at a third of revenue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-allocution:
An allocution is a formal address, a speech from the throne, that the Pope gives on certain occasions. Only a secret consistory of cardinals alone hears it delivered. The ancient Romans used the term allocutio for a commander's speech to his troops, before or during a battle, to animate and encourage them. Taken into ecclesiastical usage, the term kept much of its original significance.

A papal allocution often stands in for a manifesto once a clash pitting the Holy See against the secular powers turns acute. It then sums up the points at issue and recounts the Holy See's efforts to preserve peace. It notes the Pope's concessions and the limit principle sets on any further ones. A secret consistory of cardinals, unlike a public one, frames the address as the Pope's own act. He speaks among his counsellors alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambition:
Ambition is the undue craving for honour, from Rome's candidates going about, ambire, soliciting votes. Honour manifests reverence for a person's worth or good qualities, and excessive desire for distinction sins not by wishing respect but by seeking it without sound reason's mandates. The disorder takes three chief forms. One wants homage for merit one lacks. Another forgets that credited goods are God's not one's own. A third absorbs himself in esteem instead of using excellence for others' welfare.

Ambition itself is not mortal sin, but becomes so through its means, as simony seeking church dignity, or through harm to another. It also acts as a canonical impediment for those who take elevation to church dignity for granted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ammon:
Ammon, Egyptian Amun or Amen, the hidden one, Hebrew Amon, Greek Ammon, was the Egyptian pantheon's supreme divinity. Chief god of Thebes at first, his worship later predominated in Egypt and spread to Libya and Ethiopia, Thebes remaining its centre, called Ne-Amun, city of Amun, Hebrew No-Amon. Jeremiah calls him Ammon of No, that is, of Thebes.

Under several names he bore different attributes. Under the name Ammon-Ra he was the sun god, chiefly worshipped at Thebes. As Khem or Min, reproduction's god. As Khnum, creator of all things and maker of gods and men, ram-headed or ram-horned, he was best known thus to classical writers. Khnum's chief temple stood in the Ammon oasis, now Siwah, where Alexander worshipped him. Greeks and Romans matched Ammon to Zeus or Jupiter, naming Thebes Diospolis, City of Zeus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce:
Macon, in Burgundy, was once capital of the Maconnais and now in the department of Saone-et-Loire. It became a city in the fifth century, when it was cut off from Aeduan territory. Christianity reached it early from Lyons, and Hugh, Archbishop of Lyons in the eleventh century, called Macon the eldest daughter of the Church of Lyons.

The bishopric came later than expected. Late in the fifth century it was still a bishop of Lyons who fed the famine-stricken people of Macon. Clovis seized the city at the end of that century, routing Arianism and foreshadowing Frankish rule. Duchesne traces the see, suffragan to Lyons, to a Merovingian understanding after the Burgundian state fell. Its first known bishop is Saint Placidus, from 538 to 555, followed by saints such as Florentinus. The see ended with the French Revolution, and its title now rests with the Bishop of Autun.

Vaison was suppressed by the Concordat of 1801, and its land now lies in the dioceses of Avignon and Valence. Its oldest bishop is Daphnus, who attended the Council of Arles in 314, though an earlier name, Saint Albinus, was placed here in error. Bishops include Saint Quinidius, from 556 to 579, who resisted the patrician Mummolus. Joseph-Marie de Suares, from 1633 to 1666, died at Rome as Vatican librarian and left many works.

Vaison, capital of the Voconces, mattered in Celtic and Roman times, then passed to Visigothic and Austrasian rule. In the twelfth century counts of Provence and bishops, each holding half the town, quarrelled, until a treaty in 1251, negotiated by the future Clement IV, ended the dispute. The apse of Saint Quenin's church dates from the eighth century, among the oldest in France. The cathedral dates from the eleventh. Councils on Gallican discipline met in 442 and 529, the latter under Saint Caesarius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andre-guijon:
Andre Guijon, bishop and orator, was born in November 1548 at Autun and died in September 1631. His father Jean Guijon, a physician and Oriental scholar, travelled in the East and brought back to France an eleventh-century Greek manuscript copy of the New Testament. Three brothers, Jacques, Jean, and Hugues, all lawyers, writers, and scholars, shared the family's fame.

Philibert de la Mare, counsellor at the Parliament of Dijon, gathered the four brothers' chief works into one quarto volume of 612 pages in 1658. Its title was Jacobi, Joannis, Andreae et Hugonis fratrum Guionorum opera varia. It held both prose and Latin poems. Andre served as vicar-general to Cardinal de Joyeuse, then became Bishop of Autun. He travelled to Rome for consecration and returned to France in 1586. His Remontrance to the Parlement of Normandy on fulminating sentences survives, while his funeral praise of Pierre Jeannin has not been preserved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andre-terraso:
Andre Terrason, a French preacher, was born at Lyons in 1669 and died at Paris in 1723. The eldest son of a Lyons court councillor, he entered the Oratory and gave himself to preaching, winning high reputation. He preached the Lenten sermons of 1717 before Louis XIV, then at the Court of Lorraine, and twice in Paris with great success. The last series broke his health and led to his death.

His diction, aided by outward action, joined nobility and simplicity with force and freedom from artifice. Good judgment kept him from mere brilliance and clever tricks, though he could seem cold, perhaps from Jansenist leanings. About fifty discourses, mostly Lenten lectures, survive in a Paris edition of four volumes from 1726 and 1736. His brother Gaspard, born in 1680 and dead in 1752, also preached for the Oratory. Jansenist writings brought condemnation, loss of the pulpit, and nine years confined at Vincennes and Argenteuil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andreas-of-ra:
Almost everything known about Andreas of Ratisbon, also called Andreas of Regensburg, comes from scanty details in his own works. This historian of the later fourteenth and earlier fifteenth century was ordained priest at Eichstätt in 1405. In 1410 he joined the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine at Ratisbon, where he gave himself to historical study.

His main works are De statu urbis Ratisbon, antiquo et de variis Haeresibus, and the Chronicon Generale. A third, the Chronicon de Ducibus Bavariae, runs to 1439 and gained him the title of the Bavarian Livy. He later turned it into German and carried it on to 1452. He stands as the chief forerunner of Aventinus, the famous Bavarian historiographer, and his chronicles remain a source for Bavarian and Ratisbon history in his time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-gordon:
A Benedictine monk and physicist, Andrew Gordon was born at Cofforach in Scotland in 1712 and died at Erfurt in 1751. After wide travel on the Continent, he became a Benedictine, and in 1737 the University of Erfurt made him professor of natural philosophy. His works on electricity soon won him considerable reputation.

Those works on electricity appeared in 1744, 1745, and 1751-52. Where von Guericke had used a sulphur ball and Newton a glass globe, Gordon put in a glass cylinder, making an efficient frictional machine. Two further inventions stand out. One is the light metallic star on a sharp pivot, its pointed ends bent at right angles to the rays, commonly called the electrical whirl. The other is the device known as the electric chimes. The whirl matters most as an electrostatic reaction motor, the earliest of its kind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelique-bul:
Angelique Bullion was born in Paris at the start of the seventeenth century, daughter of Guichard Favre and Madeleine Brulart de Sillery. Her husband Claude de Bullion served Louis XIII as Keeper of the Seals and Superintendent of Finances. Each year Cardinal Richelieu rewarded his intelligent and disinterested administration with a bonus of 100,000 livres. When he died in 1640, her four children were well provided for, and she followed the advice of the Recollet Father Rapin.

In 1641-42 she gave 60,000 livres to found Ville-Marie, now Montreal, Canada. In 1643 she founded and endowed a Hotel-Dieu in honour of Saint Joseph. Mademoiselle Mance had begun it at Ville-Marie in 1642, and in 1657-59 it was entrusted to the Sisters of Saint Joseph. She gave more than 20,000 livres for defence against the Iroquois, helping to save New France from destruction. In her donation deeds she insisted on being named only as an unknown benefactress.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anselm-of-lao:
Known from his learning as Doctor Scholasticus, Anselm of Laon died on 15 July 1117 as one of the Middle Ages' famous theologians. He learned at Bec abbey under Saint Anselm of Canterbury, who introduced him to the new scholastic theology. From 1076 he taught with much distinction at Paris, working with William of Champeaux to establish the university there. Near the end of the eleventh century he went back to Laon and set up a theological school.

That school grew so famous that Abelard, then thirty and teaching philosophy at Paris, moved to Laon to study theology under him. Anselm's chief work is the Glossa interlinearis, a commentary on the whole Vulgate, published at Antwerp in 1634. With Walafrid Strabo's Glossa ordinaria, it counts as one of the Middle Ages' two chief works of biblical interpretation. His known writings appear in Migne, Patrologia Latina, CLXII, 1187-1660.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-parki:
Anthony Parkinson, historian, was born in England in 1667 and died there on 30 January 1728. Douai's Franciscan Convent made him professor of philosophy in 1692, and the next year approved him for preaching and hearing confessions. He reached the English missions in 1695. Warwick's Franciscans had him as president from 1698 to 1701, Birmingham's from 1701 to 1710, and he served as Definitor of the province from 1707 to 1710.

He was also nominal guardian of Worcester from 1704 to 1707 and of Oxford from 1710 to 1713, and twice he governed the hidden English Province as provincial, in 1713-16 and 1722-25. In that role he attended the Order's General Chapter at Rome in May 1723. His chief work, the Collectanea Anglo-Minoritica, gathers the antiquities of the English Franciscans, or Gray Friars, in two parts, with an appendix on the English Nuns of Saint Clare. It appeared at London in 1726, and some unedited manuscripts of his survive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antidoron:
Antidoron, Greek for a gift instead of, is what remains of the loaves from which portions are cut for consecration in the Greek Mass. Those remains are collected on a salver in the sanctuary and kept on the prothesis, or side-altar, through Mass. They are cut into small fragments. When Mass ends and the celebrant has retired, the deacon, or the priest where there is no deacon, carries the salver out through the royal doors.

Before the iconostasis, he gives each fasting worshipper a fragment of blessed bread, eaten before leaving church. Russians, Greeks, and Syrian Christians of Saint Thomas on the Malabar coast regularly follow this giving. The entry also traces the custom's history. An early Western mention appears in Saint Augustine's letter to Januarius, and it spread in the East in the ninth and tenth centuries. It served as a substitute for those unable to receive Communion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiphon:
Antiphon, Greek antiphonon, sounding against, alternate chant: an antiphon is one or more psalm verses or Scripture sentences. They are sung or recited before and after each psalm and the Magnificat at Matins and Vespers. The antiphon text holds the psalm's fundamental thought and viewpoint. It gives the key to the psalm's liturgical and mystical meaning for the feast. More widely, the name also covered the early Mass Introit, Offertory, and Communion.

Of the psalm itself, originally sung complete, only one verse and the doxology survive for any Introit, so the antiphon is now paramount. Antiphon melodies, especially before Vesper psalms, are generally simple, often syllabic, forming a prelude to the psalm tune. Vesper antiphons are almost universally sung to Gregorian melodies, while Mass antiphons have fed figured settings by polyphony masters and modern writers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-touro:
Antoine Touron, a French Dominican historian born in 1686, wrote twenty-nine volumes on his order and its saints. After teaching philosophy and theology at Toulouse, he gave his later years to biography, history, and defence of the faith. His name became illustrious in his order, though little was written about the man himself.

His best work told the life of Saint Thomas Aquinas, and he also wrote lives of Saint Dominic and other Dominican worthies. A general history of America from his pen was in truth a church history of the New World. Later Dominican historians drew freely on his work, and the entry calls it essential for students of the order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apolytikion:
An apolytikion is a dismissal prayer or hymn said or chanted at the end of the Greek liturgy and at other moments during Matins and Vespers. First sung at the end of Vespers, it resembles the Roman collect or post-communion prayer in changing with each feast day of the year and honouring that feast's subject. Each apolytikion thus sums up the day's celebration in a short, set text.

Two examples show the form at work. For Christmas it hails Christ's birth as light of knowledge rising on the world, teaching star worshippers by a star to adore the Sun of Righteousness. For the Annunciation it calls the day the crowning of salvation and the unveiling of a mystery from eternity, ending with Gabriel's greeting to Mary. The entry is a brief guide to a hymn that closes worship by naming the feast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-suc:
Apostolic succession is the claim that bishops today stand in an unbroken line from the apostles. This article argues that the Catholic Church holds it while separate churches do not, above all the Anglican church. Apostolicity as a mark of the true church is treated elsewhere; here the task is proof. To succeed means to follow in office, as Victoria followed William IV, so Roman pontiffs, the article argues, follow Peter in place and function.

Proof therefore turns on showing that Peter came to Rome and ended his pontificate there, and that later bishops of Rome held his office in the church. Once the question passed from partisan theologians to impartial historians in the last half century, the article says, it found a solution no scholar now dares to dispute. Readers get the Roman case stated as history and logic, with Anglican claims tested against it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-approbation:
Approbation is the act by which a bishop or other lawful superior grants a cleric the actual exercise of ministry. Full church power given by Christ to the apostles resides solely in bishops. From the bishop, centre of the Christian community, flow government and care of souls, the teaching of doctrine and giving of sacraments. Parish priests, their vicars, and co-workers help the bishop in pastoral ministry, holding power by episcopal delegation through many differing acts.

Permanent fitness and appointment to church service in general come through holy orders. Actual appointment to ministry in a set sphere comes from conferring a church office, recognized as a permanent charge that should follow special proof of fitness. Approbation is the further step that lets an ordained and appointed priest actually exercise ministry in a given place. The entry untangles office, orders, and permission in church law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-appropriation:
Appropriation means attributing a special character to a person or thing. In theology it is used of the three Persons of the Trinity, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It consists in assigning certain names, qualities, or works to one Person in preference to the others, though not to their exclusion. The qualities belong essentially to all three, yet revelation leads us to link some traits more clearly to one Person.

Thus the Father is marked above all by omnipotence, or all power, the Son by wisdom, and the Holy Spirit by love. Yet all three possess equal power, wisdom, and love by nature. Appropriation is not arbitrary labelling, the article argues, but a way of speaking that follows how each Person is revealed in Scripture. Readers get a precise term for a common habit of Christian speech.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arason-jon:
Jón Arason, the last Catholic bishop of Iceland before Protestantism took hold, was born in 1484 and died on 7 November 1550. Consecrated bishop of Hólar in 1524 by his archbishop at Nidaros, now Trondheim in Norway. He was a typical Icelander of extraordinary talent, poorly versed in Latin and openly careless of celibacy law. Devoted to the church's cause, he acted more as a war chief than a bishop.

When Christian III of Denmark ordered a change of faith in Iceland in 1538, Arason joined Bishop Ögmundur Pálsson of Skálholt in resistance. Ögmundur, old and blind, was seized by the royal leader Kristoffer Huitfeldt and died aboard ship bound for Denmark in 1542, and Lutheran bishops succeeded him. Leadership of Catholics then fell to Arason, who held the defence until 1548, when Skálholt's see was remade on the new pattern.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arbitration:
Arbitration, in general, is a method of settling differences by referring them to a disinterested outsider's judgment. The parties agree in advance to accept that outsider's decision as binding in some way. The whole process covers reference of issues, investigation, decision, and acceptance or enforcement. It is invited where persons of equal or nearly equal power who disagree obstinately over a right, privilege, or duty, refusing to settle it themselves.

Its assumptions are that self-interest and obstinacy dull each side's sense of fairness, and that a capable neutral judge will come closer to justice and equity. Its motive lies in society's wish to remove force as the sanction of right and to bring ethical principles into dispute settlement. Courts, rules, and custom frame the practice, and the long article traces arbitration from private quarrels to public and international disputes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archange-de-l:
Archange de Lyon, whose birth name was Michael Desgranges, was a Capuchin preacher born at Lyons on 2 March 1736 and dead there on 13 October 1822. He joined the Capuchins in 1751 and served as lector, or reader, in theology toward the end of the 18th century. In 1789, after preaching against the States General, the French assembly, he was forced to leave France.

He returned in secret to Lyons about 1796 and became curé, or parish priest, of the Carthusian parish. When his order was re-established at Chambéry he resumed his habit there in 1818. He gave himself to preaching missions and stations across Savoy and France until, in 1821, he could reopen his order's former convent at Crest in Valence. Regarded as the restorer of the Capuchins in France, he also wrote on Jews and Christians, Catholic education, and Chateaubriand's Genius of Christianity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archdeacon:
An archdeacon held an ecclesiastical office dating to antiquity and, until the fifteenth century, of high importance in diocesan administration, above all in the West. The term first appears in the fourth century, in Optatus of Mileve's account of the Donatist schism, written about 370. Toward the end of the fourth and start of the fifth century it grows frequent in Latin and Greek writers.

Other names sometimes marked the office, such as the Greek phrase for head deacon of the choir, and the title soon gained fixity as the archdeacon's duties sharpened. The entry follows a deputy who stood beside the bishop, managed diocesan business, and slowly built a jurisdiction of his own, before later reforms cut that power back. Readers get the biography of an office, not of a person.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arni-thorlaks:
Árni Thorlaksson, an Icelandic bishop born in Iceland in 1237 and dead at Bergen in 1297, visited Norway as a deacon in 1262 and befriended Bishop Magnus. Ordained priest, he was soon made administrator of the Hólar diocese and stood out for zeal over celibacy law. He assisted the bishop of Skálholt in 1267 and succeeded him, consecrated in 1269 at Nidaros, now Trondheim, in Norway.

Back in Iceland he set about organizing church administration. Since Norway's hierarchy was regulated in 1152, Iceland's bishops had been suffragans of Nidaros's metropolitan, and in 1264 Iceland grew still more dependent politically on Norway's king. Until then Iceland had been a republic ruled by the Althing, an assembly of ninety-six councillors, forty-eight chiefs, and a law announcer as president. Its chiefs had built churches on their lands and taken church roles with them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-artemon:
Artemon, or Artemas, is named as leader of an anti-Trinitarian sect at Rome in the third century, of whose life little is known for certain. Eusebius calls him a forerunner of Paul of Samosata, a view confirmed by acts of a council at Antioch in 264, which link the two names in communion and support. Eusebius and Theodoret describe his teaching as denying Christ's divinity and asserting he was a mere man. They also accuse him of falsifying Scripture and appealing to tradition for his errors.

Both authors cite refutations: Eusebius an untitled work, and Theodoret one called The Little Labyrinth, attributed to the Roman priest Caius and recently to Hippolytus, supposed author of the Philosophumena. The entry is a brief dossier on a shadowy teacher, known only through opponents who answered him and through a council that tied his name to a better-known heretic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arthur-richar:
Arthur Richard Dillon, a French prelate, was born at St-Germain-en-Laye near Paris in 1721 and died in London in 1806. The fifth-born son of Arthur Dillon, an Irish officer outlawed as a Jacobite who passed into French service, he was educated for the church and became curé of Elan near Mézières. He became vicar general of Pontoise in 1747, bishop of Evreux in 1753, archbishop of Toulouse in 1758, and archbishop of Narbonne and primate of France in 1763.

A man of wide sympathies and varied accomplishments, and a Catholic, he nevertheless applauded recognition of Protestant marriages in the Clergy Assembly of 1788. He presided over that assembly. His Narbonne appointment made him viceroy of Languedoc, where he won popularity not only as bishop but as promoter of public works: roads, bridges, canals, harbours. Rather than take the revolutionary constitutional oath, he emigrated to Coblenz with French nobles, then to London.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ascalon:
Ascalon was a titular see of Palestine whose bishops' list from 351 to 930 or 940 is given in Gams. It was one of the Philistines' five chief cities, named in Joshua 13:3. Its site on the sea shore between Gaza and Jamnia rendered it a stronghold, held by Arabs after their seventh-century conquest.

Crusaders later took the city, but Sultan Baybars destroyed it in 1270 and blocked its port to stop it ever falling again into Christian hands. Its extensive ruins still stand, presenting a scene of mournful desolation. The entry compresses a Philistine city, an Arab stronghold, and a Crusader prize into a short note on a place whose harbour was deliberately closed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ascension:
The Ascension is Christ's elevation into heaven by his own power before his disciples on the fortieth day after his rising. It is told in Mark 16:19, Luke 24:51, plus the first chapter of Acts. Though its place is not distinctly stated, Acts suggests Mount Olivet, since disciples return to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, near Jerusalem within a Sabbath day's walk.

Tradition consecrated that spot as the Mount of Ascension, and Christian devotion raised a basilica over it. Helena built the first memorial, destroyed by Persians in 614, restored in the eighth century, destroyed again, then rebuilt a second time by Crusaders. Muslims also destroyed that church, leaving only the octagonal structure enclosing the stone said to carry the imprint of Christ's foot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aston:
Aston is the name of several English Catholics of note gathered in one entry. Sir Arthur Aston, of a knightly family, was an able officer in Charles I's army and governor of Oxford. He was made governor of Drogheda in Ireland in 1649. He was killed at the siege of that town by Cromwell's forces, his brains knocked out with his wooden limb during the massacre that followed its capture. Murphy's Cromwell in Ireland relates the account.

Herbert Aston, a poet born at Chelsea in 1614 and third son of Walter, the first Lord Aston of Forfar, accompanied his father to Madrid on his father's second embassy in 1635. He authored Tixall Poetry, collected in 1658. Walter Aston, Herbert's father and son of Sir Edward Aston from Tixall in Staffordshire, educated under Sir Edward Coke, was sent as one of two ambassadors to Spain in 1619. Their task was to negotiate a royal marriage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-attrition:
Attrition, also called imperfect contrition, means sorrow for sin driven by motives other than love of God. The Council of Trent defined contrition as sorrow of soul and hatred of sin, with a firm purpose not to sin again. When that hatred springs from love of an offended God, the sorrow is perfect contrition. When it springs from fear of hell, loss of heaven, or the ugliness of guilt, it is attrition, from Latin for wearing away by rubbing.

Trent taught that such fear-born sorrow is a gift of God and an impulse of the Holy Spirit. It readies the sinner for grace in Penance, though it cannot by itself justify. The entry traces the debate that followed: must attrition include some beginning of love of God to work in the sacrament? Pope Alexander VII left that question open in 1667. Benedict XIV later taught that it remained undecided.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auguste-caray:
Auguste Carayon was a French author and bibliographer born at Saumur in 1813 who died at Poitiers in 1874. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1848 and served at times as librarian and procurator, the order's business manager. Between 1864 and 1874 he edited many historical works. The entry calls him a leading authority on the history of his order, above all in New France, the French lands in North America.

His chief works include a historical bibliography of the Company of Jesus, published at Paris in 1864. His eighteen-volume Documents inedits on the Company appeared at Poitiers between 1863 and 1874. Other titles cover the first Jesuit mission to Canada, the Jesuits' banishment from Louisiana, and the prisons of the Marquis de Pombal. He also wrote devotional treatises between 1854 and 1863.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auguste-nelat:
Auguste Nelaton was a famous French surgeon born in Paris in 1807 who died there in 1873. He graduated in medicine in 1836 with a thesis on tuberculous disease of the bones. He became agrege, a certified teacher, in 1839 after a treatise on tumors of the breast. In 1851 he became professor of clinical surgery, and his thesis won wide notice and a German translation.

On the staff of the St Louis Hospital he devised new operations, first proposed tying both ends of arteries in hemorrhage, and advanced plastic, abdominal, and pelvic surgery. His probe with a porcelain knob located a bullet in Garibaldi's ankle in 1862. He was praised as a great teacher and a master operator. His fame as a writer rests on his five-volume Elements of Surgical Pathology, and he became a senator of the French Empire in 1868.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-avicebron:
Avicebron, properly Salamo ben Jehuda ben Gebirol, was a Jewish poet of religion, a moralist, and a philosopher. He was born at Malaga in 1020 or 1021, died at Saragossa in 1070, and spent his life there on philosophy and religious verse. The Schoolmen, mistaking him for an Arabian, called him Avicebron. His chief philosophical work, written in Arabic, reached Hebrew as Mekor Chayim and Latin as Fons Vitae, the Fountain of Life.

His thought joins traditional Neo-Platonism to the religious teaching of the Old Testament. From Neo-Platonic sources he took emanation: from God flows the Universal Intelligence, from it the World-Soul, and from the World-Soul comes Nature, the direct source of material things. Later Schoolmen split over him. Dominican teachers, including Aquinas, refuted him on this point. Duns Scotus, Alexander of Hales, and other Franciscans adopted his doctrine as part of their theory of angelic nature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-avignon:
Avignon, written Avennio in ancient texts, takes its name from the house or clan Avennius. The Cavari, a Celtic people, founded it, and it became the center of a Phocaean colony from Marseilles. Under Rome it ranked among the flourishing cities of Gallia Narbonensis, and during the barbarian inroads it passed to Goths, Burgundians, Ostrogoths, and Frankish kings of Austrasia. Saracens seized it in 736, and Charles Martel drove them out.

When Boso became King of Provence in 879, Avignon left Frankish rule, and in 1033 it passed with Arles to the empire under Conrad II. Distant German rulers let the city set up a republic between 1135 and 1146, while counts of Forcalquier, Toulouse, and Provence held only nominal sway. During the crusade against the Albigenses, its citizens shut the gates on Louis VIII and the legate, then yielded after a siege in 1226. The entry continues through later centuries with a source list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-babylon: Babylon is the curial title of a Latin archbishopric, and also of a Chaldean patriarchate and of a Syrian archbishopric. The whole entry is a single line, giving those three titles and nothing more. No history, holder, place, or date is described for any of the three titles. Readers seeking more must look to the articles on those sees themselves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-de-mont:
Baron de Montyon was a famous French philanthropist, born at Paris in 1733, who died there in 1820. Son of a wealthy Exchequer official, he became king's advocate at the Châtelet, earning the name Grenadier of the Bar for inflexible integrity. He entered the Great Council in 1758, became master of petitions in 1760, and intendant of Auvergne in 1767. There his liberality to the poor endeared him, spending some twenty thousand francs yearly of his own income on needy families.

Refusing to install Maupeou's magistrates, he was moved to Provence and La Rochelle, then recalled to Paris as councillor of State in 1775. He also wrote on economics, winning Academy distinction for his Eloge de Michel de l'Hôpital in 1777. His great concern was anonymous philanthropy, and he founded Academy prizes to reward virtue and works useful to morals. His will left the bulk of his property to Paris hospitals and homes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beatific-visi: The beatific vision is the immediate knowledge of God enjoyed in Heaven by angels and the souls of the just. It is called vision because it differs from the mediate knowledge of God that minds can reach in this life. Since beholding God face to face gives created intelligence perfect happiness, the vision is called beatific.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beatification:
Beatification and canonization are traced by some writers to pagan apotheosis, a view Benedict XIV refutes at the outset of his classic work. He shows substantial differences between the institutions, so no clear thinker need confuse or derive one from the other. Apotheosis was the imperial family's exclusive privilege, often resting on one witness's tale of an eagle or peacock carrying the spirit heavenward. No regard went to virtues or deeds: Romulus was deified by his slayers, Poppaea by Nero after he kicked her to death.

The entry then traces canonization's own history apart from apotheosis, through its processes and decrees. Its closing pages publish the costs of Leo XIII's canonizations of Anthony Maria Zaccaria and Peter Fourier. Decoration, lights, and labor alone ran 152,840 lire, and the whole totaled 221,849 lire, about $42,817 in 1913 money. The figures were published by Diomede Panici, then Secretary of the Congregation of Rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-de-mo:
Bernard de Montfaucon, a French Benedictine scholar, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1655 at Soulatge in Languedoc, he died in Paris in 1741 at St-Germain-des-Prés. Trained first for the army at Perpignan, he left soldiering after his father's death and joined the Benedictines, turning to ancient languages and manuscripts.

His edition of St. Athanasius, issued in 1698 with brother scholars, won wide praise, and Italian library journeys widened his command of Greek, Hebrew, Syriac, and Coptic. As curator of coins at St-Germain, he joined numismatics, the study of coins, to patristics, the study of the Church Fathers. The entry presents a founder of modern manuscript scholarship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berthold-of-r:
Berthold of Ratisbon, a Franciscan preacher, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born about 1210, probably to a well-to-do Ratisbon family named Sachs, he died in 1272 as the most powerful preacher of repentance of his century. Classical learning in his sermons and knowledge of secular life suggest a mature man before he entered the monastery.

In 1246 a papal legate made him inspector of the Niedermünster convent, the first fixed date of his life. Crowds flocked to his open-air sermons calling hearers to penance, and his German sermons survive as models of popular preaching. The entry presents a friar whose voice moved towns to tears.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethdagon: Bethdagon is the name of two cities in Palestine. One, in the tribe of Judah's lowland between the hills and the sea below Joppa, has an uncertain site. The other, in the tribe of Asher near Zebulun, is thought to be Tell Daouk, southeast of Acre. The entry is a short note distinguishing the two towns of one name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biblical-acco:
Biblical accommodation, the use of Scripture words in a sense different from the author's, receives a careful entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It first defines the practice, then shows it in Scripture itself, then sets rules for its use. A sinner quoting Eve's serpent deceived me to excuse his own fault is the opening example.

New Testament reuse of Old Testament words with a changed meaning, and mistranslations born of double Latin meanings, illustrate the borders of the practice. The entry allows accommodation in preaching and devotion when the new sense is clearly not claimed as the author's. It is a guide to quoting Scripture honestly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biblical-intr:
Biblical introduction, the science preliminary to studying Scripture, receives a long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. The term covers both a branch of learning and the books that teach it. Its general aim is to give students the knowledge needed for sound interpretation of the Old and New Testaments.

Because the Bible is inspired as well as ancient, its introduction must also treat inspiration, integrity, and truthfulness, questions no introduction to a merely human book must face. General introduction covers all books together, while special introduction treats each book alone. The entry maps the doorway every serious Bible reader must pass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bilocation:
Bilocation asks whether one body can be in two places at once. The question is treated in a philosophical entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It grows from the Eucharist, in which Christ is truly present in every consecrated host, wherever it lies. Thinkers sort out kinds of presence: by place, by power, and by the sacrament itself.

Catholic thinkers hold bilocation against the known laws of matter, yet not beyond God's power as such. Tales of saints seen in two places are weighed against these fine points. The entry is a careful piece of thought built on a point of faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bination:
Bination, a priest's saying Mass twice in one day, receives a historical entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. In the earliest years public Mass came only on Sundays, then on Wednesdays and Fridays, with Saturday added especially in the East. Augustine, who died in 430, reports Mass on Sundays alone in his own time in some places.

Custom multiplied Masses on great feasts, with three on Easter and three on Christmas, and the pope saying two on the feast of Peter and Paul. Innocent III ended the tangle, ruling one Mass daily for a simple priest, Christmas excepted, and Honorius III spread the rule to dignitaries. The entry traces a discipline settling into law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-hugh-farin:
Blessed Hugh Faringdon, also called Cook, abbot and martyr of Reading, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Probably born at Faringdon in Berkshire, he died at Reading in 1539. Elected Abbot of Reading in 1520, he hosted Henry VIII in 1521, served as royal chaplain, and sat in Parliament from 1523.

In 1536 he signed Convocation's articles at the king's desire, yet he would not surrender his abbey to Henry's commissioners. Tried for treason on a charge of aiding rebels, he was hanged, drawn, and quartered at Reading with two companions. The entry presents an abbot who paid for loyalty to his house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-james-thom: Blessed James Thompson, also known as James Hudson, was a martyr born in or near York, where he lived most of his life and died on 28 November 1582. He reached Allen's college at Reims in 1580 and, though so ill he could hardly stand, was ordained at Soissons within twelve days in May 1581. Sent to England that August, he was arrested at York within days and confessed his priesthood before the Council of the North.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-felto:
Blessed John Felton, a martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His birth date and place are unknown, and he was executed in St. Paul's Churchyard, London, on 8 August 1570. His crime was fixing a copy of Pope Pius V's bull excommunicating Queen Elizabeth to the London bishop's palace gates on the night of 24 May.

His daughter Frances Salisbury tells the story: her father, a small, dark, wealthy Norfolk gentleman living at Bermondsey Abbey, had brought bull copies from Calais. One copy, given to William Mellowes, was found, and racking forced the name out. Felton, thrice racked in the Tower, confessed and gloried in his deed from the first, and died uttering the name of Jesus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-marie-de-l:
Blessed Marie de l'Incarnation, known in the world as Madame Acarie, founder of Carmel in France, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born Barbara Avrillot in Paris in 1566 to a high bourgeois family, she died at Pontoise in 1618. Schooled with the Poor Clares of Longchamp, she kept a cloister vocation through a life in the world.

Married life brought charity to Paris hospitals and a house visited by Vincent de Paul and Francis de Sales, her director for six months. Reading Ribera's life of St. Teresa late in 1601 fired her to bring the Discalced Carmelites to France. The entry presents a laywoman who founded a contemplative order from her parlour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-richard-fe:
Blessed Richard Fetherston, priest and martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Chaplain to Catherine of Aragon and schoolmaster to her daughter Mary, he died at Smithfield in 1540. A doctor of sacred theology, he defended Catherine's marriage before legates Wolsey and Campeggio in the divorce case, writing a treatise against Henry's divorce that no longer survives.

In Convocation in 1529 he was among the few who refused the Act of Supremacy's premises. Attainder for treason followed, and he was hanged, drawn, and quartered. The entry presents a court theologian who would not sign away his queen's marriage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-robert-joh: Blessed Robert Johnson, a martyr, was born in Shropshire and entered the German College at Rome in 1571. He took priestly orders at Brussels, through the English College at Douai, in April 1576, and sailed at once for England. A Rome pilgrimage in 1579 came before his return in 1580. He was jailed in the Poultry Counter, then the Tower, where he was racked in December. He was condemned at Queen's Bench in November.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-thomas-joh:
Blessed Thomas Johnson, a Carthusian martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. He died in Newgate gaol, London, on 20 September 1537. On 18 May 1537 the London Charterhouse monks were ordered to take the Oath of Supremacy, and Johnson with two other priests and a deacon refused, as did six lay brothers.

Sent to Newgate on 29 May, they were chained standing to posts with hands tied behind them and left to starve, though Margaret Clement smuggled them food until the gaoler feared discovery. Companions died through June, but Johnson lived until September, and Horne survived for a later execution. Leo XIII beatified all ten Carthusians in December 1886.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-john-:
Blessed John Houghton, protomartyr of Henry VIII's persecution, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Essex in 1487, he died at Tyburn in 1535. Cambridge degrees in law and divinity led to ordination in 1501 and the London Charterhouse novitiate in 1505, with profession in 1516.

Sacristan, procurator, prior of Beauvale, prior of London from 1531, and provincial visitor, he led his house against the oath of supremacy. A month in the Tower with Humphrey Middlemore ended in trial and the gruesome death of hanging, drawing, and quartering. The entry presents the first Carthusian to die for the old faith.

Blessed John Nelson, an English Jesuit martyr, was born at Skelton near York in 1534 and died at Tyburn on 3 February 1578. He went to Douai in 1573, followed by two of his four brothers into the priesthood, and was ordained at Binche in 1576. Sent to London's mission that November, he was arrested on 1 December 1577 while saying Matins at night and committed to Newgate as a suspected Papist, then executed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bonaventura-b:
Bonaventura Baron, an Irish Franciscan theologian, philosopher, and Latin writer, defended the Scotist system from Rome's Irish College of Saint Isidore. Born at Clonmel in 1610, he was nephew to Luke Wadding, founder of the college. He studied philosophy at Louvain, taught theology at Saint Isidore's, and published widely on theology, philosophy, and history.

Leaving Rome about 1651 after trouble with the master of the sacred palace, he moved through Schwaz, Salzburg, Hungary, Paris, Wurzburg, and Lyons. He declined the Archbishopric of Cashel, became historiographer to Cosimo de' Medici in 1676, and joined Florence's academy. His last work traced the Order for Redemption of Captives from 1198 to 1297, and he died at Rome in 1696.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boniface-asso:
The Boniface Association, one of Germany's most successful Catholic societies, supports Catholics scattered among Protestants. Suggested by Dollinger at the 1849 Ratisbon congress, it maintains churches, missions, and schools where Catholics are few. A general committee at Paderborn guides it, while local committees control their own gifts and choose their objects with their bishop's approval.

About $9,250,000 has been collected since its founding, and some 2,600 churches have been built or aided. A collecting branch begun in 1885 gathers tin-foil, stamps, coins, and other trifles, raising over $625,000 for orphanages and first-communion training. A university branch, founded at Munster in 1867, counted thirty-six groups with 750 members by 1907. Its work reached places where Catholics lived far from any parish of their own.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boston:
Boston's archdiocese covers five Massachusetts counties across 2,465 square miles, holding 850,000 Catholics where its first bishop found barely one hundred. Erected on 8 April 1808 and made an archbishopric in 1875, it once ruled all New England. Eight dioceses now share that ground with about 2,100,000 Catholics, growth driven by immigrants drawn to New England mills.

Irish came first, then French Canadians, Italians, Poles, Portuguese, and peoples from nearly every land. Early sections trace Irish emigration in three waves from 1621 to 1775, warning that not all were Catholic, and recall Ann Glover, hanged at Boston in 1688 after Cotton Mather's witchcraft mania. Later parts profile bishops from Cheverus to O'Connell, with social progress and statistics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brian-walton:
Brian Walton, editor of Walton's Polyglot Bible, gave England its first book published by subscription. Born near York in 1600 and schooled at Cambridge, he served as curate, schoolmaster, and rector of Saint Martin's Orgar in London, with Sandon added in 1636. Accused of popish innovations, he lost both rectories in 1641 and spent a year in prison.

Free again, he planned at Royalist Oxford a Bible in many tongues side by side. After Oxford fell in 1646, he issued his prospectus in London in 1652 at ten pounds a set and soon raised nine thousand pounds. Aided by Castell, Pococke, Hyde, and other scholars, he edited the Polyglot himself and defended a liberal view of the Hebrew text against John Owen's narrow doctrine of vowel-points and accents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brook-of-cedr:
The Brook of Cedron, the ravine east of Jerusalem, runs from the Tombs of the Judges to the Dead Sea. The city lies on one side of it and the Mount of Olives on the other. Its name likely comes from a root meaning dark, its exact sense unknown. The valley begins northwest of Jerusalem, a mile and a quarter out, bending past the Tombs of the Kings. It deepens to 100 feet deep and 400 feet broad by Saint Stephen's Gate.

Olive trees shade its bed, an old bridge crosses it, and below lie Gethsemani, the Virgin's tomb church, and the tombs of Josaphat, Absalom, and James. Farther on stand the Virgin's Fountain, Siloe village, and Job's well, where Warren found a rock aqueduct in 1868. Dry most of the year, it bears names like Valley of Nuts, Valley of Mary, Valley of Josaphat, and Valley of Fire along its course.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brothers-of-c:
The Brothers of Christian Instruction, founded at Saint-Brieuc in 1817 by Jean-Marie-Robert de la Mennais, teach youth where a single brother must work alone. La Salle's rule barred his brothers from lone missions, leaving many places with need and means for only one teacher. La Mennais's first novices trained under the Christian Brothers and largely adopted their rule.

Rome recognized the congregation in 1851 and erected it canonically in 1891, under simple vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience. It spread from Ploermel to England, Africa, Asia, America, and Oceania, reaching Montreal in 1886 and the United States soon after. The 1901 French Law of Associations moved its mother-house to Taunton, England. By 1903 it counted 3,000 members, 420 institutions, and 75,000 students.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bruno-the-sax:
Bruno the Saxon, an eleventh-century German chronicler, wrote the chief Saxon account of the war against Henry IV. Little is known of his life, but he seems to have been a Saxon monk in Archbishop Werner of Magdeburg's household. Werner opposed Henry IV and led the Saxon rising, and after his death at peasants' hands in 1078, Bruno joined Werner of Merseburg.

To that bishop he dedicated his De Bello Saxonico in 1082. It traces Henry's youth, Adalbert of Bremen's sway after Anno of Cologne's stern rule, and the rebellion's causes and course to Hermann of Luxemburg's election as king in 1081. Critics call him a partisan who lowered Henry's name, yet the entry defends his sincerity and purpose to tell the truth. His vivid contemporary picture gains value from the Saxon bishops' letters and documents he prints.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-burlington:
Burlington is the diocese covering the whole state of Vermont, set up on 14 July 1853. Catholics reached Vermont early: Champlain gave the state its name in 1609, and the first Mass within its bounds was said in 1666 at Fort Saint Anne on Isle La Motte. Jesuit and other missionaries crossed the state in the years that followed, and by 1734 fourteen Catholic families gathered round a chapel at Alburgh.

Vermont passed from Quebec's care to the Diocese of Boston in 1810. Its first resident priest, Jeremiah O'Callaghan of Cork, came to Burlington in 1830 and built Saint Peter's church there in 1832. John D. Daly served the southern missions from 1837, and other pioneer priests spread through the state before the see was erected.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canon:
A canon belongs to a chapter, a body of clerics living by rule under one of their number. Whether the title comes from canon as rule or canon as list of a church's servants is much debated. The fuller definition is simply a member of a chapter, since chapters differ in rule, rights, and privileges. Some derive it from the regularity of the canons' common life, others from their names standing on church lists.

The latter view, held by Thomassinus and most writers, fits the fact that today's cathedral chapters continue the ancient bodies of presbyters who formed the bishop's senate in each church. It is hard to say when canons first stood out as a body apart from other clergy, though many churches had their own clergy from the first ages. The first certain Western evidence is Chrodegang of Metz's rule of common life of 763.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-ado:
Adoption in law is the act by which a person, with public authority's cooperation, takes as his child one who is not his own. Roman law called adoption of an adult adrogatio, and giving in adoption by one with power over the child datio in adoptionem. Full adoption put the child under the adopter's control, gave the adopter's name, and made the child necessary heir. Less full adoption lacked the natural tie of kinship.

The Church took over Roman adoption law, which Pope Nicholas I called venerable when urging it on the Bulgarians. Under the name legal relationship it became a diriment bar to marriage. It covered civil paternity between adopter and adopted with the adopted's lawful children, civil brotherhood with the adopter's lawful children, and affinity with each spouse's kin. Justinian's Code later ruled that adoption by a stranger did not strip the child's natural parentage rights.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-inq:
Canonical inquisition takes two forms, extra-judicial and judicial, the first like a coroner's inquest in civil law, the second like a grand jury's investigation. An extra-judicial inquiry, advised in civil cases, is absolutely required in criminal matters, except where the case is notorious. A bishop may not even admonish a supposedly delinquent cleric without first holding a summary inquiry into the rumors, denunciations, or charges against him.

The bishop runs the inquiry himself or through a prudent, trustworthy, and impartial deputy, as secretly as possible and without judicial form, though witnesses and experts may still be heard. Great care must guard the cleric's good name, lest the bishop face a damages suit. Acts with evidence go to the archives; acts without evidence, or with only slight evidence, are destroyed. The outcome may leave matters as they are, order extra-judicial correction, or open a public action.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-ins:
Canonical institution is the church-law process by which a cleric gains a benefice, a church office that carries income and duties. The entry separates the broad sense, any lawful way of gaining such an office, from three narrower senses that canon lawyers use. Chief among them is the grant of title. There a lawful authority confers the office on a candidate put forward by someone holding the right of presentation.

A second form puts the holder in real possession through installation, with rites set by local custom. A third form is the bishop's approval for ministry when a lesser authority granted the title. The entry also sets time limits for parish cases and the bishop's right to test candidates. It explains what happens when institution is refused. Readers get a compact map of a term that links patronage, appointment, and possession.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-vis:
Canonical visitation is a superior's official visit to people and places under his care. Its purpose is to uphold faith and discipline and to correct abuses. The entry roots the practice in early Christian times and notes its decline. It shows the Council of Trent restoring it with a rule that bishops visit their dioceses in person or through a deputy. The whole territory must be covered within two years.

Its stated aims are sound doctrine, good morals, and the correction of evil. Visitors pursue them by warning and encouragement as well as by remedies suited to time and place. The entry also covers who holds the right of visitation. Matters beyond a visitor's power are reported upward. Visitors without jurisdiction may correct only minor breaches of rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canons-regula:
The Canons Regular of the Immaculate Conception are a congregation founded at Saint-Antoine in the French department of Isère. Its founder was Abbé Dom Adrien Gréa. Pius IX and Leo XIII approved the community in rescripts of 1870, 1876, and 1887. Its members set out to restore early canonical life. They recited the full Divine Office day and night and kept lifelong abstinence and early fasting practices.

After French laws of 1901 drove the community from Saint-Antoine, its mother-house moved to Andora Stazione in Genoa province. Houses followed in France, Switzerland, Italy, Scotland, and Canada. Canadian foundations at Nomingue and St. Boniface anchor the work. A small body of priests, students, postulants, and lay brothers serves there, with priests working in settlement and in teaching the young.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardinal-de-b:
Emmanuel Théodore de la Tour d'Auvergne, Cardinal de Bouillon, was a French prelate and diplomat. He was born at Turenne in August 1643 and died at Rome in March 1715. Son of Frederick Maurice, Prince of Sedan, and kinsman of Marshal Turenne, he became a canon of Liège in 1658. He took a Sorbonne doctorate in 1667 and became a cardinal in 1669 at twenty-four, with benefices and the post of chief almoner to Louis XIV.

Minister Louvois, hostile to the house of Turenne, blocked his family claims. Bouillon's satire on the king helped bring his fall at court. He failed to win the Prince-Bishopric of Liège, regained favor as ambassador to Rome, and there backed Fénelon against Bossuet, resisting condemnation of Fénelon's Maxims of the Saints. Recalled yet refusing to obey, he spent years abroad pleading his case before regaining his revenues and a Roman retirement.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-castile-and-a:
Castile and Aragon form the united kingdom born from the 1469 marriage of Isabella of Castile to Ferdinand, King of Aragon, known as the Catholic. Columbus sailed as agent of their Catholic Kings, and the union grew into the Spanish kingdom, or more precisely the Spains. Castile's name is disputed, but likely comes from the castles Romans built against the Cantabrians and Christians later built against the Moors.

Castile's central Spanish region is bounded by Biscay, the Basque provinces, Navarre, Aragon, Valencia, Andalusia, Estremadura, Leon, and the Asturias. It is divided into Old and New Castile. Later sections give the histories of Castile and Aragon and their relations. They cover civil and church divisions, judiciary, military, education, and church life, with a table of dioceses closing the survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-bene:
The Catholic Benevolent Legion was a fraternal assessment life-insurance society founded in Brooklyn, New York, on 5 September 1881. Its charter members included Dr. George R. Kuhn and nine other men, and Bishop Loughlin of Brooklyn served as spiritual adviser of its supreme council, the governing body that secured its legal incorporation.

The Legion aimed to unite Catholic men between eighteen and fifty-five for social, benevolent, and intellectual improvement, offering life insurance up to $5,000 with assessments set by the member's age. By 1908 it had paid $19,000,000 in death benefits, counted 20,000 members out of 74,188 enrolled since its founding, and held councils in six states.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-miss:
The Catholic Missionary Union is the legal name of a society governed by directors drawn from the bishops, seminaries, parishes, and missionary organizations of the United States. Its purpose is to recruit priests and laymen as missionaries to non-Catholics in America. It supports them, spreads Catholic literature, and helps bishops build home missions in their dioceses. It was formed by the Paulist Fathers to pursue the lifework of their founder, Isaac Thomas Hecker.

The movement rests on a sense of duty toward the spiritual good of Catholics, of baptized non-Catholics, and of all others called to the knowledge of the truth. In practice each diocese formed bands of diocesan priests. Working under their bishop, they gathered non-Catholics and explained Catholic doctrine to them. A monthly magazine, The Missionary, spread accounts of the work and encouraged charitable gifts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-youn:
The Catholic Young Men's National Union was organized on 22 February 1875 at a meeting in Newark, New Jersey, called by Very Rev. George H. Doane, its first president. It embraced about one hundred organizations, representing some 30,000 persons, with a western reach to Mankato, Minnesota. Its aims were practical unity and the spiritual, intellectual, moral, and physical advance of Catholic youth.

The means were the practice and profession of the faith, the founding of young men's clubs, libraries, reading rooms, and gyms, and fraternal unity among like-minded bodies. An athletic league served boys of the parochial schools, and members of one organization could be received as guests by others. Though run by volunteers, the Union's growth called for a salaried staff and an endowment fund.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholics-and:
Catholics and evolution asks what an educated Catholic should make of the theory of evolution. Should it be cast aside as unfounded and hostile to the faith? Or taken as sound and in line with a Christian view of the world? The answer turns on four distinctions. They are the theory as science versus as philosophy, and on theistic grounds versus atheistic grounds. The last two set the theory against Darwinism, and the theory in plants and animals against the theory applied to man.

As science, the theory traces the order of plant and animal species through the ages of the earth. It draws on fossils and on the study of form, embryos, and life habits. The article holds that man's soul, being of a spiritual kind, could not have grown from a brute soul. Its origin must be a creative act of God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-centurion:
A centurion commanded a Roman century or company, whose strength ranged from fifty to one hundred men. In the Vulgate and Douay Version the term also covers a Hebrew army officer. New Testament times saw sixty centurions to a legion, two per maniple and six per cohort, with ranks that differed.

The centurion of the first century in a maniple outranked the second, and rank rose with the maniple and the cohort. The chief centurion of the legion was the primipilus, the leading centurion of the first cohort's triarii. He kept charge of the legion's eagle, sat in councils of war, and in a superior's absence took command of the legion. Auxiliary cohorts held six or ten centurions, and these ranked below the legionary centurions. A vine-branch staff marked the rank, and with it centurions at times chastised their men.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ceylon:
Ceylon is an island 266 and a half miles long and 140 and a half broad, southeast of India. It is joined to India only by the reefs and sandbanks called Adam's Bridge. Flat, low maritime districts contrast with a mountainous center. Two monsoons shape the climate: the southwest blows from May to September, the northeast from November to February. Pidurutalagala, at 8,296 feet, is the highest mountain. Adam's Peak, at 7,353 feet, holds the legendary footprints of Buddha and draws yearly pilgrims.

Rivers water the island well, the Kelani-ganga reaching the sea at Colombo, the capital, and the Mahaviliganga at Trincomalee. The article surveys the island's history and people, civil government, law and courts, marriage, education, and religion. Its closing statistics count 570 schools with 45,549 pupils, five seminaries, and hundreds of priests, religious, and sisters in educational and charitable work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chalcedon:
Chalcedon was a titular see of Asia Minor founded in 676 B.C. by Megarians on the Bithynian coast, opposite the site where Byzantium would later rise. Captured by the Persian general Otanes, allied by turns with Athens and Sparta, it eventually joined Bithynia and passed to the Romans in 74 B.C., who lost it briefly to Mithradates. Under the empire it was a free city, though Valens dismantled it between 364 and 378, and the Persians held it from 616 to 626.

Chalcedon gave the world Xenocrates, Plato's disciple in philosophy, and the sculptor Beotes, and the virgin St. Euphemia suffered martyrdom there under Galerius. In her magnificent church the Fourth General Council against Eutyches met in 451. After the council the city became a metropolis, though without suffragans, and its bishops are listed by Lequien.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-berin:
Charles Berington, titular Bishop of Hiero-Caesarea, was born at Stock in Essex in 1748 and died in 1798, after a life of disappointed hopes. Sent to Douai's English College at thirteen, he showed ability but never applied himself, and four years later he was moved to St. Gregory's Seminary in Paris. He did little better there, though he took his doctorate at the Sorbonne in 1776. Back in England he became chaplain at Ingatestone Hall, then spent two years travelling with a young Mr. Giffard of Chillington.

Back home he became Bishop Thomas Talbot's coadjutor in the Midland District, where Talbot served as Vicar Apostolic, a stronghold of Cisalpine opinion with which Berington fully sympathised. In 1788 he joined the Catholic Committee, then agitating for repeal of the Penal Laws, though its members were willing to minimise Catholic principles. He died of a sudden apoplexy on the ride home from Sedgley Park.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-carro:
Charles Carroll of Carrollton was an American statesman born at Annapolis in 1737 and dead near Baltimore in 1832. His grandfather emigrated from England in 1688. His father, Charles Carroll of Annapolis, opposed the political disabilities of Maryland Catholics. His biographer splits his life into three thirty-year spans: preparation, public service, and retirement.

Carroll first made his name opposing the Stamp Act fees, arguing against Daniel Dulaney that fees were taxes and taxes needed the consent of representatives. In 1774 he entered the provincial convention despite Catholic disfranchisement. He served on the Canada committee with Franklin and Samuel Chase. He helped move Maryland to authorise independence in June 1776 and signed the Declaration of Independence that August as its wealthiest signer. Later a Federalist senator, he backed Hamilton's funding measures. He gave up his United States seat in 1792 to keep his Maryland Senate place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-eysto:
Charles Eyston was an antiquary born in 1667 and dead in 1721. He belonged to the ancient Eyston family of East Hendred. Their house kept the Blessed Sacrament continuously, a rarity in England. Eldest son of George Eyston and Ann Dormer of Peterley, he inherited the family estates on his father's death in 1691. In 1692 he married Winefrid Dorothy Fitzherbert of Swinnerton, Staffordshire, by whom he had a large family.

A good scholar, he became a friend of Thomas Hearne through antiquarian research. Hearne praised his charity to the poor, his sweet temper, his scholarship, and a modesty that never sought mention. His son Charles succeeded him on his death. Another son, William George, entered the Jesuits in 1736 but left almost at once, and several daughters became nuns. Eyston wrote a short monument to Glastonbury Abbey and borough, published by Hearne in 1722, and a history of dissolved foundations in England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-franc:
Charles Francois Baillargeon was a French-Canadian bishop born at Ile-aux-Grues in 1798 and dead in 1870. He studied theology at the Quebec Seminary, where he taught rhetoric, and was ordained in 1822. He served in turn as chaplain at St. Roch, pastor of St. François on the Isle of Orléans, and pastor of the joint parishes of L'Ange-Gardien and Chateau-Richer. As rector of Notre Dame de Quebec he showed apostolic zeal and charity through three cholera visitations, in 1832, 1834, and 1849, and the typhus horrors of 1847.

On 23 February 1851 he was made Bishop of Tloa and coadjutor to Archbishop Turgeon of Quebec, the first Canadian bishop since the conquest chosen without British Crown involvement. He became administrator in 1855 and succeeded as Archbishop of Quebec in August 1867. He attended the Vatican Council.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-janua:
Charles Januarius Acton was an English cardinal born at Naples in 1803 and dead there in 1847. His father was Sir John Francis Acton, and Charles was his second son. After his father's death in 1811, Charles and his elder brother were sent to school in England, with the understanding that their religion would not be interfered with.

At twenty Charles went to Rome and entered the Academia Ecclesiastica, which trains ecclesiastics seeking public office. An essay caught the eye of Secretary of State della Somaglia, and Leo XII made him chamberlain and attaché to the Paris Nunciature, a fine school of diplomacy. Recalled by Pius VIII and later made assistant judge of Rome's Civil Court by Gregory XVI, he became Auditor of the Apostolic Chamber in 1837. He was proclaimed Cardinal-Priest of Santa Maria della Pace in 1842.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-thoma:
An entry on Charles Thomas Maillard de Tournon, the papal legate whose mission to China ended in imprisonment and death. Born at Turin in 1668 of a noble Savoyard family, he studied canon and civil law at Rome. He won the trust of Clement XI, who named him legate to India and China in 1701. His charge was to bring harmony among missionaries and enforce Rome's ruling against the Chinese rites.

Those rites meant sacrifices to Confucius and ancestors and the use of Chinese names for God. Tournon forbade them, first for the Malabar rites in India in 1704, then by decree at Nanking in 1707. Emperor Kangxi, who had welcomed him at Peking, demanded that missionaries keep the rites and ordered Tournon confined at Macao. The legate died there in confinement in 1710, a cardinal whose firmness had wrecked his own embassy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-water:
An entry on Charles Waterton, an English naturalist and explorer who turned his Yorkshire estate into a sanctuary for wild life. Born at Walton Hall near Wakefield in 1782 to a staunch Catholic and Royalist family, he was schooled at Stonyhurst, where his passion for birds and beasts already showed. After years managing family estates in British Guiana from 1804, he explored the Guiana hinterland at four-year intervals.
