Waterton studied the deadly wourali poison and showed that its effects could be held off by artificial breathing. More lastingly, his knowledge of living animals and his new way of preserving skins raised taxidermy, the stuffing of animals, from craft to art. Back at Walton Hall, he walled his park, banned killing within it, and lived plainly, giving freely to the poor. Darwin visited him there, and he died in his own park in 1865 after tripping on a briar root.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charleston:
The Diocese of Charleston now covers the whole state of South Carolina. Founded in July 1820, it first took in Georgia and North Carolina as well, before Savannah split off in 1850 and North Carolina became a vicariate in 1868. Mass was first said in Charleston in 1786 for twelve people, and by 1789 a meeting-house bought by Thomas Keating had become St. Mary's Church. An act of 1791 gave the Church legal standing in the state.

John England, consecrated at Cork in 1820, was the first bishop, and his able rule shaped the diocese until his death in 1842. His successors included Ignatius Reynolds, who published England's works and built a new cathedral, and Patrick Lynch, who bought a church for Black Catholics in 1867. By 1908 the diocese counted about 9,650 Catholics, nineteen priests, twelve churches with resident priests, and seventeen missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-and:
An entry on Christian perfection, the spiritual union with God possible in this life. A thing is perfect when nothing is wanting to its nature, purpose, or end. Yet full perfection belongs to heaven alone, where the soul enjoys the beatific vision, the direct sight of God. Perfection here is relative, compatible with human miseries, wayward passions, and even venial sins.

This perfection consists in charity, in love of God and neighbour, as taught in Matthew, Romans, Galatians, and Corinthians. Charity joins the soul to God as its supernatural end and clears away what blocks that union. Suárez explains that charity counts as perfection substantially, principally, and entirely, since other virtues accompany it and serve it. Faith and hope prepare the way but do not themselves constitute perfection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-n:
An entry on Christopher Norton, martyr, executed at Tyburn in May 1570. His father Richard Norton of Norton Conyers, Yorkshire, known as Old Norton, had kept the Catholic faith through Henry the Eighth and Edward the Sixth. He governed Norham Castle under Mary and served as sheriff of Yorkshire in 1568. Pardoned once for the Pilgrimage of Grace, he joined the northern rising of 1569 with his brother Thomas, nine sons, and many kin.

Attainted, Old Norton fled to Flanders with four sons, two sons were pardoned, and one apostatised, leaving the faith. Christopher, the seventh son, and his great-uncle were captured and proved steadfast Catholics, then hanged, disembowelled, and quartered. The apostate Edmund and a sister live on in Wordsworth's White Doe of Rylstone, a poem that keeps the Norton name joined to loyalty, loss, and a ruined house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-circumcision:
Circumcision, the cutting away of the foreskin, is practised by peoples across the world. Egyptians, Colchians, and Ethiopians knew it in ancient times, as did tribes in Sumatra, New Guinea, Samoa, Australia, and the Americas. Herodotus traced it to Egypt, but its wide spread casts doubt on a single origin. Suggested reasons range from tribal marking and initiation at puberty to cleanliness, nobility, and religious offering.

For Jews it was the sign of the covenant given to Abraham, and the article weighs its relation to Gentile practice. Muslims keep it by tradition, not by Koranic command, usually between seven and twelve years. In Catholic teaching it was no mere ceremony but a sacramental rite. Augustine and Aquinas held it conferred remission of original and actual sin, though not full release from temporal punishment as baptism does.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-citation:
A citation is the legal act by which a judge calls a person before a tribunal for trial. A verbal citation has the judge send an apparitor to summon the accused to a fixed day. It is edictal when issued by public summons, and real when the person has been arrested by officers of the law. Citations are simple or peremptory. The simple form fixes a day without threats. The peremptory form binds strictly and warns that no later summons will follow.

Ordinarily a citation is so necessary that its omission voids every later act of the trial. Exceptions cover a person caught red-handed, an accused already before the tribunal, and danger in delay. A valid citation must name plaintiff and defendant, state the cause, and fix day and place, binding the case to the judge who issued it. Contumacy by a defendant raises a presumption of guilt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-dablon:
Claude Dablon, a Jesuit missionary born at Dieppe in February 1618 and dead at Quebec on 3 May 1697, entered the Society of Jesus at twenty-one and reached Canada in 1655. Sent at once with Chaumonot to the Iroquois at Onondaga, he kept a diary picturing the journey's terrors. In 1661 he went with Druillettes toward Hudson Bay, seeking missions and perhaps a passage to the China Sea, but the expedition failed.

In 1668 Dablon joined Allouez and Marquette on Lake Superior, the trio Bancroft calls illustrious, and he first told the world of the region's rich copper mines. He chose Marquette for the expedition that found the Upper Mississippi and published Marquette's letters and charts. He also proposed a half-league prairie canal from Lake Michigan to the Illinois River. After founding Sault Sainte Marie he led the Canadian missions from 1670 to 1680 and again from 1686 to 1693.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clifton:
Clifton, a diocese of England covering Gloucestershire, Somersetshire, and Wiltshire, was founded by Pius the Ninth when he restored the English hierarchy in 1850. Before that it belonged to the Western District, one of four vicariates set up by Innocent the Eleventh in 1688, covering Wales and six south-western counties. In 1840 Wales became a separate vicariate, leaving the district to the English counties alone.

As the vicars apostolic lived chiefly at Bath, Joseph William Hendren, the Western District's last vicar apostolic, became the first Bishop of Clifton. The diocese thus represents the old vicariate, and its bishop keeps the Western District archives, a prime source for English church history from 1780 to 1850. Earlier papers perished in the Gordon Riots of 1780. Hendren moved to Nottingham a year after the foundation, succeeded by Thomas Burgess. A cathedral chapter of a provost and ten canons rose on 28 June 1852.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-co-education:
Co-education now generally means educating the sexes together, but it carries several meanings. Mere juxtaposition uses the same buildings, equipment, and teaching staff for both sexes without the same methods or regimen. Co-ordinate education teaches both sexes by the same methods and teachers, but each sex keeps its own classes and, at a university, its separate college. Identical education teaches both sexes the same things together, in time and place, by the same faculty and methods, admitting age and proficiency but not sex.

It is this third and narrowest sense that has drawn widespread discussion, growing rapidly in the United States, slowly in Europe. Co-education is practically universal in American public elementary grades and common in private schools, including Catholic parochial schools. In secondary schools, the Commissioner's Report for 1905 to 1906 counted 7,962 public co-educational high schools with 283,264 boys and 394,181 girls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-colophon:
Colophon, a titular see of Asia Minor and one of the twelve Ionian cities, fills Sophrone Pétridès's entry. It lay between Lebedos and Ephesus. Two sons of Codrus, King of Athens, founded its colony in Greek antiquity. It gave birth to the philosopher Xenophanes and the poet Mimnermus. Lysimachus, a successor of Alexander, later destroyed it. Notium served as its port, and nearby stood Clarus, with its famed temple and oracle of Apollo Clarius.

Colophon's cavalry won renown, and its pine trees yielded a rosin, colophony, prized for musical instrument strings. Under Rome the city lost weight, and its name moved to the site of Notium. The Notitiae still list Colophon as a suffragan of Ephesus into the twelfth or thirteenth century. Lequien names only four bishops, two of them legendary. Its ruins lie at Ghiaour-Keui, a small village near Smyrna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communion-ant:
Adrian Fortescue's entry traces the Communion antiphon, from Communio, once sung while the people received the Blessed Sacrament. It now follows that moment, displaced from its old place. In the Ambrosian Rite it is called the Transitorium, since the celebrant crosses to the Epistle side to read it. It is the fourth and last changeable choir part of the Mass, after Introit, Gradual, Offertory. It dates at least to the fourth century. Augustine, who died in 430, defended its use in Africa against Hilary.

Two changes mark its history: removal to a place after Communion, and shortening. Fortescue notes its present form and sources in the rubrics and in Duchesne and Benedict XIV. The entry gives singers and students a compact history of a short chant. It runs from early African controversy to a settled place in the Mass, sung by the choir as the faithful communicate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-compensation:
John Augustine Ryan's entry treats compensation as the price paid for human labor. Wherever free men could sell their labor, they saw its pay as a matter of right and wrong. Christian lands shared that conviction. Early in the fourth century, Diocletian's edict fixed maximum prices and set a wage schedule for nineteen classes of workers. Its preamble claimed justice for the people as its motive. Through the Middle Ages and nearly to the nineteenth century, most European lands regulated wages by law.

Church Fathers implied a laborer's right to life-sustaining pay, holding that God meant the earth for all. Today Catholic teaching is precise on the just minimum. It sets that ethical floor without declaring what full justice in pay would demand. The entry leans on Levasseur, Brants, Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum, and Ryan's own Living Wage of 1906.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comte-de-forb:
Camillus Maes's entry follows the Comte de Forbin-Janson, Bishop of Nancy and Toul, founder of the Holy Childhood. Born at Paris on 3 November 1785, he was a Knight of Malta from childhood, a soldier at sixteen. Napoleon made him Auditor of the Council of State in 1805. His family hoped for a statesman, but in 1808 he entered Saint-Sulpice seminary. Ordained in Savoy in 1811, he became Vicar-General of Chambéry, then chose French missionary work with Abbé de Rauzan.

Refusal to sign the Gallican Declaration drew persecution, and exile forced him from France in 1830. Gregory XVI sent him touring the United States in 1839. Louisiana first felt his zeal, and he gave a third of Spring Hill College's price near Mobile. From New York to Quebec, his missions stirred Catholics, and French Canada kept his memory. Back in France he founded the Holy Childhood in 1843, dying near Marseilles in 1844.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concelebratio:
Adrian Fortescue's entry defines concelebration as the rite where several priests say Mass together, all consecrating the same bread and wine. Once common in East and West, it survived late into the ninth century, when priests stood around their bishop and consented to his sacrifice. Rome modified the rite, perhaps under Pope Zephyrinus from 202 to 218, so each priest consecrated a separate host, held by deacons in patens or corporals, while all shared one chalice.

By the sixth century the rite marked all station days. By the eighth it remained only for the greatest feasts: Easter, Christmas, Whitsunday, and Saint Peter. Other days saw priests assist without consecrating. In the Latin Church it survives only at ordinations of priests and bishops. There the new priests consecrate with the bishop and receive under one kind. At a bishop's consecration, the new bishop instead communicates with his consecrator under both kinds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concepcion:
F. M. Rudge's entry covers Concepción, a diocese in Chile suffragan to Santiago de Chile. It takes in the provinces of Arauco, Bío-Bío, Concepción, Ñuble, Maule, Linares, and Malleco, across 27,901 square miles. Pius IV issued its erection bull on 22 May 1563. Since then, except for a vacancy from 1818 to 1832, a bishop has always sat at Concepción. Its institutions include an orphan asylum and a Capuchin missionary college.

Ten congregations of men and seven of women work in the diocese, among them the Sisters of Providence, Mercy, Christian Charity, Good Shepherd, and Sacred Heart, numbering 393 in all. The Catholic population runs to 835,790, with 52 parishes, 190 priests, 91 secular and 99 regular, and 135 churches and chapels. College and seminary stand beside nine Catholic schools with 2,550 pupils. The entry points readers to Chile for the wider story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-condition:
Francis Aveling's entry defines condition, from Latin conditio, as what is needed, or at least helpful, for a cause to act, without itself causing the effect. Light suits my writing, yet I, not the light, cause the writing. A condition is a circumstance in which a cause acts readily, or alone can act. It differs from a real principle giving existence to an effect. Conditions split into the sine qua non, without which a cause lies inoperative and irreplaceable, and the merely helpful kind, where one of several conditions may serve.

Combustion of wood offers an irreplaceable case. Some modern philosophies treat condition as accidental modification. Writers professing theism yet defining God through conditions, removing imperfections toward plenitude, miss the strict sense, Aveling argues. The entry closes with Thomas's third way in the Summa, on knowing whether God exists, where conditions frame the proof without causing its conclusion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confirmation:
Thomas Scannell's vast entry treats Confirmation, the sacrament where the Holy Ghost comes to the baptized to make them strong Christians, soldiers of Jesus Christ. Names vary: bebaiosis, a making fast; teleiosis or consummatio, a perfecting tied to baptism; Sacrament of the Holy Ghost; Sacrament of the Seal; imposition of hands; chrism anointing. West says confirmatio, Greeks myron. The entry moves through practice, doctrine, rite, minister, matter, form, recipient, and effects.

In the West the bishop usually administers it, opening with hands imposed and prayer, then anointing. The East drops the opening imposition and prayer, anointing with words on the seal of the Spirit's gift. The bishop alone serves as ordinary minister. Only the baptized, unconfirmed, in grace, may receive. Confirmation stands to baptism as growth to generation, adding grace, not removing sin. The entry closes amid Anglican debate, noting some Catholics conceding no visible sign ordained by God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Blanche Mary Kelly's entry covers the Sisters of Notre-Dame de Sion, founded at Paris in May 1843 by Marie-Théodore and Marie-Alphonse Ratisbonne. Théodore, sub-director of the Archconfraternity of Our Lady of Victories, gained Gregory XVI's leave to work among Jews. With his brother he raised a congregation under Our Lady of Sion, mother-house at Paris. Affre, Sibour, and Cardinal Fornari encouraged it warmly, and Pius IX granted indulgences on 15 January 1847.

Holy Land foundations led the expansion, chiefly a convent, orphan asylum, and school near Jerusalem's Ecce Homo arch, with Saint John's founded from it. Saint Peter's orphanage added art and manual schools. At Ecce Homo 170 pupils, Jews, Mohammedans, and schismatics, studied beside 100 day scholars. Houses followed in London, Rome, Versailles, Trieste, Vienna, Prague, Galatz, Bucharest, Jassy, and Constantinople. Five hundred sisters served, guided by the Priests of Notre-Dame de Sion.

The entry surveys Immaculate Conception congregations, opening with the Conceptionists. Beatrix de Silva, sister of Blessed Amadeus, founded them at Toledo in 1484. Having fled a jealous queen's court to a Toledo Dominican convent, she lived forty years in holiness without joining. Devotion to the Virgin moved her to found a new congregation. With companions she took a castle Queen Isabella set apart. In 1489, by Innocent VIII's permission, the sisters adopted the Cistercian rule and daily Office.

Other bodies follow in turn. Lamennais founded the Missionaries of Rennes at Saint-Méen for seminary care. Georgian priest Peter Carisciarian founded Constantinople's Servites in 1864 for Georgian Christians, with sister Servites running two schools open without creed distinction. Canon Kinet founded the Sisters of Providence at Jodoigne in 1833, settled at Champion near Namur in 1836. Abbé Noailles founded Bordeaux's Sisters of the Immaculate Conception in 1820 as a Holy Family branch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-consecration:
Augustin Joseph Schulte's entry defines consecration as separating a thing from profane to sacred use, or dedicating it to God's service through prayers and rites. The custom reaches remotest times, with rites in Egyptian and pagan cults. Among Semitic tribes it formed a threefold act: separating, sanctifying, devoting to the Deity. Hebrew Law applied it to the whole people, Moses's People of God.

Exodus 24 describes altar and twelve stones, with twelve youths performing the holocaust. Aaron and his sons received consecration in Exodus 29; Levites represented the first-born. The Church distinguishes consecration from blessing. The Roman Pontifical holds one of persons, a bishop's, and four of things: altar, altar-stone, church. Eastern prayers carry the same import. Unqualified, consecration ordinarily means the Mass act changing bread and wine. A bishop's consecration marks priesthood's plenitude, its day a Sunday or Apostle's feast, its rite most splendid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-consubstantia:
Thomas Scannell's entry treats consubstantiation, a heretical doctrine attempting to hold Christ's Real Presence in the Holy Eucharist without Transubstantiation. Under it, Christ's Body's substance exists together with bread's substance, and His Blood's substance together with wine's. Hence the name. How two substances coexist finds various explanations. The subtlest theory holds that, just as God the Son took a human body without destroying its substance, so in the Blessed Sacrament He assumes bread's nature. Hence the theory also bears the name Impanation, founded on Incarnation's analogy.

Full treatment belongs with the general doctrine of the Holy Eucharist. Here the entry traces the heresy's history briefly. Earliest ages set the background, while Berengarius and his modern followers appealed chiefly to reason and the Fathers for their opinions. Cited works span Harper, Franzelin, Schwane, Vernet, Streber, Hedley, Waggett, and Gore, grounding the sketch in Eucharistic theology across Catholic and Anglican writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-contemplation:
Augustin Poulain's entry treats contemplation through mystical theology, since neither explains clearly without the other. Supernatural acts no effort of ours can produce, even slightly or for an instant, are called mystical. Seeing one's guardian angel, independent of effort, counts as mystical.

Mystical states bear names: supernatural or infused, and extraordinary. Ordinary prayer and acquired contemplation follow in four degrees: vocal prayer, meditation, affective prayer, and prayer of simplicity. The last two, prayers of the heart, border mystical states. Mental prayer rich in affective acts counts as affective. Feeling neither relish nor facility for certain acts, one should not force them. Higher contemplation, or mystical union, unfolds in four stages, from incomplete union, the prayer of quiet, to full, semi-ecstatic union. After Saint Teresa, Saint John of the Cross holds first place for observation, though his classifications confuse, and both tower over later repeaters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-contrition:
Edward Hanna's entry treats contrition, Latin contritio, a breaking of hardness. Holy Writ abounds in repentance calls: Ezekiel's call to turn and live, Luke's warning that without penance all perish. At times repentance includes exterior satisfaction, but always implies knowing wrong done to God, hating evil, and desiring to turn and do good. Psalm 50 voices this pattern, as does the Pharisee and publican parable.

Nature follows: inward repentance theologians call contrition. Need stands firm: until the Reformation no theologian denied contrition's need for pardon. Catholic teaching splits hatred of sin in two: perfect contrition, from love of God offended, and imperfect contrition, its lesser twin. Marks require contrition, perfect or imperfect, to be inward, from grace, whole, and supreme. Inward means real heart sorrow, not mere outward show. Supernatural means prompted by grace and faith's motives, not merely natural ones. Whole, per Trent, includes firm purpose against future sinning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conversion:
Benedict Guldner's entry traces conversion, from Latin converto and conversio, change. In the Vulgate, in patristic Latin, and in later ecclesiastical Latin, conversion means moral change. It means turning to God and the true religion, passing into modern languages. Conversion usually means an infidel's turn to the true religion, or a schismatic's or heretic's turn to the Catholic Church.

Every man must seek the true religion, embrace it when found, and live by its precepts. The normal process begins with examining the Church's credentials, often painful labour. Since the duty rests on Divine right, no civil law can forbid fulfilling it. Reception follows abjuration of heresy or profession of faith, conditional baptism, and sacramental confession with conditional absolution. Force, violence, or fraud may never bring an unbeliever's conversion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-core-dathan-a:
Florentine Bechtel's entry treats Core, Dathan, and Abiron, revolt leaders against Moses and Aaron in Numbers 16. Core, son of Isaar, came from the Caathite Levite family. Dathan and Abiron were sons of Eliab, son of Phallu, of Ruben's tribe. A fourth leader, Hon, son of Pheleth, also a Rubenite, never appears again, suggesting textual corruption. Core headed the rebellion, hence the sedition of Core, and the rebels, the congregation of Core.

Many people, unreconciled to the exclusive Sinai priesthood, wanted the old order restored, with priestly functions exercised by each family's oldest member. Yet all shared jealousy of Amram's house, where civil and religious authority concentrated, aiming at its overthrow. Core's sons did not perish, and later descendants appear among the singers. The critical school reads the story as a combination of three narratives, one telling a revolt under Dathan and Abiron against civil authority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coronation:
Herbert Thurston's entry treats coronation under five headings: Constantinople's emperors; Visigothic and Celtic elements; English coronation orders; the Western Empire and the Roman Pontifical; and other ceremonials. A coronation rite, ideally, creates the monarch, though changing succession theory may make it rather the ratification of an accomplished fact.

Down to Constantine's reign, coronation properly speaking did not exist, for he first used the diadem. The next epoch-making change introduced the Patriarch to set the diadem on the elected sovereign's head. Phocas in 602 became the first emperor crowned in church. Records of procedure stay somewhat defective, yet church crowning certainly continued from that time. One passage suspects the adoration's timing, just after the emperor received the Host, was motived by some design. Western inauguration rites show first coronation-order traces in Spain and Great Britain, with close liturgical relations via Celtic channels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corporation:
John Willis's entry treats corporation, Latin corpus, a body. A corporation is an association recognized by civil law and regarded in law as an artificial person. Chief Justice Marshall of the United States Supreme Court defined it as an artificial being, invisible, intangible, existing only in contemplation of law. Being law's mere creature, it holds only those properties its creation charter confers, expressly or as incidental to its existence.

Chancellor Kent of New York defines a corporation as a franchise possessed by one or more individuals subsisting as a body politic. English law distinguishes corporations first as aggregate or sole, then as ecclesiastical or lay. Under English common law, corporations depended on a charter, Latin charta, a paper, granted by the king. Ecclesiastical corporations as such find no recognition in United States law, federal or state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-ch:
The Council of Chalcedon, the Fourth Ecumenical Council, sat from 8 October to 1 November 451 in Bithynia, Asia Minor. Its chief task was to defend orthodox teaching against Eutyches and the Monophysites, who so stressed Christ's unity that his two natures blurred into one. Discipline and jurisdiction also claimed the fathers' attention.

Session by session, the council heard testimony and read the fathers, and on 22 October proclaimed Christ true God and true man, one person in two natures. Bishops signed amid acclamation, and later sessions settled jurisdiction, including Jerusalem's bounds. Monophysite refusal persisted in Palestine, Syria, Armenia, and Egypt, where followers remain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-a:
This long reference entry surveys the councils held at Avignon across eight centuries, from a little-known meeting in 1060 to a synod in 1849. It treats each council in turn, noting who presided, what was decided, and how the decisions touched clergy, laity, and rulers in southern France.

Early meetings deposed a usurping bishop, excommunicated the people of Toulouse for sheltering Albigensian heretics, and defended church property and clerical rights. Later councils regulated confession, urged regular attendance at parish churches, and protected would-be crusaders who had failed to depart. The 1849 council closed the sequence with ten chapters on faith and discipline, and the entry cites its sources throughout for readers who want to dig deeper.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-covington:
A diocesan entry covers Covington, the Kentucky see east of the Kentucky River, established in 1853 by dividing the Diocese of Louisville. It spans 17,286 square miles, with a total population near 900,000, of whom about 54,000 were Catholics at the time of writing.

Early congregations were served by clergy in the tradition of Flaget, Badin, David, and Nerinckx. German Catholics predominated in Covington and Newport, while the Irish were the majority inland at Lexington, Frankfort, and Paris. The entry lists bishops, parishes, schools, and religious orders, and notes how a lack of industry south of the Mason-Dixon line handicapped the region.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-creation:
A long doctrinal entry defines creation as God's act of bringing a thing's whole substance into being out of nothing. It distinguishes this from ordinary making, where material already exists, and explains that nothing here is not a stuff from which things are made. It means the absence of any prior material.

The entry then traces the idea through history: its scriptural roots, its statement by the Fathers against pagans and Gnostics, and its fuller development by the Scholastics with Aristotle's theory of causes. Arguments for creation follow, along with a discussion of creation and evolution. Readers get a systematic account of one of Catholic theology's central doctrines, with a full bibliography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cremation:
A long entry traces cremation, the burning of the dead, from ancient practice to modern Church law. Pre-Canaanites burned their dead until about 2500 BC, while Jews, Egyptians, and Persians largely did not. Greeks and Romans varied with their views of the afterlife, and by the fifth Christian century the practice had ceased in the West under Christian influence.

Church legislation then made burial in earth or tomb part of Christian burial, and later Roman decrees forbade cremation. The entry explains the motives: in modern times cremation was often tied to a public profession of irreligion and materialism, promoted first by Freemasons. It closes by asking whether cremation marks culture, and answers that the Church could conform if the custom ever became universal without offence to faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dagon:
A scriptural entry examines Dagon, a Philistine deity whose name most scholars derive from the Semitic root for fish, meaning little fish. The Bible's account at Azotus suggests a figure with face, hands, and a fish-like lower body. Coins of Philistine and Phoenician cities match it, showing a composite being, human above and fish below.

Dagon was the foremost god of maritime cities such as Azotus, Gaza, Ascalon, and Arvad, and was sometimes paired with the half-fish goddess Derceto or Atargatis. A minority view, resting on Philo Byblius, makes him a god of corn and agriculture instead. The entry also notes the Ark's sojourn in Dagon's temple and the Syrian peoples' religious abstinence from eating fish, naturally linked to a fish god's worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-beaton:
A biographical entry traces David Beaton, Cardinal Archbishop of Saint Andrews, born in 1494 and murdered on 29 May 1546. A younger son of John Beaton of Balfour, he studied at Saint Andrews, Glasgow, and Paris, and in 1519 became James V's resident at the French court. His uncle, Archbishop of Glasgow, gave him the rectories of Campsie and Cambuslang and the abbacy of Arbroath.

Returning in 1525, Beaton sat in Parliament and became Lord Privy Seal. He negotiated James's French marriages, attended the king's wedding at Notre-Dame in 1537, and rose to cardinal and primate. As Scotland's leading churchman he opposed English influence and Protestant reform, and his murder by Protestant lairds in Saint Andrews Castle opened a new phase of Scotland's Reformation struggle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-william:
A biographical entry follows David William Bacon, first Bishop of Portland, Maine, born in New York in 1813. He studied classics at Montreal's Sulpician College and theology at Mount Saint Mary's, Emmitsburg, and was ordained at Baltimore in 1838. After missions at Utica, Ogdensburg, New York City, and Belleville, he founded Brooklyn's third parish in 1841, completing a suspended priest's unfinished church.

Named first Bishop of Portland in 1855 and consecrated at Saint Patrick's Cathedral, he found only six priests and eight churches in all Maine. Know-Nothing bigotry, the Civil War, and Portland's great fire of 1866 all hindered him, yet his zeal, tact, and energy prevailed. At his death he left 63 churches, 52 priests, 23 parish schools, and about 80,000 Catholics to his successor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dedication:
A liturgical entry treats dedication, the setting aside of places for a sacred purpose, though the word is sometimes used of persons consecrated to God's service. Christians believe God fills all space, yet they reserve special spots for communion with the Creator and worship. Old Testament precedent runs from Jacob and Moses to Solomon's temple dedication.

The New Law surely kept the custom by apostolic usage, though persecutions make early references rare. A fragment ascribed to Jerome notes Rome's dedication of the first church built and consecrated by Peter. The first authentic accounts come from Eusebius and Sozomen, on Tyre's cathedral in 314 and Constantine's Jerusalem church. Etheria's pilgrim narrative fully describes Jerusalem's dedication festival as witnessed in the fourth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deduction:
A philosophy entry explains deduction, from Latin for leading out, in two parts: as an argument and as a method. As an argument it moves from known truths to other truths that must follow from them. As a method it is the chain of such moves by which we learn more.

The typical form is the syllogism, whose essential feature is necessary connection between premises and conclusion. Granted the premises, the conclusion must follow, with no greater certainty than the premises themselves. The entry shows this in hypothetical and categorical forms, treats demonstration as certain deduction, and contrasts deduction's descent from general to particular with induction's ascent. Both, it argues, rest on abstract necessary truths. In plain terms, if the start is true, the end must be true too. That must is the whole point of the move, and it is what makes the thought safe to trust.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-degradation:
A canon law entry defines degradation, a penalty by which a cleric is entirely and perpetually stripped of all office, benefice, dignity, and power from ordination. By a set rite he is made a layman, loses clerical rights, and passes to the civil power. Yet degradation cannot remove the character conferred in ordination, nor free him from celibacy or the Breviary.

Degradation is twofold: verbal, the mere sentence, and real, its execution, parts of one punishment, not two penalties. Unlike deposition, it strips him wholly of orders, rule, and church rights, and leaves him fully under civil rule. Any bishop may speak the sentence, but only a consecrated bishop can carry it out, and only Rome can lift it. Today dismissal with perpetual deprivation usually takes its place. In short, he keeps the mark of ordination for life, but loses post, pay, and place among clergy for good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-delegation:
A canon law entry defines delegation, from Latin delegare, as commissioning another to exercise jurisdiction in the delegator's name. Jurisdiction itself is the power of one holding public authority and pre-eminence to rule and govern others. Roman law used delegation for substituting one debtor for another, and modern civil law uses it for committees acting for parliament or courts.

Canon law distinguishes delegation by a person, ab homine, from delegation by law, a jure, which may come from a juridical or moral person. Thus bishops hold certain powers over exempt regulars as delegates of Trent. One acting as delegate of the Apostolic See faces appeal to the pope, since the jurisdiction is really his. Sections cover delegated powers for liceity and validity, the delegate's duties, and the end of delegation by death or completion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demonic-posse:
A doctrinal entry that separates two kinds of attack by evil spirits. Obsession strikes the body from outside, while possession takes control of it from within. The soul itself, the entry insists, can never be seized or robbed of freedom, though its command over the body may be blocked.

Cases range from frequent reports among ancient pagan peoples to a single case in the Old Testament, then to the fuller Gospel record. Later pages test whether the phenomenon is real, answering writers who deny evil spirits or their power over the body. Church practice for dealing with the possessed is left to companion entries on exorcism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denunciation:
A canon law entry on denunciation, the act of laying another's crime before a superior. Evangelical denunciation follows Matthew's steps: speak alone first, then bring witnesses, then tell the church, all aimed at reform rather than revenge. Judicial denunciation, by contrast, seeks punishment as well as correction once the Church built a criminal process.

A denouncer differs from an accuser by bearing no duty to prove the charge, and modern diocesan courts put a promotor fiscalis in the accuser's place. False accusers once faced the penalty they sought for others, though that reprisal rule has lapsed. Denunciation is strictly required only in set cases, such as marriage impediments, abuse of the confessional, and leaders of secret societies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deposition:
A canon law entry on deposition, a lasting penalty that strips a cleric of office, benefice, and the exercise of orders. Total deposition takes all powers, while partial deposition takes only some, and no penance alone earns release, though a superior may restore a truly amended man. It bars future offices too, which sets it apart from simple privation and from suspension.

Early centuries already expelled guilty clerics to lay communion while leaving their ordained character intact. Use of the word itself is traced to the Synod of Agde in 506, and down to the twelfth century the two penalties meant the same thing. Later law drew the lines that separate deposition from degradation, which alone takes away clerical privilege.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-derogation:
A canon law entry on derogation, the partial repeal of a law, set against abrogation, its total repeal. Roman jurist Modestinus first framed the distinction, and canon law took it up, though loose speech still uses derogation for either kind. Dispensation differs again, easing named persons rather than cutting the law itself.

Papal rescripts often carry derogatory clauses, and their absence can flaw the document's form. Rules for reading derogations demand strict and specific terms, with no need for fresh promulgation when nothing contrary is imposed. General laws do not sweep away special ones by accident, since superiors are presumed unaware of the particular law they never meant to touch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-desecration:
An entry on desecration, the loss of the sacred character that consecration or blessing gives to places and things. Objects set aside for worship gain a stamp that bars profane use, and they lose it when they cease to be what they were. As a rule they keep their blessing while they stay morally the same and fit for their first purpose.

A broken chalice unfit for the altar loses its consecration on its own, with no ceremony needed. A sound vessel that only needs regilding cannot be stripped by rite at all, though the bishop's leave is sought before a craftsman handles it. Churches, altars, and altar stones each have their own listed triggers, from ruin to a cracked stone or a broken anointed corner.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-desertion:
A canon law entry on desertion, the culpable abandonment of a state whose duties one freely accepted. Leaving the faith counts as apostasy, as does a cleric quitting his orders or a religious quitting solemn vows. Quitting a congregation under simple vows is mere desertion instead: no excommunication follows, though clerics face suspension and the path usually ends in dismissal.

Later cases cover a cleric who abandons his benefice, judged under rules from the Council of Trent, and desertion in marriage, where malice must be weighed by the proper judge. Sources point readers to the canonists on non-resident clerics, to appeals, and to Sanchez on marriage. Each strand turns on the same question: what duty was freely taken, and how was it left?
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-detraction:
A moral theology entry on detraction, the unjust harming of another's good name by telling a fault the person truly has, or is honestly believed to have. Calumny differs at once: the slanderer states what he knows is false, while the detractor tells what he takes to be true. As a breach of both charity and justice, detraction is generally a mortal sin.

Guilt shrinks to venial when the matter is slight or little heed was paid to the harm. Weighing a case means weighing the charge itself, the detractor's standing for truth, and the standing of the person attacked, since a small flaw can wound a high reputation deeply. A duty to pay for money loss follows the detractor, and that burden passes even to his heirs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-devolution:
A canon law entry on devolution, the right of a higher church authority to fill a benefice when the rightful patron or collator fails. Failure may mean neglect or naming an unfit candidate, and the loss of right lasts only for that vacancy, never for good. When a chapter or private patron leaves a post empty six months, the diocesan bishop steps in.

Neglect by the bishop moves the right to the metropolitan, and where bishop and chapter share the power, the faithful partner keeps it alone. A vacant see needs a vicar capitular within eight days or the metropolitan names one, while chapters electing an archbishop, bishop, or abbot get three months before Rome takes over. Law aims both to cure neglect and to punish misuse.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moral-aspect-: May scientists experiment on living animals? catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mortification: Mortification is the ascetic discipline of the senses, and this entry explains its purpose, its kinds, and its place in the spiritual life. A balanced treatment of a demanding practice. Dying to self, that the spirit may live: the entry distinguishes true asceticism from excess.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mosaic-legisl: The Mosaic legislation is the Law given through Moses: the Ten Commandments, the ritual codes, and the civil statutes of ancient Israel. This entry surveys its parts, its spirit, and its fulfillment in Christ. The Torah, systematically explained: its 613 precepts ordered Israel's worship and life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-muratorian-ca: The Muratorian Canon is the oldest known list of New Testament books, drawn up around 170 AD and discovered by Muratori in Milan. This entry explains its contents, its date, and its immense importance. The first table of contents of the New Testament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nathaniel-bac: Nathaniel Bacon led Virginia's frontier rebellion in 1676, burning Jamestown before dying of fever. This entry covers his revolt, its causes, and its place in colonial history. The rebel of the Old Dominion: his uprising exposed the colony's deep divisions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nerses-of-lam: Nerses of Lambron was the Armenian archbishop who labored for union with Rome and translated the liturgy with exquisite learning. This entry covers his career, his writings, and his ecumenical vision. The bridge-builder of the Armenian Church: his translations adorned the liturgy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-atki: Nicholas Atkinson was an English priest martyred for his faith under Elizabeth I, one of the many who died for the old religion. This entry traces his mission, his capture, and his death. A martyr of the penal years: his name stands among the English martyrs of the Reformation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-de-br: This biographical entry profiles Nicolas de Bralion, a French Oratorian of the 1600s, tracing his career, his writings, and his place among the scholars of his congregation as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's French gallery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-pavil: Bishop Nicolas Pavillon of Alet was the saintly Jansenist whose resistance to the formulary made him a hero of Port-Royal. This entry traces his episcopate, his rigor, and his long struggle. The bishop who would not sign: his diocese became a model of pastoral reform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-talon: This biographical entry profiles Nicolas Talon, a French Jesuit of the 1600s, tracing his career, his writings, and his place among the scholars of his order as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Jesuit gallery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nikon: Patriarch Nikon reformed the Russian liturgy and split the Church, creating the Old Believers, then quarreled with the tsar and fell. This entry covers his reforms, his schism, and his tragedy. The patriarch who broke Russia's Church: his reforms split the faithful forever.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nomination: Nomination is the prince's right to name bishops for the pope to institute, and this entry explains its history, its concordats, and its canon law. The politics of episcopal appointments: kings and popes bargained over every see in Christendom for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nomocanon: The Nomocanon was the Byzantine collection that wove the Church's canons together with the emperor's laws. This entry explains its compilation, its authority, and its influence. Two laws, one book: its collections governed the Eastern Church for a full millennium.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-northampton: Northampton became a cathedral city of the restored English hierarchy, serving the Midlands' Catholics. This entry covers its diocese, its bishops, and its history. The faith in England's heartland: its cathedral serves the Midlands' Catholics to this day from its Northampton see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-obligation: Obligation is the moral bond that binds the will to do or avoid something, and this entry examines its kinds, its sources, and its force in moral theology. A precise scholastic treatment of duty. What binds the conscience: the entry distinguishes moral, legal, and religious bonds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-obreption: Obreption is the concealment of truth in a petition to Rome that can void the rescript obtained. This entry explains its canon law, its effects, and its remedies. The hidden flaw in a papal favor: the entry explains when concealment voids the grant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-occult-compen: Occult compensation was the disputed doctrine that a defrauded man might secretly take his due. This entry explains the theory, its limits, and the moralists' debates. Justice taken in secret: the moralists debated its limits for centuries without ever agreeing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-odo-of-cherit: Odo of Cheriton was the Cistercian preacher whose fables taught morals to medieval England. This entry covers his sermons, his stories, and his influence. The friar who preached with beasts: his fables moralized the animal kingdom for England's medieval preachers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-omission: Omission is the sin of leaving undone what duty requires, and this entry examines its kinds, its gravity, and its place in moral theology. The sin of the things we failed to do: the entry weighs its kinds and gravity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-the-: The Presentation Sisters were founded by Nano Nagle in 1775 to teach Ireland's poor Catholic children. This entry traces their foundation, their schools, and their worldwide spread. The ladies of the lantern: Nagle carried her lamp through the slums of Cork.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oregon: Oregon's Catholic story runs from the Hudson's Bay missionaries to the archdiocese of Portland. This entry covers its bishops, missions, and institutions. The faith in the Beaver State: its missions followed the fur traders ever westward toward the far Pacific.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orestes-augus: Orestes Brownson was America's great convert publicist, whose Review argued the Catholic cause for forty years. This entry traces his conversion, his writings, and his influence. The Yankee who became Rome's champion: his conversion shook Protestant America in the 1840s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-our-lady-of-a: This entry profiles the shrine of Our Lady of Arcachon, tracing its pilgrims, its miracles, and its place in French devotional life as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact sketch from the encyclopedia's French gallery, preserved among its Marian shrines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-arbitra: Papal arbitration was the medieval world's supreme court, with popes settling the disputes of kings. This entry traces its history, its great cases, and its principles. The peacemaker of Christendom: its famous awards once divided the whole vast New World.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-ander: This biographical entry profiles Patrick Anderson, a Scottish Jesuit of the 1600s, tracing his career, his mission work, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Jesuit gallery, preserved among its Scottish missionaries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-scarron: Paul Scarron was the burlesque poet whose Roman Comique mocked the heroic age. This entry covers his career, his satires, and his famous marriage to the future Madame de Maintenon. The cripple who made France laugh: his burlesques mocked the mighty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-antonio: Pedro Antonio de Alarcón wrote The Three-Cornered Hat, the sparkling novel behind Falla's ballet. This entry covers his career, his novels, and his fame. Spain's storyteller of the 1800s: his sparkling novels captured the colorful Andalusian life of old Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perpetual-ado: Perpetual Adoration is the unbroken worship of the Blessed Sacrament, day and night. This entry traces its origins, its societies, and its practice. The never-ending prayer before the Host: its worldwide confraternities now span the entire Catholic globe today in prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-persecution: Persecution is the Church's ancient trial, from Nero to the modern age. This entry surveys its causes, its martyrs, and its theology. The blood of the martyrs, through the centuries: its brave theology consoles the persecuted faithful of every age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-person: Person is the great term of theology and philosophy, meaning the rational individual. This entry examines its history, its definitions, and its mysteries. The word that holds the Trinity: its classic definition took many long centuries to fully forge at last.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-hutton: This biographical entry profiles Peter Hutton, an English Jesuit of the 1600s, tracing his career, his ministry, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Jesuit gallery, preserved among its records of English preachers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petun-nation: The Petun were the Tobacco Nation of Ontario, kin to the Hurons and evangelized by the Jesuits. This entry by Arthur Jones notes their territory, their customs, and their tragic dispersal in the Iroquois wars. The people of the tobacco fields.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philemon: Philemon is St. Paul's tender letter pleading for the runaway slave Onesimus. This entry examines its occasion, its message, and its place in the canon. The shortest letter of the Apostle: its tender plea for Onesimus is a small masterpiece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-reping: Philip Repington was the bishop who first followed Wyclif and then condemned him. This entry traces his career, his recantation, and his episcopate. The convert of the Lollard crisis: his fiery sermons once shook the great medieval universities of England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philipp-melan: Melanchthon was Luther's gentle scholar, the Praeceptor Germaniae who systematized the Reformation. This entry covers his career, his theology, and his legacy. The mild reformer of Wittenberg: his famous Loci Communes shaped all Protestant theology for centuries afterward in Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippe-pier: This biographical entry profiles Philippe Pierson, a French churchman of the 1800s, tracing his career and his service as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's French gallery, preserved among its records of France's 19th-century clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-physical-effe: This article examines the bodily consequences of abortion from the medical knowledge of 1913. It surveys the physical dangers, the moral context, and the Church's condemnation. A sober medical-moral study of its day, grounded in the medical science of 1913.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-physiological: This scientific article explains how living bodies take in and transform nourishment, from the biology of 1913. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-chaign: This biographical entry profiles Pierre Chaignon, a French Jesuit of the 1800s, tracing his career, his spiritual writings, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Jesuit gallery, preserved among its spiritual directors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-charro: Pierre Charron was the moralist whose De la Sagesse taught a stoic wisdom just short of faith. This entry covers his career, his book, and his influence. The skeptic in a cassock: his dangerous wisdom book guided the French libertines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-coton: Père Coton was the Jesuit confessor of Henry IV who guided the king's return to the Church. This entry traces his direction, his influence, and his writings. The confessor of the Béarnais: his powerful sermons converted the skeptical royal court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-d-aubu: Pierre d'Aubusson was the Grand Master who held Rhodes against Mehmed II's great siege. This entry traces his defense, his rule, and his fame. The shield of Christendom in 1480: his mighty walls broke the surging Ottoman tide at Rhodes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-de-lau: Pierre de Lauzon was the Jesuit superior who governed the Canadian missions in their heroic age. This entry traces his superiorship, his labors, and his times. The superior of the martyrs' missions: his sad term saw the glorious Huron martyrdoms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-de-voy: Pierre de Voyer d'Argenson was the governor of New France in its struggling years. This entry traces his administration, his challenges, and his recall. The governor of the infant colony: his sudden recall ended a troubled term in utter disgrace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-talon: This biographical entry profiles Pierre Talon, a French explorer of the 1600s, tracing his voyages, his discoveries, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's gallery of explorers, preserved among its Mississippi pioneers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ponce-de-leon: Ponce de León was the conquistador who sought the Fountain of Youth and found Florida. This entry traces his voyages, his governorship, and his death. The discoverer of the Flowery Land: his fabled fountain proved a cruel mirage at last.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-conon: Conon was the Sicilian pope of 687, old and sick at his election. This entry notes his brief pontificate and the scant records. The venerable elder of the seventh century: his peaceful election pleased all the warring Roman factions at once.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-porphyreon: Porphyreon was a city of ancient Phoenicia important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Levantine coast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-postcommunion: The Postcommunion is the Mass prayer after the faithful have received. This entry explains its form, its history, and its meaning. The thanksgiving of the sacred banquet: its brief prayer seals the holy Mass each day worldwide in ancient Latin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-postulation: Postulation is the canonical petition for a dispensation or favor. This entry explains its kinds, its procedure, and its effects. The Church's formal asking: its humble petitions seek the pope's gracious favor in eternal Rome itself today still heard gladly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pragmatic-san: The Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges asserted the French Church's liberties. This entry explains its articles, its fate, and its significance. The charter of Gallicanism: its bold articles curbed the distant pope in Rome itself in 1438's hot July days of Bourges.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-preconization: Preconization is the consistory's formal naming of a bishop. This entry explains its rite, its history, and its law. The pope's public choice: its solemn rite names the chosen bishop-elect in papal Rome itself in solemn consistory hall today still.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-predestinatio: Predestination is God's eternal decree of the elect's glory. This long entry examines its mystery, its schools, and the Catholic doctrine. The secret of the chosen: its awful mystery humbles the proudest human mind to lowly dust in holy awe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prescription: Prescription is the moral theologian's term for rights acquired by time. This entry explains its conditions, its kinds, and its applications. The theology of time's title: its silent years vest the hidden right in moral conscience at last in peace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-presumption: Presumption is the sin of rash hope in God's mercy. This entry explains its kinds, its gravity, and its remedies. The counterfeit of true hope: its blind rashness offends a holy and just heaven itself in foolish pride and folly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-promulgation: Promulgation is the publication that makes a law binding. This entry explains its forms, its necessity, and its effects. The birth of the law: its solemn act makes the dead statute live at last in binding force of holy law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psalms-of-sol: The Psalms of Solomon are the apocryphal hymns of the Pharisees' age. This entry examines their origin, their contents, and their value. The songs of the Hasidim: their fervent hope awaited the promised Messiah in prayer and fasting and tears.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psychological: Psychological assimilation is the mind's digestion of new knowledge. This entry explains its process and its place in teaching. The learning that becomes one's own: its quiet digestion feeds the growing mind in school each passing day in turn unbroken.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quilon: Quilon became the diocese of India's Malabar coast. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history as of 1913. The faith on the pepper coast: its old churches dot the Kerala lagoons in India's sunny south in living faith today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ratisbon: Ratisbon became the diocese of Regensburg. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The faith on the Danube's north bank: its twin-towered cathedral crowns the old city of Ratisbon in Bavaria's green heart of faith and ancient stone and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-breto: Raymond Breton was the Dominican missionary of the Caribs. This entry notes his grammar, his missions, and his labors. The apostle of Guadeloupe: his great dictionary saved the Carib language from oblivion in printed form forevermore in print and ink.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-caron: Raymond Caron was the Irish Franciscan theologian. This entry notes his works, his teaching, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A quiet name of the Friars Minor: his subtle theses filled the Irish schools of theology in Louvain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reason: Reason is the mind's power of knowing truth. This long entry examines its nature, its rights, and its relation to faith. The lamp of the intellect: its clear light serves the Catholic faith in truth and charity and hope and reason.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-recollection: Recollection is the gathering of the mind into God's presence. This entry explains its practice, its degrees, and its fruits. The silence that finds the Guest: its daily habit stills the restless soul in quiet prayer and holy peace and love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-redemption: Redemption is Christ's buying back of fallen man. This long entry examines its nature, its price, and its fruits. The ransom of the world: its precious blood bought the sinful slaves of Satan and sin and death and hell itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regeneration: Regeneration is the new birth of baptism. This entry examines its nature, its effects, and its theology. The washing of the second birth: its cleansing water renews the sinful soul in baptismal grace and light and life eternal and new.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religion: Religion is man's bond with God expressed in worship. This long entry examines its nature, its history, and its necessity. The virtue that honors the divine: its true worship crowns the humble soul with grace and peace and joy and light.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-con: The Congregations of the Presentation are the sisterhoods of Mary's feast. This entry notes their foundations, their schools, and their works. The daughters of the Presentation: their quiet convents dot the dioceses of France and beyond the seas in prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-of-: The Religious of Perpetual Adoration are the adorers of the Host. This entry notes their foundation, their rule, and their houses. The watchers before the tabernacle: their holy hours never cease day or night in prayer and praise and song.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-pro: Religious profession is the solemn taking of the vows. This entry explains its kinds, its effects, and its rite. The marriage to Christ: its solemn vows bind the soul to Christ forever in love and fidelity and joy and peace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-tol: Religious toleration is the state's patience with differing faiths. This entry examines its principle, its limits, and the Catholic doctrine. The peace of the mixed city: its civil law permits the sects to worship in peace and quiet and order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-edouard-: René-Édouard Caron was the Quebec jurist and lieutenant-governor. This entry notes his career, his offices, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A French-Canadian statesman: his judicial robes graced the bench of Quebec's courts in the 1800s' decades.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-renunciation: Renunciation is the giving up of a right or office. This entry explains its kinds, its conditions, and its effects. The surrender of the claim: its solemn act frees the office for another's hands in law and peace and order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reparation: Reparation is the making amends to the Sacred Heart. This entry explains its devotion, its practices, and its theology. The atonement of the loving heart: its holy hours console the Heart of Jesus in love and tears and prayer and song.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reservation: Reservation is the pope's keeping of benefices to himself. This entry explains its kinds, its history, and its law. The papal hold on the appointment: its ancient right names the bishop of Rome's choice in conclave's vote of scarlet cardinals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-restitution: Restitution is the paying back of what was unjustly taken. This entry examines its obligation, its measure, and its theology. The repair of the stolen good: its stern debt binds the conscience till paid in full and just measure of right.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-revelation: Revelation is God's speaking to man of Himself. This long entry examines its nature, its modes, and its completion. The divine unveiling of truth: its living word ends in Christ Jesus our Lord and King and God and Man and Savior.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-revocation: Revocation is the withdrawing of a grant or privilege. This entry explains its kinds, its conditions, and its effects. The recall of the favor: its formal decree annuls the papal grant in law and fact and right and deed and name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-angel: Richard Angelus Mason was the English Franciscan of the penal years. This entry notes his career, his works, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A friar of the hidden church: his brown habit braved the penal laws.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-archd: Richard Archdeacon was the Irish Jesuit of the penal age. This entry notes his ministry, his sufferings, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A priest of the hedgerows: his secret Mass hid in the Irish hills at dawn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-broug: Richard Broughton was the English priest-historian. This entry notes his writings, his ministry, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A chronicler of the recusants: his faithful pen recorded the suffering recusants of England's north in the 1600s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-malco: Richard Malcolm Johnston was the Georgia storyteller of the Old South. This entry notes his tales, his humor, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A humorist of the plantation: his warm tales charmed the South in print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-samps: Richard Sampson was the bishop turned royal servant. This entry notes his sees, his compliance, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A prelate of the Henrician schism: his ready pen served the king in schism and divorce.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-simps: Richard Simpson was the priest of the English mission's peril. This entry notes his ministry, his sufferings, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A laborer of the secret church: his secret altar hid in the attic of the manor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-uller: Richard Ullerston was the Oxford theologian of the fifteenth century. This entry notes his writings, his teaching, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A doctor of the schools: his learned lectures filled Oxford's halls in the 1400s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-wilto: Richard Wilton was the Oxford theologian of the thirteenth century. This entry notes his writings, his teaching, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A scholastic of the schools: his subtle questions filled Oxford's schools in the 1200s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-right-honoura: John Thompson was the Catholic premier of Canada. This entry traces his career, his faith, and his death. The prime minister of the Dominion: his daily Mass steadied the cabinet in Ottawa's halls of power in the 1890s' winters of snow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-right-of-excl: The right of exclusion is the veto of Catholic crowns in conclave. This entry explains its history, its exercise, and its end. The royal no to the papabile: its last veto fell in 1903's conclave in Rome's Sistine Chapel forever.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-right-of-opti: The right of option is the canon's choice of a prebend. This entry explains its nature, its conditions, and its law. The choosing of the vacant stall: its senior canon claims the prebend in chapter's vote of canons in choir.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-right-of-pres: The right of presentation is the patron's naming of the priest. This entry explains its origin, its exercise, and its law. The founder's voice in the appointment: its lay patron names the rector of the parish church in England's shires.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-right-of-volu: The right of voluntary association is the natural right to unite. This entry examines its basis, its limits, and the Catholic doctrine. The freedom of the guild and union: its natural right guards the workers of the world in justice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-henrys: Robert Henryson was the schoolmaster-poet of Dunfermline. This entry notes his fables, his Testament, and his art. The Chaucer of Scotland: his moral fables charmed the north of Scotland in Scots tongue and rhyme and wit and wisdom and grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-of-cou: Robert of Courçon was the cardinal-legate of the Albigensian age. This entry notes his legation, his statutes, and his death. The reformer of Paris's schools: his stern statutes bound the masters of Paris in 1215's August heat and dust of summer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rockhampton: Rockhampton became the diocese of central Queensland. This entry covers its bishops, its parishes, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the Australian bush: its hardy priests ride the ranges of Queensland's interior in the saddle in the 1880s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roger-anderto: Roger Anderton was the Lancashire priest of the penal mission. This entry notes his ministry, his sufferings, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roger-bacon: Roger Bacon was the Franciscan doctor of experiment. This entry examines his science, his Opus Majus, and his fame. The wonderful doctor of Oxford: his brave lenses foresaw the future in the 1260s' Oxford of friars and scholars and saints.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roscommon: Roscommon became the county of the western plain. This entry covers its churches, its abbeys, and its history. The faith of the Connacht land: its ruined abbeys dot the plain of Connacht's west in Ireland's green land of lakes and bogs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-francis: The Saint Francis Mission served the Sioux of the Rosebud. This entry covers its Jesuits, its schools, and its history as of 1913. The mission of the Lakota plain: its mission school teaches the Sioux in Dakota's Rosebud in the 1880s.

complete-project-gutenberg-collection-of:
Three memoir collections by various insiders of Napoleon's court fill this large Project Gutenberg gathering. Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne, Napoleon's private secretary and school friend from Brienne, anchors the volume. His memoirs, edited by R. W. Phipps, show the emperor at work and at home. Bourrienne claims impartial aim, praising and blaming his old master in turn.

Constant, the emperor's premier valet de chambre, adds Recollections of the Private Life of Napoleon in Walter Clark's translation. Stewarton's Memoirs of the Court of St. Cloud close the set as secret letters from Paris to London. Together the three give campaigns, councils, dress, temper, and table talk from men who stood in the room. Editors extended Bourrienne past the Elba abdication through Waterloo to the death at St. Helena. Napoleon readers who want the private man behind the battles, in slippers as much as in uniform, start with these witnesses.
concept-great-power-mattison:
Ages of the world roll past in a short apocalypse from the Nag Hammadi codices. The Concept of Our Great Power, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives that vision in English. The power of the title is the high God, whose plan the seer lays bare.

The text moves from creation through the flood and the age of flesh to fire and final rest. It tells how the savior comes, how the rulers fail, and how the saved are known. The sweep is vast for so brief a book. Mattison's free rendering lets readers trace that sweep in one sitting.
coningsby-or-the-new-generation: Coningsby, or The New Generation, Benjamin Disraeli's political novel. The young politician. This book preserves that classic. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
country-life-in-canada-fifty-years-ago-p:
Canniff Haight's Country Life in Canada Fifty Years Ago gathers the personal recollections of a sexagenarian looking back on pioneer Ontario. Haight dedicates the book to the young men of Canada, on whose integrity and energy, he writes, the future of their great heritage rests.

The recollections cover clearing land, building homes, travelling rough roads, worship, school and neighbourly life in a colony still close to the forest. Haight writes as a man who lived the changes he describes, contrasting the hardships of early settlement with the settled country of his old age. Readers interested in Canadian social history will find here a first-hand, unpretentious account of how ordinary settlers actually lived.
criticism-and-fiction:
William Dean Howells argued the case for literary realism in Criticism and Fiction, a collection of his critical essays. Howells asks whether any lasting standard of taste exists. Quoting John Addington Symonds, he answers that fashion changes but truth endures. What is simple, natural, and honest in art, he argues, stays beautiful. Fantastic and artificial work pleases briefly, then fades.

Essays take up fiction's aims, the role of the editor, and the faults of romantic storytelling. Howells praises novels that study ordinary life honestly. He attacks false sentiment and stagey plots. His manner is conversational, full of asides about dress, furniture, and painting. Readers get the clearest statement of the realist creed that shaped Howells's own novels and his editing of a generation of American writers.
