One hundred twenty engineers and scientists met at Marshall Space Flight Center on October 5 and 6, 1967, for this conference. The topic was molecular radiation and its use in diagnostic techniques. R. Goulard of Purdue University edited the proceedings; W. K. Dahm chaired with him.

Glowing molecules betray temperature and composition, which is why rocket engineers care. The meeting reviewed current work and weighed new research directions. An open forum on the second day was transcribed in full. The catalog record names rocket base heating and the behavior of liquid rocket propellant plumes among the subjects.
nasa-tm-19680012351-aerobee-350-rocket-i:
C. D. Tackett, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, documents the Aerobee 350 sounding rocket's nerve system in this report. It describes the rocket's instrumentation and telemetry, the gear that measures the flight and radios the results down. Three launches had flown by the time of writing.

The first launch checked that the rocket and its Wallops Island launcher worked together. The next two carried heavily instrumented payloads for ionospheric and solar physics groups. Tackett describes the flight gear in detail. He also describes the ground equipment that checked the rockets out and received and recorded their data.
nasa-tm-19680013786-measurement-of-pilot:
Rodney C. Wingrove and Frederick G. Edwards of NASA's Ames Research Center address a measurement problem in flight testing in this 1968 memorandum. Engineers use pilot describing functions to sum up how a pilot responds to control inputs. Under normal flight test conditions, a known error distorts those measurements.

The error comes from a link between the input error signal and the pilot's own output noise. Shifting the input signal during computer work by the pilot's time delay cuts that error down. A simulated pilot model shows how the method works in practice. Real records from the retrofire phase of the Gemini X flight then prove the method works with normal spacecraft data.
nasa-tm-19680023796-an-ion-exosphere-wit:
R. E. Hartle of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this August 1968 preprint, numbered X-615-68-303, on the ion-exosphere of a planet. The exosphere is the outermost air layer, where particles so rarely collide that many escape. Its base, the baropause, is where Hartle lets conditions vary, improving an earlier model by Eviatar, Lenchek, and Singer.

That earlier model held density and temperature uniform across the baropause of a nonrotating planet. Hartle allows both to differ even between magnetically linked points on that surface. He then builds the ion and electron speed patterns for the varied case. From them he derives densities, currents, pressures, and temperatures, and compares each against the uniform case.
nasa-tm-19680024850-complex-stochastic-n:
John H. Painter of Langley Research Center and Someshwar C. Gupta, of Southern Methodist University in Dallas, presented this paper at a June 1968 communications conference in Philadelphia. Their subject is complex stochastic noise and modulation: random signals, and the signals that carry messages, treated with one shared mathematics. Radio engineers need such tools whenever noise crowds a channel.

The authors use distribution theory to write random modulation and noise as smooth analytic time functions. That move makes the random case as workable as the orderly signals engineers already handled this way. Applying the method, they obtain new results on recovering single sideband angle-modulated signals buried in noise. The paper builds the theory step by step toward that payoff.
nasa-tm-19680024874-a-sinusoidal-pulse-t:
James T. Howlett and Dennis J. Martin of Langley Research Center propose a new vibration test technique in this paper, presented in May 1968. Many environmental tests rest on shock spectra and slowly swept sine inputs. The input needed to mimic a transient depends heavily on the test item's damping.

Standard practice uses a single damping value for setting test levels. That choice heavily overtests systems with low damping, the authors note. Their method instead sends a spaced sequence of sinusoidal pulses. Pulse frequency, amplitude, and count are chosen to account for response variation with damping. The technique aims for fair tests across structures with different damping levels.
nasa-tm-19690013440-proton-energy-into-t:
D. J. Williams and C. O. Bostrom of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this April 1969 paper on proton entry into the magnetosphere on May 26, 1967. A solar proton event had begun three days earlier, flooding near-Earth space with fast protons. The pair compare proton readings over the polar cap with outside readings. Their sources span interplanetary space and the magnetosheath, just outside Earth's magnetic bubble.

Their results indicate that diffusion, a slow random spreading, controlled the protons' entry at that time. The protons reached the whole figure-eight current pattern of the geomagnetic tail, they find. Explorer 34 supplied the outside readings, while a second satellite watched the polar cap. Only a rough upper limit could be set for where the tail diffusion began.
nasa-tm-19690014116-applications-of-auge:
Isidore Adler presented this talk on Auger and photoelectron spectroscopy in March 1969, to the Washington-Baltimore chapter of the Society of Applied Spectroscopy. Goddard Space Flight Center issued the text in April 1969. A co-author's name is poorly rendered in the scan, so only Adler is named here. Both methods read the electrons atoms give off, and from them name the elements present.

Adler begins with first principles, in his own plain style. Strike an inner electron out of an atom, and an outer electron drops to fill the gap. The freed energy either leaves as a characteristic X-ray, or knocks out a second electron, the Auger electron. The talk then covers the instruments and the practical uses of both methods.
nasa-tm-19690028204-a-preliminary-survey:
J. P. Heppner, B. G. Ledley, T. L. Skillman, and M. Sugiura, of Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this preprint, X-612-69-429. They survey the distribution of micropulsations in the magnetosphere from OGO 3 and OGO 5 data. Micropulsations are small rhythmic wiggles in the magnetic field, sorted here into seven period bands plus irregular types.

Scanning is still incomplete, the authors caution, yet the main patterns already stand out near the equatorial plane. One wave family shows a broad dayside maximum, roughly independent of distance from Earth. Its character matches the same family's well known behavior at the surface exceptionally well. Separate chapters cover the magnetosheath waves and activity indices built from them.
nasa-tm-19700015418-evaluation-of-integr:
John W. Fairbanks of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in September 1969. It evaluates solar cells whose protective covers are built right onto the cell surface. In space, bare silicon cells face radiation damage, so a cover matters. A built-in cover also promised lower cost and better power for its weight.

Goddard funded three separate efforts to make such covers, and Fairbanks compares how each one worked. One approach fused borosilicate glass onto the cell, while the other two used forms of sputtering. The report then tests the covered cells for coating quality, soldering, heat and damp exposure, and proton damage. A long closing section weighs the results and draws conclusions.
nasa-tm-19700024852-deposition-of-ion-th:
John V. Staskus and Robert J. Burns of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 electric propulsion conference at Stanford. It studies what ion thruster exhaust leaves on spacecraft surfaces. The test craft was SERT II, which flew ion engines in orbit.

Mercury vapor from the thrusters can settle on nearby surfaces and foul them. An experiment aboard SERT II was built to catch this contamination in flight. Earlier estimates counted how much material escaped, the authors note. They did not show where the particles spread. The flight test gave the first direct check of the problem in space.
nasa-tm-19700025433-lm-landing-radar-tes:
The Systems Analysis Branch at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston issued this Apollo internal note, number MSC-EG-69-14. It covers the lunar module landing radar test for the F mission. Mission F was Apollo 10, the final rehearsal before the first landing attempt, flown in lunar orbit.

Earlier radar flight tests used aircraft over White Sands, bouncing signals off Earth's surface. Those tests could not reach the highest speeds and heights of an actual lunar descent, though. So a test was set for the F mission itself, using the Moon as the reflecting surface. The study fixes antenna position and craft attitude for the test, and estimates how many seconds of usable beam data to expect.
nasa-tm-19700026394-flight-analysis-of-t:
NASA issued this Apollo working paper, number 1196, as a flight analysis of the Apollo propulsion systems. It studies how the program's rocket engines actually performed in flight. Such studies compare flight data with what designers expected before launch, and they feed lessons into the next flights.

Aims are set for each stage of the work: before flight, during flight, and after flight alike. Analysis served two uses, checking performance and hunting the causes of malfunctions. Flight data were adjusted by weighted least squares to give best estimates of performance values. Models of the flight path and of each propulsion system supported that fitting, including a careful measure of specific impulse.
nasa-tm-19700026409-dynamic-spacecraft-s:
NASA issued this Apollo working paper, number 1178, on dynamic spacecraft simulation. The work concerns the signals that tracking stations receive from a moving spacecraft. Motion shifts those signals through Doppler effects and time delays, and test gear had to copy those shifts faithfully on the ground.

First come the signal traits of the unified S-band ranging system, described in detail. A realistic copy of both Doppler shift and range delay, the summary states, can be achieved. The technique uses frequency translation to copy radio and clock Doppler effects. Range delay is copied by digitally holding back parts of the ranging code, and each step of the method is set out in turn.
nasa-tm-19700026799-a-graphical-approach:
James C. Taylor of the Astrionics Laboratory wrote this report on September 26, 1969. It comes from the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama. It presents a graphical approach to convolution, a math operation that blends two curves into a third, met throughout signal and systems work.

Taylor argues that most writing on convolution is either rigorous analysis or narrow specialty material. His paper instead draws the operation, with just enough analysis to make each step plain. Worked cases cover two similar pulses, two unlike pulses, and a function combined with an impulse. Later sections treat scanning and superposition traits, the response of a linear system, and the convolution theorem.
nasa-tm-19700032730-effect-of-pressurant:
Steven G. Berenyi of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in October 1970. It studies how the shape of a pressurant inlet changes liquid outflow in weightlessness. A pressurant gas pushes liquid out of a tank, and in space the liquid floats free.

Berenyi reports tests in both normal gravity and a weightless setting. The normal tests set up known pressure patterns inside the tank first. The weightless tests then measured how much liquid stayed behind. The key moment came when vapor, not liquid, began to leave the tank. Tank designers used such results to waste less fuel in orbit.
nasa-tm-19710004951-future-fields-of-con:
NASA issued this volume on future fields of control application. It gathers work from a symposium on where control theory would next be put to use. Automatic control guides everything from aircraft to factory machines, and its reach was growing fast into fields far from engineering.

One sample talk takes up new technology in mass media communication, meaning the printing trade. The speaker calls progress in the graphic arts appalling for two centuries after Gutenberg. Lately, though, a rush of new developments had thrown the industry into ferment. Talks like this one let specialists in very different fields compare how new control and communication tools were changing their work.
nasa-tm-19710007347-field-tests-using-de:
William C. Mastin and Peter H. Broussard Jr. of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on January 18, 1971. It gives field tests of remote navigation for a lunar surface vehicle. Drivers on Earth would steer the vehicle using dead reckoning and a single camera view, with no direct sight of the ground it crossed.

The tests ran ordinary vehicles, a Jeep and a Travelall, fitted as remote driving rigs. Objectives and ground rules come first, then how the system was put together and what happened. Appendices study how gyro updates affect the accuracy of closing a traverse. Driving tests in a crater field, and a sortie log, show the method working over rough, Moon-like ground.
nasa-tm-19710008032-space-flight-with-el:
NASA issued this survey under the title Space Flight with Electric Propulsion. It treats the development and the traits of electric propulsion systems. Such engines serve both crewed and uncrewed spacecraft on long missions, trading a weak but steady push for great savings in propellant.

The survey opens with the fundamental relations of propulsion in space, then historical highlights. Electric thrusters get a full section, and power generation another, covering nuclear and solar-cell options. Mission chapters treat the SERT test craft and auxiliary uses for electric engines. Primary propulsion for uncrewed and crewed craft is weighed last, before a look at other advanced methods such as the nuclear rocket.
nasa-tm-19710017435-artificial-meteor-ab:
Maxwell B Blanchard of the Ames Research Center burned natural iron minerals in a hot air plasma stream to mimic meteors. The minerals were mostly magnetite and hematite, the iron oxides found in real meteor material. Ablation is the melting and stripping a meteor suffers as it dives through air. Blanchard then examined the melted debris grain by grain.

Most debris grains mixed two or more minerals. A rare unstable mineral, wustite, appeared often in the products. The more volatile elements dropped by about a third during the burn. Iron grew richer as other elements left and its oxidation state fell. Blanchard concluded that such lab made debris carries clear fingerprints. Their shapes, textures, and odd minerals can identify real cosmic dust.
nasa-tm-19720007228-space-shuttle-stagin:
Charles E Hall of the Marshall Space Flight Center and Rex D Agler of Northrup Corporation wrote this report on December 27, 1971, as NASA TM X-64631. Hall worked in the Aero Astrodynamics Laboratory. They describe a new computer program that simulates space shuttle staging. Staging is the risky moment when a spent booster separates in flight. A good simulation lets engineers rehearse it safely many times.

The program's special strength is its treatment of separation hardware. It can model linkage type separation devices, not just simple push off systems. It also covers the other common separation methods. The report lays out the program's overall capability in detail. Shuttle designs of the day depended on safe, clean booster separation.
nasa-tm-19720007232-atlas-centaur-26-int:
Kennedy Space Center issued this operations summary on October 7, 1971, for the Atlas Centaur 26 mission. The launch carried the Intelsat 4 F3 communications satellite. The summary runs to thirty six pages and carries the center's report number TR-1132. It records how the mission was planned and run from the Florida launch site. Intelsat satellites formed the backbone of global commercial communications.

Six subjects structure the account. They run from mission objective and mission plan through launch operations. Post launch operations and communications equipment follow. Test operations close the list, and illustrations support the text. Such summaries preserved a full record of a launch campaign. Later mission teams could study what the earlier crew had done.
nasa-tm-19720022032-emitter-surface-temp:
Richard B Lancashire, Eugene J Manista, James F Morris, and Arthur L Smith of the Lewis Research Center mapped heat on a tiny emitter in August 1972, as NASA TM X-2588. The emitter belonged to a miniature thermionic diode, nicknamed a diminiode. Its glowing face measured barely over half a centimeter across. Even heating matters, because output depends on surface temperature everywhere. The team read brightness temperatures at five spots.

Five tiny cavities, called hohlraums, were spaced evenly across a diameter. Each cavity's glow revealed the local temperature at that point. The surface sat in a test setup mimicking the diminiode layout. Heat came from behind the surface, as in real operation. The readings showed how evenly the small emitter truly heated. Diode designers used such maps to judge their models.
natural-history-of-the-mammalia-of-india:
Robert A. Sterndale published his Natural History of the Mammalia of India and Ceylon in 1884. Thacker firms in Calcutta, Bombay, and London issued the book. It carries 170 pictures drawn by Sterndale, T. W. Wood, and others, with a tiger as frontispiece.

Sterndale says his preface aim was a popular handbook of Indian mammals. Older works, he notes, covered only the peninsula and missed Assam, Burmah, and Ceylon. He widened the range to lands a sportsman from India might reach. He also dropped the stiff form of older natural histories. The book thus served hunters, officers, and general readers across the region.
nature-near-london:
Richard Jefferies wrote Nature Near London, shown here in a fine paper edition from Chatto and Windus in 1905. Jefferies also wrote The Life of the Fields and The Open Air. The contents list short pieces named Woodlands, Footpaths, and Flocks of Birds.

Other pieces follow a nightingale road, a brook, and a London trout. A barn, wheatfields, and crows get chapters of their own. Each title points to wild life found close to a great city, not far from it. The book suits readers who walk the edges of London and want to notice what lives there.
norwegian-life-an-account-of-past-and-co:
Ethlyn T. Clough edited and arranged Norwegian Life, an account of past and present conditions in Norway and Sweden. First chapters cover prehistoric and early historic times. Norway in the nineteenth century, then Sweden in the same century, follow. The religion of the Northmen gets a chapter of its own.

Later chapters treat the literature of both lands, then their government and politics. Army and navy, public education, and charitable work come next. Haakon the Seventh, new king of Norway, and Sweden's royal family are introduced. Roads, railways, waterways, manners, health, newspapers, folk songs, and women fill the rest. English readers got a whole survey in one book.
observations-upon-the-windward-coast-of-:
Joseph Corry based this account on travel in 1805 and 1806. It was printed in London in 1807. Corry describes the Windward Coast of Africa. He writes about religion, character, and customs of the people there. He also describes natural and trade resources.

Corry proposes a plan to spread European ways in the region. He hopes readers will learn more about the African interior. An appendix holds his letter to Lord Howick. That letter urges a simple, strong way to end the slave trade. The book mixes travel report, trade survey, and reform appeal. His dedication thanks Lord Castlereagh for support and permission.
of-captain-mission:
Daniel Defoe wrote the life of Captain Misson and his crew. It opens volume two of The History of the Pyrates. That second part appeared in 1728. The introduction notes Defoe hid behind the name Captain Charles Johnson. Scholars identified him as the author only in 1932.

Misson is presented as a pirate with unusual ideals. The editor calls the tale one of Defoe's finest neglected fictions. It follows the manner of the first pirate volume. Yet it reads more like an invented moral adventure. Readers value it as bold early pirate fiction. The Clark Memorial Library editors prepared this modern reprint edition.
old-john-brown-the-man-whose-soul-is-mar:
Walter Hawkins wrote this short life of abolitionist John Brown. The preface is dated at Kilburn in May 1913. Hawkins wrote for busy people short on time. He relies much on Sanborn's Life and Letters of Brown. Chapters run from Brown's childhood vow to Harper's Ferry.

Hawkins treats the Underground Railway and Brown's call to act. He ends with the march of Brown's soul after death. The famous song claimed Brown's body moldered in the grave. Hawkins argues the story deserves fuller English attention. Chapter heads trace the Long Waiting-Time and How the Call Came. A later head joins Bible and Sword as twin themes.
on-our-selection:
Steele Rudd wrote these comic tales of Australian bush life. His real name was Arthur Hoey Davis. He dedicated the book to Australia's unnamed pioneers. Good Old Dad receives a special, fond dedication. The contents follow a family starting a selection farm.

Chapters treat harvests, deeds, drought, and a wolf at the door. Dad, Dave, and Kate face snakes, hunts, and weddings. A circus, a bear venture, and corn years add humor. Dry outback humor runs through every hard season. The tales honor settlers who toiled in lonely country. Heads name a night watch for wallabies in the bush. Kate's wedding and Dan's homecoming add warmth to the set.
on-the-brink-of-a-chasm-a-record-of-plot:
L. T. Meade published this novel in New York in 1899. Chatto and Windus issued the London edition that year. Meade had written The Medicine Lady before this book. Chapter one is titled Undone, chapter two A Man's Revenge. The subtitle promises a record of plot and passion.

Catalog notes say Nurse Clara uses hypnotism in the tale. She rescues a young aristocrat from a villain. Hypnotism was a daring, fashionable device for fiction then. Meade blends sensation, romance, and moral danger. The title hints at a life near ruin. The book suits fans of Victorian popular novels.
ontario-normal-school-manuals-science-of:
Ontario's Department of Education issued this teacher manual in Toronto. The Ryerson Press printed it, with copyright in 1915. The minister of education authorized the manual for normal schools. A second printing came in 1919, a third in 1923. Part one sets out the principles of education.

Chapter one treats the nature and purpose of education. It covers growth, human worth, and social efficiency. Chapter two treats instinctive, habitual, and conscious reactions. Experience and its relative value receive careful attention. Chapter three turns to the process of education itself. The manual trained Ontario teachers in a shared science.
oonomoo-the-huron:
Edward Sylvester Ellis wrote this frontier adventure for young readers. Hurst and Company copyrighted this edition in 1911. Ellis also wrote The Trail-Hunter and Hunter's Cabin. Chapter one introduces a comic figure, Hans Vanderbum. Oonomoo meets the Shawnees in chapter three.

A young lieutenant and Cato enter in chapter four. The home of the Huron and adventures follow. A plan for a rescue shapes the middle chapters. Hans performs an exploit before a new danger rises. The tale ends in a short concluding chapter. Ellis writes fast frontier fiction with Native characters. Mary Prescott appears among the pictured figures.
origin-world-mattison:
Creation gets a strange new telling in a Sethian book from the Nag Hammadi codices. On the Origin of the World, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives that bold text in English. Its makers held that the world was made by lesser, flawed powers, not by the high God.

The book tells how chaos bred rulers, how the first man was formed, and how wisdom slipped into the world. Flood, paradise, and the serpent all appear in turned-around form. Scholars prize the text for its wild map of the cosmos and its mix of myths. Mattison's version opens the strange work to all readers.
our-changing-constitution: Charles W. Pierson's Our Changing Constitution argues that the Constitution changes in practice while its text stands still. It was published in New York in 1922. The hosted sample shows the title page and a contents list with detailed chapter summaries, but no body text. The summaries promise chapters on national and state power. They also cover the Supreme Court and its power to strike down laws. Causes of change follow, from wars and railroads to immigration. This note follows the contents alone.
our-government-local-state-and-national-: Our Government: Local, State, and National, in its Idaho edition, is a school civics textbook. J. A. James and A. H. Sanford wrote it, and Scribner's issued it in 1903 and 1913. The hosted sample shows the title page and contents only. Part One covers local government: counties, origins, and cities. Part Two runs from the Union's formation through Congress and the presidency. The Constitution itself sits in an appendix. No lesson text appears in the sample.
our-vanishing-wild-life-its-exterminatio:
William T. Hornaday, director of the New York Zoological Park, opened Our Vanishing Wild Life with an indictment. He reprints an 1857 Ohio Senate report that refused to protect the passenger pigeon. Wonderfully prolific, the senators said. The birds travel hundreds of miles, here today and elsewhere tomorrow. No ordinary destruction could lessen them. The snipe, too, would take care of itself.

Facing the report stands a photograph of the last living passenger pigeon, twenty years old in 1912, in the Cincinnati Zoological Gardens. The folly of 1857 and the lesson of 1912, Hornaday captions it. His book, subtitled its extermination and preservation, became a founding blast of the American conservation movement, written by the man who had helped save the bison.
out-of-doors-california-and-oregon: J. A. Graves's Out of Doors — California and Oregon collects sporting and travel sketches from the West. It was published in 1912 and profusely illustrated. The hosted sample shows the contents and list of illustrations only. A motor trip in San Diego's back country is promised. So are boyhood days in early California, and an auto trip through the Sierras. The illustrations run to Klamath Lake in Oregon. No sketch text appears.
outlines-of-english-and-american-literat: William J. Long's Outlines of English and American Literature introduces the chief writers of two nations. Their books and their times come with them, as the subtitle promises. The hosted sample shows the title pages and a dedication to the author's sister. A long caption discusses the Chandos portrait of Shakespeare. The preface begins just as the sample ends. No page of Long's literary history itself appears here.
over-the-top-with-the-third-australian-d: G. P. Cuttriss's Over the Top with the Third Australian Division is a brief volume of sketch and story. Major-General Sir John Monash, the division's commander, provides its introduction. The book is dedicated to the fadeless memory of the heroic dead. Those who lost them share the dedication. The hosted sample shows the title pages and that dedication. A contents heading follows, and the text stops. No sketch or story appears.
paraphrase-shem-mattison:
Derdekeas, a heavenly revealer, opens the secrets of the cosmos to Shem in a Sethian apocalypse. The Paraphrase of Shem, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives that Nag Hammadi text in English. Shem is the son of Noah, here made the hearer of the end of things.

The vision maps the powers above and below, the flood, and the wars of light and dark. Its tongue is dense, its scenes vast, and its world stern. Scholars wrestle with its codes to chart Sethian thought at its most obscure. Mattison's version gives readers a firm path through the dark text.
paul-faber-surgeon: The hosted sample stops at the front matter of Paul Faber, Surgeon, the title page and a long table of contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names George MacDonald as the author, in a 1900 printing. The contents map an English village world of rectory, manor house, cottage, and pulpit, with chapters named for Paul Faber's dressing-room and study, a character called Juliet. Other chapters name places such as Owlkirk, Nestley, and Glaston.
peg-woffington:
Charles Reade inscribed Peg Woffington in December 1852 to T. Taylor, his partner in the stage comedy Masks and Faces. He calls it a dramatic story and dedicates it to the memory of Margaret Woffington, the Irish actress, whom he says was falsely summed up until today. The novel sets out to do her justice.

The first chapter opens in the mid-eighteenth century with Triplet, a threadbare scene painter, actor, and writer of bad plays, asleep in a poor lodging. His wife comes home exhausted from playing a queen at the theatre. Around such strugglers, Reade builds his portrait of Peg and the London stage.
peter-ibbetson:
George Du Maurier's Peter Ibbetson is presented as a manuscript edited by the author and introduced by Peter's cousin, who signs herself Madge Plunket. Peter calls himself a poor scribe, ill-versed in wielding words. He says he has been an object of pity and contempt to all but one person, yet counts himself perhaps the happiest of men.

His outer and inner lives, he warns, lie as far apart as the poles. The felicity he found is in regions open to all, if they learn his clue. The novel became famous for that clue: a shared life lived in dreams, beyond prison and disgrace.
plum-pudding-of-divers-ingredients-discr:
Christopher Morley published Plum Pudding in nineteen twenty-one, a book whose full title promises divers ingredients, discreetly blended and seasoned. Morley was an American essayist and novelist, and the volume came out in Garden City, New York, from Doubleday, Page and Company, with pictures by Walter Jack Duncan.

Copyright pages show the pieces first appeared in print between nineteen ten and nineteen twenty-one. Venues named include the Public Ledger, the New York Evening Post, the Outlook, and the Atlantic Monthly. So the book gathers periodical writing into one volume, in the playful, old-style dress of its title page, which lists it among other works by the same author modestly offered to readers.
poemata-latin-greek-and-italian-poems-by:
John Milton wrote poems in Latin, Greek, and Italian alongside his famous English work, and Poemata gathers those pieces in English dress, translated by William Cowper. Milton composed much of this verse as a young man, including elegies sent to his friend Charles Diodati and poems for teachers, churchmen, and Italian patrons. The collection shows the great epic poet working in the classical languages of his education.

Contents open with complimentary pieces addressed to Milton, then move through his elegies. Among them poems on the Gunpowder Plot, the approach of spring, and the deaths of university and church figures. A second section of poems in various metres adds pieces to his father, to singers in Rome, a version of Psalm 114, and the Death of Damon. Cowper's translations let English readers meet the young, learned Milton behind Paradise Lost.
poems-by-adam-lindsay-gordon:
Adam Lindsay Gordon, a British-born Australian steeplechase rider and poet who lived from 1833 to 1870, wrote the verse collected in this 1893 edition. Gordon became the first poet to give the Australian bush its own galloping voice. The book opens with a long memorial poem mourning him as the singer of the first great songs these lands can claim as their own.

Four sections organize the work: Sea Spray and Smoke Drift, Bush Ballads and Galloping Rhymes, miscellaneous poems, and Ashtaroth, a dramatic lyric. The ballads made his name, full of horses, racing, and the risks of bush life, written by a man who rode the country he described. Gordon died before his fame settled; this posthumous collection is how generations of Australians met him.
poems-of-passion:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox made her name with Poems of Passion, published in Chicago by the W. B. Conkey Company in 1883, when she was a young Wisconsin writer. The book's frank treatment of love and desire startled reviewers and delighted readers, and it launched a career that made her one of the best-selling poets in America. A portrait frontispiece and a list of her other books show a publisher already building a brand.

An opening address warns readers that songs are only shells cast up by waves of thought, hiding the soul's real mysteries like the sea hides its depths. The poems that follow speak of love in its heats and sorrows, in the direct, rhymed, emotional style that became her trademark. Dismissed by high critics then and since, Poems of Passion remains a landmark of popular American poetry and of women's writing about desire.
poetic-edda-bray-translation:
Olive Bray translated Part One of the Poetic Edda, the great store of Norse myth in verse. The Edda gathers old Icelandic poems about gods and heroes. Saemund's name was long tied to its keeping.

These poems tell of Odin seeking wisdom, Thor fighting giants, and doom at Ragnarok. Bray renders the verse in plain, strong English. Her version keeps the stark humor and fate-haunted tone of the source. The Edda anchors all Norse myth study. Any reader who loves Tolkien or northern lore will find its roots here, raw and strange.
police-operation:
H. Beam Piper published Police Operation in Astounding Science Fiction in July 1948, a novelette of his Paratime series. The epigraph from Charles Fort imagines an occult police force that diverts human suspicion from beings who exploit the earth. Piper makes the idea literal: a secret police patrols alternate timelines, and when a creature from another world line escapes onto ours. An operative must hunt it down without letting the locals learn that parallel worlds exist.

On a Pennsylvania farm, a dead heifer and a dog torn apart open the case, with a game protector and angry farmers demanding action. The hunter must work with inadequate means, since advanced weapons would blow his cover. Piper's cool, procedural treatment of an impossible beat made the story a foundation of his career and of the whole alternate-history tradition in science fiction.
practical-argumentation:
George K. Pattee, assistant professor of English and rhetoric at Pennsylvania State College, wrote Practical Argumentation and dedicated it to Fred Lewis Pattee. His preface picks a fight with the critics: argumentation courses, they said, were purely academic, mere stepping-stones to law, or excuses for intercollegiate debating contests. Pattee answers with a textbook grown in his own classroom, every rule tested time and again over years of teaching.

Illustrations come from contemporary magazines, newspapers, books, and recent speeches rather than from student themes or criminal trials. Since the average student will rarely argue a murder case but will argue everything else. Argumentation, he insists, is one of the four branches of rhetoric, a practical subject for citizens, not a sport. The book's authority is its method: a department's collective experience, printed so other teachers could run the same course.
prefaces-to-fiction:
Benjamin Boyce introduced this gathering of five early prefaces to fiction for the Augustan Reprint Society. Published at the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library in Los Angeles in 1952 as its thirty-second publication. The texts span a century of the novel's childhood: Georges de Scudéry's preface to Ibrahim of 1674. Mary Delariviere Manley's preface to the Secret History of Queen Zarah of 1705, and a letter from the Marquis d'Argens's Jewish Spy of 1744.

William Warburton's preface to the later volumes of Richardson's Clarissa of 1748 follows, with Samuel Derrick's preface to a translation of d'Argens in 1754. Together they show novelists apologizing, boasting, and theorizing before the novel had a name to defend. Why romances may teach virtue, how secret histories claim truth, and what readers were promised. For students of fiction's rise, these threshold documents are where the genre first explains itself.
prisoners-fast-bound-in-misery-and-iron:
Mary Cholmondeley, already known for her novel Red Pottage, published a new novel with Dodd, Mead and Company of New York in 1906. A verse from Julian of Norwich about failing love stands at the front as the book's guiding thought.

The frontispiece shows a woman looking toward something that holds the man she is thinking of, and the story promises strained hearts held fast by duty and feeling. Cholmondeley writes about English society, family pressure, and love that cannot move freely. Readers who like her earlier work get a serious tale of people bound by their own ties.
problems-of-poverty-an-inquiry-into-the-:
John A. Hobson studied the working poor of England in a book first printed in 1891 and issued here in its sixth edition of 1906. He begins by asking who the poor are, noting that the poor law counts only the fully destitute and so counts too few.

Chapters take up the effects of machinery, the rush of people into large towns, the sweating system and its causes and cures, and the state of women workers. Moral aspects and new laws close the survey. Readers get a careful, fact-based account of low-paid labour and its reform.
proportional-representation-a-study-in-m:
John H. Humphreys, secretary of the Proportional Representation Society, explained new ways of voting in a study first printed in 1911. Lord Courtney of Penwith added an opening essay praising the book as timely for a coming reform of the House of Commons.

Humphreys weighs the claims for and against giving each party seats in line with its votes, then shows how an election under the favoured plan would work. He notes fast gains for the idea across northern Europe and France. Readers get a clear, fair guide to ballot reform in Britain.
public-opinion:
Walter Lippmann opened his study of public opinion with Plato's picture of prisoners in a cave who see only shadows on a wall. The passage, set at the front of a book signed at Wading River, Long Island, in 1921, states his theme in advance.

Lippmann argues that people act on pictures in their heads, built from news, habit, and feeling, rather than on the world itself. He examines how those pictures form, how they are steered, and what they mean for democracy. Readers get a founding work of media study, still quoted wherever news and power are discussed together.
pulpit-and-press-6th-edition:
Mary Baker Eddy issued a sixth edition of her volume of sermon and press pieces in 1897, again presenting herself as discoverer and founder of Christian Science. The contents show the book's two halves plainly: her own pulpit words and the newspapers' answers.

First come the dedicatory sermon, an account of her textbook, and hymns for laying a corner stone. Then a long run of clippings follows from papers in Chicago, Boston, New York, Washington, Kansas City, Montreal, Baltimore, Toronto, and smaller towns. Readers can watch a new church being praised, doubted, and debated across North America.
pygmalion:
Pygmalion is a play by Bernard Shaw, dated 1912, preceded by a long preface headed "A Professor of Phonetics." Shaw warns that the play needs not a preface but a sequel, which he supplies in its due place, and then turns on the English and their speech.

The English, he argues, have no respect for their own tongue. They spell it so badly that no one can learn its sounds from the page. They judge each other the moment a mouth opens. His hero is a phonetics expert, in a line that runs from Melville Bell and Alexander J. Ellis to Henry Sweet, the best of them all, whose scorn for Oxford kept him from fame.
q-e-d-or-new-light-on-the-doctrine-of-cr:
Q.E.D., or New Light on the Doctrine of Creation, is by George McCready Price. Price taught chemistry and physics at Lodi Academy in California. The book was published in 1917. It is dedicated to the scholar William Cleaver Wilkinson. Price argues from science back to Genesis, as his Browning motto puts it, to set the reader square with the Bible again.

Eight chapters move from the origin of matter and of energy to the rule that life comes only from life. The cell, the meaning of species, and Mendel's laws on heredity follow, then geology and its lessons, and a closing chapter on creation and the Creator.
quotes-and-images-from-chesterfield-s-le:
Quotes and Images from Chesterfield's Letters to His Son draws short extracts from the Earl of Chesterfield's famous letters of advice, headed with the years 1766 and 1771. The extracts run in alphabetical order, one crisp maxim after another, giving the letters in miniature.

Early entries warn that a little learning is a dangerous thing. A joker is near akin to a buffoon, they say. A favor may make an enemy. An injury may make a friend. Chesterfield urges absolute command of the temper, warns against speaking of oneself, and notes that advice is seldom welcome, a creed of polish and self-command throughout.
rabbi-saunderson: Rabbi Saunderson, by Ian Maclaren, published in London by Hodder and Stoughton in 1898 with twelve illustrations by A. S. Boyd, is shown here by its front matter and contents. The book is dedicated to Mrs. Williamson of Glenogil, praised for a gift of witty speech. Six pieces are listed: A Supra-Lapsarian, Kilbogie Manse, The Rabbi as Confessor, The Fear of God, The Wounds of a Friend, and Light at Eventide.
ralph-waldo-emerson: Ralph Waldo Emerson, by Oliver Wendell Holmes, belongs to the American Men of Letters series. Charles Dudley Warner edited that series. The title page is dated 1891. Holmes's note of thanks is signed at Boston on November 25, 1884. The note thanks Emerson's family. They lent letters and gave information. The pages shown give the contents in summary form. Emerson is settled as colleague of the Reverend Henry Ware. He is married to Ellen Louisa Tucker. Her death follows. His difference with parishioners comes next. His resignation of the pastorate closes the summary.
reminiscences-of-tolstoy-by-his-son:
Count Ilya Tolstoy recalled his father in this memoir, translated by George Calderon. Part one opens not with Ilya's own words but with a letter from Tolstoy to his great-aunt, Alexandra Andreyevna Tolstoy. In it the novelist describes each of his children in turn, with a father's sharp eye.

Sergei, the eldest, is gentle and patient, and moves his father to tears when he cries. Ilya himself, the third child, is hot-tempered, tender-hearted, and fond of eating and lying still. Tanya at eight delights in looking after children, while baby Masha, with her deep, serious eyes, is called one of life's riddles.
reno-a-book-of-short-stories-and-informa:
Lilyan Stratton, also named Lilyan Stratton Corbin, published this book of short stories and information about Reno in 1921. It opens by quoting the Holy Bible, from Deuteronomy chapter twenty-four, on a man who writes his wife a bill of divorcement and sends her from his house. Scenic views by the Van-Noy Interstate Company of San Francisco picture the place.

Stratton dedicates the book to all good husbands, and to her own in particular. Her chapter list divides the matter in two: Part 1, Social and Industrial Life, and Part 2, Reno Tragedies. Tales and facts together treat the Nevada city famed for quick divorce.
rest-harrow-a-comedy-of-resolution:
Maurice Hewlett named this novel for a plant, quoting Weathers at the front: rest harrow grows in any soil, and it is a British plant. Frank Craig drew the pictures, though they are not available in this edition. The story is billed as a comedy of resolution, in five books.

Book one serves as prologue, dealing with a bruised philosopher in retirement. Book two brings Sanchia to Wanless Hall, and book four takes her to London. The recluse philosopher returns in an interlude between them. A fifth book, of the nature of an epilogue, deals with Despoina and closes the tale.
retrospection-and-introspection:
Mary Baker Eddy, author of Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures, looks back on her own life in this book. Copyright of 1891 and 1892 stands on the title page, renewed in 1919 and 1920. The trustees under her will published it at Boston as authorized literature of the First Church of Christ, Scientist.

Contents open with Ancestral Shadows and a set of autobiographic reminiscences. Voices Not Our Own and Early Studies follow, then a girlhood composition kept from her youth. A theological reminiscence closes the list shown. Eddy mixes family history, early writing, and the growth of her faith in one short volume.
return-loads-bureaus-to-save-waste-in-tr:
Bulletin number one of the Highways Transport Committee, dated April 2, 1918, tells how return-loads bureaus could save waste in transportation. The committee worked under the Council of National Defense at Washington, and the Government Printing Office printed the bulletin. A Council resolution at the front approves the widest use of the motor truck.

The plan would relieve railroads choked by delays and embargoes during the war. State councils, chambers of commerce, war boards, and motor clubs were building a system already working in Connecticut. Trucks that haul freight out often return empty, the bulletin notes. Matching them with return loads would shift short hauls from rail to road.
revelations-of-a-wife-the-story-of-a-hon:
Adele Garrison tells the story of a honeymoon in this novel, under copyrights of 1915, 1916, and 1917. A picture caption shows a man pleading, Look at me, Margaret. The first chapter vows, I will be happy, three times over, setting the bride's resolve at the start.

The second chapter brings the first quarrel, and the marriage is tested from there. Lillian Gale, known to fame, and a girl on a train cross the couple's path. Chapters promise a friendly warning, a tragedy averted, and a quarrel and a crisis. Lost and found, and the words But I love you, mark the later turns of Garrison's tale.
robert-louis-stevenson:
Walter Raleigh, professor of English literature at Oxford, wrote this essay on Robert Louis Stevenson, most of it given as a lecture at the Royal Institution on May 17, 1895. Edward Arnold of London issued the fourth impression in 1906. Raleigh opens by refusing the question a nervous age asks when a popular writer dies: will he live?

No question is idler, he argues, for time buries fathers in short memories. Yet Stevenson's fame is made of good stuff, spreading from the few to the many as lasting fame does. His essays and travel books were treasured by a small company long before Treasure Island and Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde felled the British public.
roderick-hudson:
Henry James's novel Roderick Hudson is laid out in thirteen chapters of contents, from Rowland and Roderick to Rome and Switzerland. Names mark the people and places: Christina, Frascati, St. Cecilia's, Mary Garland, the Cavaliere, Mrs. Hudson, and the Princess Casamassima. Chapter one belongs to Rowland Mallet.

Mallet has arranged to sail for Europe on the first of September and spends his spare fortnight with his cousin Cecilia, a widow at Northampton, Massachusetts. Her three misfortunes, he counts, are a dead husband, lost money, and Northampton itself. Yet she is clever and has made a charming home, and Mallet, rich and idle with a tender conscience, cannot decide how to help her gracefully.
round-the-moon: Jules Verne wrote Round the Moon, headed with the year 1870. A table of contents lists a first chapter serving as a preface to the second part, then chapters timed from twenty minutes past ten to forty-seven minutes past ten. Later chapter titles include The First Half-Hour, Their Place of Shelter, A Little Algebra, The Cold of Space, and Question and Answer. The contents page is broken by long dotted leaders, and several chapter titles run on past the portion given here.
sagard-dictionaire-huron:
Sagard's Dictionary of the Huron Language came out in French in 1632. The Recollect friar built the wordbook as a tool for mission work. It stands as the first dictionary of Huron ever put in print.

Words and phrases pair Huron speech with French sense and use. A friar learning to preach, trade, or greet hosts could start here. No Iroquoian tongue had been fixed in print in this way before. The tool outlived its task and became a monument of record. It preserves Huron speech at the very moment of first contact in North America. Later scholars still mine its pages for lost words.
sailors-knots-entire-collection: W. W. Jacobs wrote Sailors' Knots, dated 1909. The contents list twelve tales: Deserted, Homeward Bound, Self-Help, Sentence Deferred, Matrimonial Openings, and Odd Man Out. The second half lists The Toll-House, Peter's Pence, The Head of the Family, Prize Money, Double Dealing, and Keeping Up Appearances. Picture captions run in the tales' own dialect. One notes a man who took a fancy to Rupert from the first. Another shows a man dashing a vase to pieces on the fender.
sallust-catiline-jugurtha-watson:
Sallust, a Roman historian of the late republic, wrote two short monographs on corruption and war. John Selby Watson translated the Conspiracy of Catiline and the Jugurthine War. Both works date from the years after Caesar's assassination.

Catiline's plot to seize Rome in 63 BCE gives Sallust his first subject. The Jugurthine War then follows Rome's long, bribery-tainted fight in Numidia. Sallust blames wealth and luxury for rotting the republic's old virtues. His sentences are short, sharp, and deliberately old-fashioned in flavor. Roman schools read him for style as much as history. The sting of his moral judgments has not faded.
samantha-at-the-st-louis-exposition:
Josiah Allen's Wife, Marietta Holley, wrote Samantha at the St. Louis Exposition, with pictures by Ch. Grunwald, dated 1904. A list of pictures gives captions in Samantha's own speech, One caption shows a man showing as much as fifteen dollars in cash in a careless way. Another shows the big crowd surging through the Pike to and fro. Chapter I opens with Samantha watching her husband. For some time, she says, she had noticed that Josiah Allen had acted queer. He would seem lost in thought now and then, and would rouse himself up and try to act natural.

Again and again Josiah would drag his old tin chest out from under the back stairway and pore over musty old deeds and papers, drawn up by his great-grandfather maybe.
samantha-on-the-woman-question:
Marietta Holley, Josiah Allen's Wife, wrote Samantha on the Woman Question, and is named as author of Samantha at Saratoga, My Opinions, and Betsey Bobbet's. The contents list ten chapters with quoted titles, opening with She Wanted Her Rights, They Can't Blame Her, and Polly's Eyes Growed Tender. Later chapters include Strivin' with the Emissary, Concerning Moth-Millers and Minny Fish, No Hamperin' Hitchin' Straps, The Women's Parade, and The Creation Searchin' Society. Pictures include Serepta wanting her rights, a visit to the Capitol, and Josiah asking whether a creature knows enough to vote.

Chapter I, She Wanted Her Rights, opens with an invitation. Lorinda Cagwin invited Josiah and Samantha to a reunion of the Allen family at her home near Washington, D.C. Washington is named as the birthplace of the first Allen they knew anything about.
samuel-johnson:
Leslie Stephen wrote Samuel Johnson, a short life of the great critic published at New York in 1878. Six chapters carry Johnson from boyhood through his rise as a writer, his circle of friends, and his years as a leading voice in letters. The book closes with his final years and a look at his writings.

Chapter one opens in Lichfield, where Johnson was born in 1709 to Michael Johnson, a bookseller. The elder Johnson sold books at market stalls in nearby towns, among them Birmingham, which then had no bookseller of its own. Respected by the cathedral clergy, he served as town magistrate and as county sheriff in his son's birth year. Stephen also notes his strong church and Tory leanings.
sappho-fragments-wharton:
Sappho sang on the island of Lesbos around 600 BCE, antiquity's most famous woman poet. Henry Thornton Wharton edited her surviving fragments with a memoir and selected renderings. Almost all her work is lost; what remains survives as quotations and scraps.

Wharton prints the Greek fragments with translations and accounts of her ancient fame. The poems speak of love, desire, jealousy, and the gods with startling directness. One nearly complete ode to Aphrodite anchors the small body of verse. Later papyrus finds added a few more pieces after Wharton's time. His edition still conveys her tantalizing mixture of genius and loss.
scaramouche-a-romance-of-the-french-revo: Rafael Sabatini wrote Scaramouche, a romance of the French Revolution, and the contents divide the novel into three books. Book I runs from The Republican and The Aristocrat through The Eloquence of M. de Vilmorin, The Heritage, The Lord of Gavrillac, The Windmill, and The Aftermath. Book II turns to the stage, with The Trespassers, The Service of Thespis, and The Comic Muse. It runs on through Exit Monsieur Parvissimus, Enter Scaramouche, and The Conquest of Nantes. It closes with Contrition and The Fracas at the Theatre Feydau.
selections-from-wordsworth-and-tennyson:
Pelham Edgar, professor of English at Victoria College in Toronto, edited this joint choice of Wordsworth and Tennyson, issued there in 1917. Edgar adds an opening essay and notes. Wordsworth leads with Michael, songs to the daisy and the cuckoo, and stern London sonnets.

Tennyson follows with Oenone, Morte d'Arthur, The Brook, and parts of In Memoriam. The pairing lets students set the older poet of nature beside the Victorian laureate of doubt and grief. Sonnets on London in 1802 sit near elegiac stanzas, so a class can trace how English verse changed across the nineteenth century.
ship-s-company-the-entire-collection:
W. W. Jacobs gathered twelve tales in this full Ship's Company set, opening with Fine Feathers. Other titles include Friends in Need, Fairy Gold, Watch-Dogs, and The Guardian Angel. Dock folk, sailors, and night-watchmen fill the pages in Jacobs's dry comic manner.

Fine Feathers opens on Mr. Jobson waking on a Bank Holiday to a theft: his trousers and red braces have vanished from their brass knob. In their place stand a tailcoat, white waistcoat, and tall silk hat that make him shudder. Jacobs builds small masterpieces of plot from such swaps, wishes, and schemes among working folk.
sir-thomas-browne-and-his-religio-medici:
Alexander Whyte delivered this appreciation of Sir Thomas Browne as the opening discourse of the British Medical Association at St. Giles' Cathedral on July 26, 1898. Oliphant Anderson issued it that year in Edinburgh and London. Whyte dedicated the piece to Sir Thomas Grainger Stewart, the association's president, at whose request he spoke.

Whyte calls the Religio Medici a known English classic, with Urn-Burial and Christian Morals worthy beside it. Chosen passages from the physician's writings follow the praise. Browne, a doctor of high standing and a famed antiquarian, speaks here in his own stately English on faith, death, and charity.
sketches-of-the-natural-history-of-ceylo:
Sir J. Emerson Tennent wrote Sketches of the Natural History of Ceylon, dated 1861, with drawings made from life. The book gives tales and short stories that show the habits of mammals, birds, reptiles, fishes, and insects on the island. One long part deals with the elephant alone, and with the ways men catch and train it.

In his opening note, Tennent says the text first formed the animal part of his larger work on Ceylon, printed in 1859. Space there forced him to cut tales and facts that showed how the animals live. Here he prints them in full, so readers get the detail that the larger work had to leave out.
sologub-the-little-demon:
Schoolteacher Peredonov's spite curdles into paranoia and madness in Fyodor Sologub's novel The Little Demon, presented here in English. A stifling provincial town supplies the chorus of gossips, officials, and schoolboys around his decline. The little demon of petty evil, a gray shifting creature of his delusions, haunts the margins of every chapter.

Grotesque, hilarious, and terrifying in turns, the novel anatomizes vulgarity until it becomes metaphysical. Peredonov schemes for a promotion, torments his pupils, and suspects plots in every teacup. Sologub, a school inspector himself, knew the world he damned. The book stands as one of the great novels of Russian symbolism. Its laughter leaves a chill that pure tragedy rarely achieves.
some-rambling-notes-of-an-idle-excursion:
Mark Twain calls his trip in Some Rambling Notes of an Idle Excursion a new thing. All his past trips had been for work. This one was for pure fun. A reverend agreed to go with him. Twain calls him a good man, though a clergyman. By eleven at night they reached New Haven. They boarded the New York boat there.

The night was too fine for bed. Twain stood at his window and heard two old men talk. The brothers came from a small Connecticut village. They were settling a grave plot. The old burying-ground had grown too full for their folk. Seth's wife could scarce be tucked in last year. Her grave lay over Deacon Shorb's lot. Plot eight cost thirteen dollars, and plot nine cost fourteen. William took plot nine all the same. The deacon's wish for it swayed him.
songs-of-action: A. Conan Doyle, author of Micah Clarke, The White Company, Rodney Stone, and Uncle Bernac, wrote Songs of Action. John Murray of London printed the seventh impression in 1916. The contents lead with The Song of the Bow, Cremona, and The Storming Party, then The Frontier Line and Corporal Dick's Promotion. A Forgotten Tale, Pennarby Mine, A Rover Chanty, A Ballad of the Ranks, and A Lay of the Links come in the first half of the list.
species-and-varieties-their-origin-by-mu: Hugo De Vries, who held the chair of botany at the University of Amsterdam, gave the talks in Species and Varieties: Their Origin by Mutation at the University of California. Daniel Trembly MacDougal edited the set. The second edition, corrected and revised, came out at Chicago from the Open Court Publishing Company in 1906, under a 1904 copyright. Three motto lines head the book: Lamarck calls the origin of species a thing of nature, Darwin an object of inquiry, and De Vries an object of trial by test.
square-deal-sanderson: Charles Alden Seltzer, author of The Boss of the Lazy Y and Drag Harlan, wrote Square Deal Sanderson, with a front picture by J. Allen St. John. Grosset and Dunlap printed the New York book in March 1922. The contents open on the North Trail, then A Man's Curiosity, and the naming of Square Deal Sanderson. Later heads speak of water and kisses, lies, plotters, plain talk, an ultimatum, and a plot that worked.
stand-by-the-union: Oliver Optic wrote Stand by the Union in The Blue and the Gray Series. Lee and Shepard of Boston published the set. The opening pages list its volumes afloat and on land. Each volume cost a dollar fifty. Taken by the Enemy stands in the sea group. Within the Enemy's Lines and On the Blockade join it. Fighting for the Right and A Victorious Union close that group. Brother Against Brother stands in the land group. In the Saddle and A Lieutenant at Eighteen join it there.
star-surgeon: Alan E. Nourse wrote Star Surgeon, printed at New York by David McKay Company under copyrights of 1959 and 1960, with a sixth printing in April 1973. Part of the book first came out in Amazing Science Fiction Stories. The contents open with The Intruder, Hospital Seattle, and The Inquisition. The Galactic Pill Peddlers, Crisis on Morua VIII, Tiger Makes a Promise, Plague, and Dal Breaks a Promise stand in the later list.
stories-from-le-morte-d-arthur-and-the-m:
Beatrice Clay retold Stories from Le Morte d'Arthur and the Mabinogion for The King's Treasuries of Literature, a series under the general editorship of Sir A. T. Quiller-Couch. The book was first issued in 1920 and reprinted in 1922 and 1924, with London and Toronto printing by J. M. Dent and Sons.

Book I, The Coming of Arthur, tells of Arthur's birth and how he became king, the founding of the Round Table, and the finding of Excalibur from the Lady of the Lake. It goes on to Queen Morgan le Fay's treachery, the loss of the sword's scabbard, Merlin, and the brothers Balin and Balan, drawing Welsh tales in beside Malory's.
strictly-business-more-stories-of-the-fo:
O. Henry's Strictly Business, subtitled More Stories of the Four Million, collects twenty-three short tales of New York life. The contents range from the title story through The Gold That Glittered, Babes in the Jungle, The Poet and the Peasant, and A Municipal Report, to The Duel and What You Want.

The title story opens with the narrator mocking what readers think they know about stage people: leading ladies, chorus girls, and shows walking back to New York on railroad ties. O. Henry's city is full of shopgirls, clerks, actors, and grafters, and his endings turn on small ironies. The set keeps the warm, slangy voice of his earlier Four Million tales.
studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-volume-:
Volume II of Havelock Ellis's Studies in the Psychology of Sex, Sexual Inversion, appears here in a 1927 printing, with a preface to the third edition. Ellis notes that the problem of homosexuality came down from the Middle Ages, which treated inverts as it treated heretics and witches for five hundred years.

Fourteen years had passed since the last edition. In that time, Ellis says, work in the field had grown hugely. Nearly every page needed rewriting. The index of authors had more than doubled. Sixteen new case histories had been added, chosen as varied and typical. He dropped shorter, less instructive histories to make room. The volume argues for study and humane understanding over persecution.
success-second-edition:
Lord Beaverbrook's Success, first published in November 1921 and reprinted the same month, collects weekly articles he wrote for the Sunday Express. A publishers' note tells the book's start. The pieces drew many requests for copies. So they were gathered into a volume. The note calls the book a sure will-tonic. It promises strength to the reader who digests its precepts.

The contents run from Success itself through Happiness and its three secrets, Luck, Moderation, Money, Education, Arrogance, Courage, Panic, and Depression. Beaverbrook was a newspaper owner. He had risen from Canada to British public life. He writes short, blunt chapters here. They treat the habits and nerve that carry a man upward. They also treat the moods that drag him down.
suetonius-twelve-caesars-thomson:
Suetonius, a Roman court official, wrote biographies of Rome's first twelve rulers around 120 CE. Alexander Thomson translated the Lives of the Twelve Caesars into English. The series runs from Julius Caesar through Domitian.

Suetonius organizes each life by topic rather than strict chronology. Battles, laws, love affairs, omens, and deaths all receive their sections. He repeats gossip alongside documented fact, often without judging between them. The result is scandalous, vivid, and endlessly mined by historians. Readers learn how emperors ate, dressed, joked, and died. Thomson's lively English keeps the imperial rumor mill turning.
tartarin-de-tarascon:
Alphonse Daudet wrote Tartarin de Tarascon in 1872, here rendered by Oliver C. Colt, whose opening pages set out the hero and his world. Tartarin is a man of the Midi in the south of France, the region where Daudet himself was born.

Colt paints Tartarin as a boastful braggart, easily fooled, yet good at heart when all is said. The tale sends this would-be lion hunter toward Algeria, then a French prize held by force of arms. Big game hunts still won praise in that age, and sea trips still ran by sail. Readers get a kind satire of tall tales and false glory, told with warmth for its fool of a hero.
tartarin-of-tarascon:
Alphonse Daudet's Tartarin of Tarascon opens with a visit to its hero's home, in a separate English rendering from the Colt version. The narrator recalls his first call on Tartarin, ten or twelve years past, as a date he will never forget.

Tartarin lived on the Avignon road, in a small white villa with green shutters and shoe-black boys at the door. Inside, the house turns heroic from cellar to garret. His garden holds no French tree at all, but gums, palms, cacti, and a small baobab, as if central Africa sat in Provence. Readers meet a dreamer whose wild gear and tales far outrun his deeds, drawn with fond mockery.
teachings-silvanus-mattison:
Wise counsel in the voice of a teacher fills a short book from the Nag Hammadi codices. The Teachings of Silvanus, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives that wisdom text in English. Its author writes as Silvanus, a name tied to a companion of Paul.

The lessons urge the reader to know himself, flee folly, and guard the mind as a city gate. Christ is praised as teacher and guide in words that mix Bible and Greek thought. Few Nag Hammadi texts speak so plainly to daily life. Mattison's clear version suits the book's own plain aim.
teddy-s-button:
Amy Le Feuvre, author of Probable Sons and Eric's Good News, published Teddy's Button in 1896, a tale for young readers built around a soldier's brass button. Chapter one is called An Antagonist.

Teddy stands bare-headed in hot sun at the heart of a ring of village boys, one hand on the great brass button at his chest. He tells how his father charged to save the regimental colors, cutting through foes as shells flew and swords flashed. His blue eyes spark and his small frame shakes with zeal as the boys hang on each word. Readers get a tale of pride, faith, and a boy who must learn what true courage asks.
tell-england-a-study-in-a-generation:
Ernest Raymond published Tell England, subtitled A Study in a Generation, in New York with George H. Doran Company in 1922. A prologue by Padre Monty leads into Book One, Five Gay Years of School, where Rupert Ray begins his own story.

Verses set before the tale vow that a full, keen life lived in death's face cannot be robbed by death itself. School chapters show boys at games, prefects, and small wars before the great war comes. Readers follow a schoolboy age group into the First World War, in a novel long read as a voice for the young men lost in that fight.
tennyson: G. K. Chesterton and Dr. Richard Garnett wrote Tennyson as a life sketch. James Pott and Company printed it in New York. Hodder and Stoughton printed it in London. Many plates fill the book. A photo of Alfred Tennyson by the London Stereoscopic Company stands at the front. Headings promise two main parts. One treats Tennyson as a force in thought. One gives a plain note on his life.
the-admirable-crichton:
J. M. Barrie wrote The Admirable Crichton as a comedy play, drawn from his plays in this printing, with act one set at Loam House, Mayfair. Stage notes in prose form tell as much of the tale as the talk does.

The play opens as the Hon. Ernest Woolley rolls up to the door, glad and sleek, with a smile that shows he is thinking of himself. Barrie's notes paint him as a man about town who is too busy over nothing to think of others. He left Cambridge of late and shines in restaurants and drawing rooms. Readers then meet Lord Loam's house, its butler Crichton, and the shipwreck that will flip rank on its head.
the-age-of-the-reformation: Preserved Smith wrote The Age of the Reformation, printed in New York by Henry Holt and Company for the American Historical Series, a set shaped by Charles H. Haskins of Harvard University. Front notes explain the copy's marks: section signs spelled out, notes moved to section ends, margin notes set in square brackets, and a small d. set in place of a death-date dagger.
the-americanism-of-washington:
Henry van Dyke's 1906 essay takes up a hard task: saying anything new about Washington, or rather unsaying old things that were never strictly true. He traces how the hero's image has passed through three hazy mediums, each one tinting his shape and color.

First came myth, with Washington as a new Saint George among ever-blooming cherry trees. Next came clouds of oratory, lifting him like a sphinx on a far peak. Last came cool criticism, which found only a decent English country gentleman, honest, brave, shrewd, slow, and above all very lucky. Van Dyke sets out to clear these vapors away.
the-art-of-interior-decoration:
A plate-by-plate study of fine rooms opens with Plate I, a composed interior praised for balance, repose, and grace. The writer pictures a tea tray brought in and two chairs drawn together so a lady and a friend may chat over their cups. No author is named on the pages shown.

Every piece in the room is placed by origin: an Italian Louis XVI mirror, French sconces, table, and chairs, and Italian vases of great worth. The vases, it turns out, are old medicine jars once used by Italian chemists for their drugs. Grey walls, green and grey curtains of antique taffeta, and green silk chair seats set the color scheme, lit through deep cream parchment shades.
the-awakening-the-resurrection:
Count Leo Tolstoi's novel appeared in New York in 1900 in a translation by William E. Smith, from Street and Smith. Tolstoi is named for War and Peace, Anna Karenina, and The Kreutzer Sonata. Scripture passages about forgiving a brother many times open the book.

Other verses warn against judging a brother's fault while missing one's own, and against casting the first stone. Those texts frame a story of sin, blame, and the wish to make amends. Even before the narrative starts, the epigraphs tell readers that mercy, not harsh judgment, is the measure the characters will be judged by.
the-babylonian-legends-of-the-creation:
Clay tablets from Nineveh tell how Babylonians and Assyrians viewed the making of the world and a fight between Bel and the dragon. The account of their finding names A. H. Layard, Hormuzd Rassam, and George Smith of the British Museum. Tablets came from the palace and library of Ashur-bani-pal, who ruled from 668 to 626 B.C.

Between 1848 and 1876 some twenty thousand fragments were worked through. Smith picked out flood legends and pieces of a creation series, though at first their order was unclear. In 1875 he summed up about twenty fragments, and in 1876 he printed translations in a book on the Chaldean account of Genesis.
the-balkan-wars-1912-1913-third-edition:
Jacob Gould Schurman issued a third edition in 1916 of his account of the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913. A postscript dated September 1, 1916, notes that Romania had joined the Allies and declared war on Austria-Hungary. Schurman also discusses Greece, split between King Constantine and Venizelos.

He quotes his own forecast from November 1914, guessing that Greece, Montenegro, Serbia, and Romania would stand with the Allies. Bulgaria, he thought, would stay neutral unless carried away by Austro-German wins. A map shows the Balkan Peninsula before the wars. The new edition thus links a recent war to the larger war then spreading.
the-bars-of-iron:
Ethel M. Dell published her novel in 1916 and dedicated it to her brother Reginald. Two Bible lines stand at the front, one about breaking bars of iron from a psalm and one about heaven opened from Revelation. A prologue and a first part called The Gates of Brass follow.

Chapter headings in part one include a jug of water, discipline, a mother's help, and life on a chain. A race, a friend in need, and a talk by the fire lead to a ticket of leave. Gloves, a star of hope, and a vision close the list, hinting at prison, release, and change.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-02-exodus-th:
Exodus, in Douay-Rheims wording, Englished from the Latin Vulgate and revised under Bishop Richard Challoner, 1749 to 1752. Rheims printed the New Testament in 1582; Douay printed the Old Testament in 1609 and 1610. An introduction notes that its events span about 145 years, from the death of Joseph to the setting up of the tabernacle.

Chapter one names the sons of Jacob who went into Egypt with their households, starting with Ruben, Simeon, Levi, and Juda. A heading says the Israelites multiplied there, then were oppressed by a new king. That king ordered their male children to be killed. Growth under hardship, and a ruler who fears it, set the stage for Moses and deliverance.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-06-josue-the:
Josue, in the English Douay-Rheims translation, based on the Latin Vulgate in the form Bishop Richard Challoner revised in 1749 to 1752. Douay issued the Old Testament in 1609 and 1610, Rheims the New Testament in 1582. An introduction draws meaning from his name, changed from Osee, as noted in Numbers chapter thirteen. Moses by his law, it says, could only bring the people within sight of their promised inheritance.

Chapter one shows Josue encouraged by the Lord and warning the people to prepare to cross the Jordan. Leadership passes from Moses to a successor whose task is entry, not wandering. The introduction links his name, rendered also as Jesus, to a fuller bringing-in still to come. Readers meet a commander, a river, and a promise at the start.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-07-judges-th:
Judges, in Douay-Rheims form, drawn from the Latin Vulgate and carried through Bishop Richard Challoner's revision, dated 1749 to 1752. An Old Testament printed at Douay in 1609 and 1610 and a New Testament printed at Rheims in 1582 lie behind the text. Chapter one opens after the death of Josue, when the children of Israel ask the Lord who should go up first against the Chanaanite.

The answer names Juda as leader, with a promise that the land is delivered into his hands. A heading notes fighting by Juda against the Chanaanites, who were tolerated in many places. That mixed outcome shapes the book: no single king, partial victories, and tribes left beside enemies. The opening question, who shall lead, has no lasting human answer in the pages that follow.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-08-ruth-the-:
Ruth, in a Douay-Rheims text based on the Latin Vulgate, as Bishop Richard Challoner revised that translation in the years 1749 to 1752. Printing history runs from Rheims for the New Testament in 1582 to Douay for the Old Testament in 1609 and 1610. An introduction calls Ruth a figure of the Gentile church and reports a view that the prophet Samuel wrote the book.

Chapter one is set in the days when judges ruled, during a famine. Elimelech of Bethlehem goes with his wife Noemi and two sons into Moab, where he dies. The sons marry Moabite wives and die without children. Noemi then returns home, and her daughter-in-law Ruth refuses to part from her. Loyalty across peoples, shown in a widow's choice, carries this short book.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-17-tobias-th:
Tobias, in Douay-Rheims English, translated out of the Latin Vulgate and later revised by Bishop Richard Challoner (1749-1752). The Old Testament first came from Douay, in 1609 and 1610; the New Testament from Rheims, in 1582. A closing summary in the introduction says the elder Tobias exhorted his son and grandsons to piety near death. He foretold the destruction of Ninive and the rebuilding of Jerusalem.

Chapter one praises Tobias's early piety and his works of mercy, especially burying the dead. He is placed in the tribe and city of Nephtali, in upper Galilee. Charity under exile defines the man before any journey or angel appears. Readers meet a righteous Israelite whose daily kindness, not rank, gives the book its centre.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-18-judith-th:
Judith, in the English Douay-Rheims translation, based on the Latin Vulgate in the form Bishop Richard Challoner revised in 1749 to 1752. Douay issued the Old Testament in 1609 and 1610, Rheims the New Testament in 1582. An introduction ends by noting a siege by Holofernes and his great army, and Judith's canticle of thanksgiving to God.

Chapter one begins earlier, with Nabuchodonosor, king of the Assyrians, defeating Arphaxad, king of the Medes. Arphaxad had brought many nations under his rule and built a strong city called Ecbatana. Empires clash before Judith herself appears. That slow build lets a later act by one widow stand against armies, kings, and walled cities already shown in force.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-19-esther-th:
Esther, in Douay-Rheims form, drawn from the Latin Vulgate and carried through Bishop Richard Challoner's revision, dated 1749 to 1752. An Old Testament printed at Douay in 1609 and 1610 and a New Testament printed at Rheims in 1582 lie behind the text. Chapter one places a king ruling from India to Ethiopia over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces.

When he sat on the throne of his kingdom, the city of Susan was its capital. Display, feasting, and royal power fill the wider chapter behind that verse. A vast empire ruled from one court sets the scale for a story in which a Jewish queen's access to that court will matter. The opening gives place and reach before any danger to her people appears.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-20-job-the-c:
Job, in a Douay-Rheims text based on the Latin Vulgate, as Bishop Richard Challoner revised that translation in the years 1749 to 1752. Printing history runs from Rheims for the New Testament in 1582 to Douay for the Old Testament in 1609 and 1610. Chapter one says there was a man in the land of Hus named Job, simple and upright, fearing God and avoiding evil. Notes explain Hus as part of Edom and simple as innocent and without guile.

Seven sons and three daughters were born to him, the next verse adds. Wealth and family stand beside his goodness at the start, so later loss can be measured. Annotations in this edition pause on single words, guiding Catholic readers through terms. Suffering, debate, and patience will test the upright man described here.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-21-psalms-th:
Psalms, in Douay-Rheims wording taken from the Latin Vulgate, with Bishop Richard Challoner's revisions of 1749 to 1752 applied. The New Testament portion traces to Rheims, 1582; the Old Testament portion to Douay, 1609 and 1610. Psalm one sets a blessed man against sinners. He avoids ungodly counsel, does not linger on their path, and does not sit with those who mock.

His will, the next verse says, is in the law of the Lord, and on that law he meditates. Two ways of life are set side by side at the very start of a songbook. Readers who continue meet praise, lament, and prayer, but the first psalm frames them all as a choice of path.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-25-wisdom-th:
Wisdom, in Douay-Rheims translation, worked from the Latin Vulgate and later put through Bishop Richard Challoner's hands in 1749 to 1752. The older printings were a Douay Old Testament (1609, 1610) and a Rheims New Testament (1582). An introduction divides it into three parts and notes many prophecies of Christ's coming, passion, and resurrection.

In the first six chapters, superiors are urged to love and practise justice and wisdom. The next three teach that wisdom comes only from God and is gained by prayer and a good life.
